chapters.chapterTitle: Ten Biblical Truths which make up the Christian Doctrine of the Trinity

elements.text:
“The Trinity is not maths badly done; it’s love, correctly counted.”
Anon.

“In no other subject is error more dangerous, or inquiry more laborious, or the discovery of truth more fruitful.”
Augustine.

elements.question: What do you think of these quotations? (Do you like them or not, and why?)
elements.answerPlaceholder: Write down your thoughts...

elements.text: Amina always felt like the Trinity was a locked room she wasn’t allowed into. Whenever she asked how God could be Father, Son, and Spirit – yet only one God – she was told, “It’s a mystery, don’t ask.” So she stopped asking. She believed in God, prayed to Jesus sometimes, and knew the Holy Spirit was mentioned in church, but in her mind they felt like three separate, slightly disconnected ideas rather than the one true, living God she was meant to know and love. It was only years later, working slowly through the Scriptures verse by verse, that the pieces began to fit together – and what had felt like an abstract puzzle became the very shape of the God who saves her.

The Trinity is not a strange piece of maths, invented to make faith harder. It is simply what happens when you take the Bible’s own testimony about God seriously.

This study walks through ten biblical truths that, together, make up the historic Christian doctrine of the Trinity; Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, three persons, one God.

elements.question: What has been your own experience? Does thinking about the Trinity feel confusing, comforting, distant, or something else?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Write down your thoughts...

elements.text: 1. There is only one God

The starting point for everything else in this study is this:
  • the God of the Bible is not one god among many, and He does not share His throne with rivals.
Israel’s daily confession – the Shema – was built on this truth, and the New Testament writers, steeped in that same conviction, never abandoned it. Whatever else we say about Father, Son, and Spirit, we must never end up suggesting there are three Gods. There is one.

elements.passageText: <sup>29</sup> Jesus answered, “The most important is: ‘ Listen, Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one .

elements.question: How does this verse show that there is only one God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus quotes the Shema as the foundation beneath the greatest commandment, affirming that Israel's God is one — not merely supreme among many gods, but singular. By stating this before giving any command to love, Jesus roots all obedience in God's identity as one. "The Lord is one" excludes the entire polytheistic framework Israel's neighbors lived by; it isn't that Yahweh outranks other gods, but that there is no category of rival deity for him to outrank. Whatever the New Testament later says about Father, Son, and Spirit has to be understood as further definition within this one God, not the multiplication of gods.
elements.questionHint: What is the 'most important' truth Jesus names before he even gives a command — and what would a people surrounded by many gods have understood 'the Lord is one' to rule out?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> Listen, Israel: The Lord is our God, the Lord is one!

elements.question: How does this verse show that there is only one God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This is the Shema, the daily confession that shaped Israel's identity among nations that worshiped many gods. "The Lord is our God" ties Yahweh to Israel by covenant, but "the Lord is one" goes further, asserting his singularity, not just his priority. It isn't "the Lord is our greatest god" but the flat claim that he is one — unified in his being, with no rival and no divine council of equals. Every truth this study explores about the Father, Son, and Spirit has to stand inside this declaration, since Scripture never abandons the conviction that at bottom there is exactly one God.
elements.questionHint: Moses commands Israel to 'listen' — what specific number does he use for the Lord, and what would that word have ruled out for a people living among nations that worshiped many gods?

elements.passageText:
5 I am the Lord, I have no peer, there is no God but me. I arm you for battle, even though you do not recognize me.
6 I do this so people will recognize from east to west that there is no God but me; I am the Lord, I have no peer.

elements.question: How does this verse show that there is only one God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Twice in two verses God says "there is no God but me," adding "I have no peer" — language that doesn't just rank him above other gods but denies that any other beings in that category exist at all. The purpose clause is telling: God arms Cyrus for battle specifically "so people will recognize from east to west" this fact, meaning his uniqueness is meant to become universally known, not just believed by Israel. This is stronger than claiming to be the best or highest; it's an exclusive, first-person claim, spoken by God about himself, to being the only reality that fits the category "God."
elements.questionHint: God says almost the identical phrase twice in these two verses — why repeat 'there is no God but me' instead of saying it once?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> For there is one God and one intermediary between God and humanity, Christ Jesus, himself human.”

elements.question: How does this verse show that there is only one God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul pairs "one God" with "one intermediary," and the parallel matters: just as there is exactly one mediator, there is exactly one deity being mediated to. The verse leaves no room for a second or third God alongside this one; instead it identifies Christ Jesus — fully human, as the text stresses — as the single bridge between humanity and the one God. What's striking is that the very verse insisting on God's oneness is also the verse building Christ into the picture as essential to reaching that one God, which is precisely the tension this study traces: strict monotheism that still makes room for what the church later called the Trinity.
elements.questionHint: Paul writes 'one God and one ___' in the same breath — what does pairing those two words together suggest about how seriously he takes the number 'one' here?

elements.question: Why does it matter that Christianity is not a form of polytheism (belief in many gods)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Write down your thoughts...

elements.text: 2. The Father is fully God

Maybe you feel like this truth needs no proof – of course the Father is God. But it sets the pattern for what follows: whatever divine status belongs to the Father belongs also to the Son and the Spirit too.

elements.passageText: <sup>27</sup> Do not work for the food that disappears, but for the food that remains to eternal life – the food which the Son of Man will give to you. For God the Father has put his seal of approval on him.”

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Father is fully God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The verse names him plainly as "God the Father," treating deity and fatherhood as the same referent without argument, as something obvious enough to state in passing. The seal of approval he places on the Son is itself an act only God could perform — authenticating the Son of Man's authority to give the food that leads to eternal life. That the Father is the one certifying eternal realities, not merely wishing them, shows him functioning here with the very authority and finality that belongs to God alone, backing his Son's mission with his own divine endorsement.
elements.questionHint: What title does Jesus use for the one who places 'his seal of approval' on the Son, and whose seal would actually be able to guarantee eternal life?

elements.passageText: <sup>25</sup> At that time Jesus said, “I praise you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and intelligent, and revealed them to little children.

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Father is fully God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus addresses the Father directly as "Lord of heaven and earth," a title claiming total sovereignty over all creation — the kind of language Scripture reserves for God alone. That Jesus himself, in prayer, ascribes this title to the Father shows it is not a courtesy but a recognition of who the Father actually is. The verse also credits the Father with sovereign control over revelation itself, hiding and revealing "these things" according to his own will, which is an exercise of divine prerogative rather than a delegated task. Jesus's own posture of praise confirms he regards the Father as fully, truly God.
elements.questionHint: What two-part title does Jesus give the Father — 'Lord of ___ and ___' — and what would controlling both of those things require someone to be?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> Now this is eternal life – that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom you sent.

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Father is fully God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus, praying to the Father, calls him "the only true God" without qualification — a direct designation of deity spoken by the Son himself. The eternal life described here consists of knowing the Father as this only true God alongside knowing Jesus Christ, which places the two in the closest possible relationship without collapsing them into each other. Far from diminishing the Father's deity by pairing him with the Son, the verse makes knowing the Father as the one true God the very substance of eternal life, the foundation the rest of the sentence is built on.
elements.questionHint: What exact phrase does Jesus use for his Father — 'the only ___ God' — and who is the one saying it, about whom?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> From Paul, an apostle (not from men, nor by human agency, but by Jesus Christ and God the Father who raised him from the dead)

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Father is fully God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul grounds his apostleship not in human appointment but "by Jesus Christ and God the Father," naming the Father outright as God and crediting him with the resurrection — an act of power only God can perform. Raising the dead is consistently, throughout Scripture, something God alone does; attributing it here to the Father identifies him as the divine agent behind Christ's resurrection. The pairing of "Jesus Christ and God the Father" as the twin source of Paul's calling also shows the Father standing alongside the Son as a distinct, fully divine person, not a lesser figure operating behind him.
elements.questionHint: What specific act does Paul say the Father performed on Jesus, and what kind of power would raising someone from the dead actually require?

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> For people everywhere report how you welcomed us and how you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Father is fully God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The contrast the verse draws is total: idols versus "the living and true God." Idols are dead, false, powerless objects, while the God the Thessalonians turned to is described with the opposite qualities — alive and true in the fullest sense those words can carry. Though this half-verse doesn't use the word "Father" outright, this is the God the whole letter identifies as Father throughout, and "living and true God" is exactly the kind of exclusive, ultimate language Scripture reserves for God alone, never for any created being or lesser power that people might turn from idols toward instead.
elements.questionHint: What two adjectives describe this God in contrast to the 'idols' the Thessalonians turned away from, and what do those two words rule out?

elements.text: 3. The Son is fully God

If people don’t know the Bible well, they can feel that it’s more natural to think of Jesus as God’s greatest servant – someone very close to God, but a notch below Him. The verses below won’t allow that:
  • They directly call Jesus God
  • They apply Old Testament descriptions of God to Him
  • They place Him alongside the Father as an object of worship.

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was fully God.

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Son is fully God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John states it as plainly as language allows: "the Word was fully God." He has already distinguished the Word as being "with God" — a distinct person — and then immediately identifies that same Word as God in essence, not a lesser divine being or a god of some diminished rank. The sentence holds together both truths this whole study is built on: real distinction ("with God") and real identity ("was... God"). John opens his entire gospel on this note specifically so that everything Jesus does and says afterward is read in light of his full deity.
elements.questionHint: John says the Word was both 'with God' and 'was ___ God' in the same sentence — how can the Word be distinct from God and also be described that way at once?

elements.passageText: Thomas replied to him, “My Lord and my God!”

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Son is fully God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Thomas doesn't say "my teacher" or even "my Lord" alone — he adds "and my God," addressing Jesus directly with the very title reserved for Yahweh. This isn't a careless exclamation of surprise; John records it as Thomas's confession of faith upon seeing the risen Christ, and Jesus doesn't correct him or deflect the worship the way an angel or a mere prophet would. The moment functions as the climactic confession of John's entire Gospel, placed right before its stated purpose statement — Thomas recognizing in the risen Jesus nothing less than God himself standing in front of him.
elements.questionHint: Jesus doesn't correct or rebuke Thomas for calling him 'my God' — what does his silence in that moment tell you about whether the title was appropriate?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> To them belong the patriarchs, and from them, by human descent, came the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever! Amen.

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Son is fully God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul traces Christ's human descent through the patriarchs and then, without pausing, calls him "God over all, blessed forever" — human ancestry and full deity affirmed in the same breath. "Over all" leaves no exceptions; this is not a regional or subordinate deity but one with universal, supreme authority, described in the doxological language ("blessed forever, amen") Paul elsewhere reserves for God the Father. The verse is one of the most direct statements in Paul's letters that the Messiah who descended from Israel's ancestors is, at the very same time, God over everything that exists.
elements.questionHint: Paul mentions Christ's human ancestry and then immediately calls him what — and what does the phrase 'over all' leave outside its scope?

elements.passageText: ... <sup>13</sup> as we wait for the happy fulfillment of our hope in the glorious appearing of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ.

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Son is fully God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The Greek grammar here binds "God" and "Savior" together under one article, pointing to a single figure described both ways: "our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ." Paul isn't describing two separate appearings — one of God, one of the Savior — but the one appearing of Jesus Christ, whom he names outright as "great God." The word "great" intensifies rather than softens the claim, and Christians are told to wait expectantly for this appearing precisely because it will be the unveiling of their own God, in person, come to them visibly.
elements.questionHint: Paul writes 'our great God and Savior' and then gives one name — whose name follows, and how many separate appearings does the verse describe?

elements.passageText: ... <sup>8</sup> but of the Son he says, “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever, and a righteous scepter is the scepter of your kingdom.

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Son is fully God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The writer of Hebrews quotes the Father addressing the Son directly as "God" — "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever." This isn't the author's own commentary but a citation of the Father's own words to the Son, making it a striking case of one divine person addressing another with the title of deity. Combined with the eternal throne and the righteous scepter, the verse presents the Son not as an exalted creature or an angel — the very contrast Hebrews 1 is building throughout — but as the enthroned, eternal God ruling in righteousness forever.
elements.questionHint: Whose words does the writer of Hebrews quote in 'Your throne, O God,' and who exactly is being addressed by that title?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> From Simeon Peter, a slave and apostle of Jesus Christ, to those who through the righteousness of our God and Savior, Jesus Christ, have been granted a faith just as precious as ours.

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Son is fully God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Just as in Titus, Peter joins "our God and Savior" to the single name "Jesus Christ," treating the two descriptions as belonging to one person rather than two. Peter, a Jewish apostle steeped in strict monotheism, opens his letter with this exact phrase, showing how thoroughly the earliest church had come to identify the risen Jesus with God himself, not merely as God's specially favored representative. The faith believers have received is described as coming "through the righteousness of" this God and Savior, placing Jesus as the very source of the righteousness that only God can grant.
elements.questionHint: What single name comes right after 'our God and Savior' in this greeting — is Peter describing two people here, or one?

elements.passageText: <sup>18</sup> No one has ever seen God. The only one, himself God, who is in closest fellowship with the Father, has made God known.

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Son is fully God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John states it for emphasis: no one has seen God, yet "the only one, himself God" has made God known. The one doing the revealing is explicitly called God — not simply God's spokesman or a heavenly messenger relaying secondhand information. His unique position "in closest fellowship with the Father" is precisely what qualifies him to reveal the Father accurately, since he shares the Father's own nature rather than observing it from the outside. The logic depends entirely on the revealer being fully God himself; otherwise he could never make the unseen God genuinely known to anyone.
elements.questionHint: What does the verse call 'the only one' before it says he is in 'closest fellowship with the Father' — why would that be necessary for making God accurately known?

elements.passageText: <sup>58</sup> Jesus said to them, “I tell you the solemn truth, before Abraham came into existence, I am!”

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Son is fully God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus doesn't say "before Abraham was, I was" — the natural way to claim to predate someone — he says "I am," present tense, echoing the divine name God gave Moses at the burning bush. He is claiming not just to have existed before Abraham but to exist in the timeless, self-existent way God exists, outside the ordinary flow of past and future that everything created is bound by. The Jewish leaders who heard him understood exactly what he meant — the next verse records them picking up stones, the standard response to blasphemy, because Jesus had just applied God's own self-designation to himself.
elements.questionHint: Why does Jesus say 'I am' rather than the more natural 'I was,' and where else does God introduce himself with those same two words?

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> For in him all the fullness of deity lives in bodily form,

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Son is fully God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul doesn't say Christ reflects God or carries some divine qualities — he says "all the fullness of deity" dwells in him, and does so "in bodily form," meaning in his actual physical, human existence. Nothing of God's nature is missing or held back; the completeness Paul stresses ("all the fullness") rules out any sense that Christ possesses only a portion of deity. That this fullness inhabits a body is itself remarkable — the eternal, unbounded God taking up residence within the limits of a human body without ceasing, even for a moment, to be fully God.
elements.questionHint: What word does Paul put before 'fullness,' and what does that word rule out about how much of God's nature Christ actually has?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> The Son is the radiance of his glory and the representation of his essence, and he sustains all things by his powerful word, and so when he had accomplished cleansing for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high .

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Son is fully God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The writer calls the Son "the radiance of his glory and the representation of his essence" — not someone who reflects God's glory from outside, but one who radiates it as its own source, the way brightness comes from a flame rather than merely borrowing light from elsewhere. "Representation of his essence" goes further still, meaning the Son bears God's own nature exactly, not a copy or a symbol of it. The verse then credits him with sustaining "all things" by his word and accomplishing the cleansing of sins, divine acts of upholding creation and atoning for sin, before he is seated at "the right hand of the Majesty," the place of supreme divine honor.
elements.questionHint: What is the difference between something that only reflects light and something that radiates its own light — and which one does the writer say the Son is?

elements.question: Which of these verses do you find clearest in showing that Jesus is fully God? Why?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Write down your thoughts...

elements.text: 4. The Spirit is fully God

The Holy Spirit is sometimes the most neglected member of the Trinity in ordinary Christian thinking – talked about less than the Father or the Son, and sometimes treated as a bit like a force or an influence. But Scripture speaks of the Spirit having a mind, being lied to as God is lied to, and indwelling believers in a way only God could.

elements.passageText: <sup>29</sup> But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven, but is guilty of an eternal sin”

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Spirit is fully God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus treats sin against the Holy Spirit with a severity reserved for sin against God himself — an "eternal sin" that will "never be forgiven." Blasphemy, by definition, is speech dishonoring God; that it can be committed specifically against the Holy Spirit, and carry eternal consequences no other sin in this passage does, only makes sense if the Spirit is himself divine. If the Spirit were merely an impersonal force or a created being, blasphemy against him wouldn't carry the same unforgivable, eternal weight as blasphemy against God — yet Jesus treats the two as functionally identical offenses.
elements.questionHint: Why would speaking against a mere force or influence be called an 'eternal sin' that can 'never be forgiven' — what does that severity require the Spirit to be?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> But Peter said, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and keep back for yourself part of the proceeds from the sale of the land? <sup>4</sup> Before it was sold, did it not belong to you? And when it was sold, was the money not at your disposal? How have you thought up this deed in your heart? You have not lied to people but to God!”

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Spirit is fully God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter's accusation moves in one breath from "you have lied to the Holy Spirit" to "you have lied... to God," treating the two statements as equivalent descriptions of the same offense. He doesn't correct himself or draw a distinction between a lesser sin against the Spirit and a greater one against God — the shift in wording is the entire point, establishing that lying to the Holy Spirit simply is lying to God. Ananias's sin was concealment aimed at a person he thought he could deceive, and Peter's words make unmistakably clear that person was fully God.
elements.questionHint: Peter uses two different phrases for what Ananias did — 'lied to the Holy Spirit,' then what one sentence later — and why use both if they didn't mean the same thing?

elements.passageText: <sup>26</sup> When the Advocate comes, whom I will send you from the Father – the Spirit of truth who goes out from the Father – he will testify about me,

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Spirit is fully God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus calls the Spirit "the Advocate" and "the Spirit of truth," describing him as sent from the Father and proceeding from the Father — language of divine origin, not merely of a divine effect or influence. The Spirit's role here is active, not passive: he "testifies" about Jesus, a personal and authoritative act of bearing witness to the truth about who Christ is. Being sent by the Father while also going out from the Father places the Spirit in the closest possible relationship to God's own being and mission, consistent with a shared, undivided deity rather than a lesser or created assistant.
elements.questionHint: The verse says the Spirit 'goes out from the Father' — what does sharing that same origin with the Father suggest about what kind of being the Spirit is?

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> God has revealed these to us by the Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God.

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Spirit is fully God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Searching "the deep things of God" requires a knowledge of God's inner life no creature possesses — Paul describes the Spirit's access to God's own thoughts, not an outside observer's best guess. This kind of comprehensive, unrestricted knowledge of God's depths belongs to God alone, since nothing hidden could remain hidden from a merely created being probing from outside. That the Spirit is the one revealing "these things to us" means he functions here as the source of divine self-disclosure, possessing the intimate knowledge of God that only God himself could have and choose to share.
elements.questionHint: What would it take to know 'the deep things' of anyone from the inside rather than the outside — and what does the verse say the Spirit does with God's own depths?

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup> For who among men knows the things of a man except the man’s spirit within him? So too, no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God.

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Spirit is fully God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul draws a direct comparison: just as a person's own spirit alone knows that person's inner thoughts, "the Spirit of God" alone knows the thoughts of God. The parallel is exact and deliberate — the relationship of the Spirit to God mirrors the relationship of a human spirit to that human being, meaning the Spirit belongs to God's own inner life the same way your spirit belongs to you. No outside knower, however wise, could substitute for this; the analogy only works if the Spirit shares in God's own self-knowledge precisely because he is himself God.
elements.questionHint: Paul compares the Spirit of God to something that belongs to a human being — what is it, and what does that comparison say about how close the Spirit is to God's own inner life?

elements.passageText: <sup>19</sup> Or do you not know that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God, and you are not your own?

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Spirit is fully God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul calls the believer's body a "temple," language that in Jewish thought meant one thing: the dwelling place of God's own presence. Calling it specifically the temple "of the Holy Spirit" identifies the Spirit as the divine presence inhabiting that temple, doing what only God himself did in the temple at Jerusalem. If the Spirit were less than God, calling believers' bodies his temple would be a strange overstatement; instead, Paul assumes without argument or explanation that being indwelt by the Spirit is being indwelt by God.
elements.questionHint: In Jewish thought, whose presence did a temple hold — and whose temple does Paul say your body has now become?

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup> Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is present, there is freedom.

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Spirit is fully God?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul makes the identification directly: "the Lord is the Spirit." In context he has just been discussing the "Lord" Moses encountered in the Exodus account, and now applies that same title to the Spirit at work among believers. The freedom Paul describes is the freedom that comes from the Lord's own presence, not a benefit conferred by some subordinate being. By using "Lord," a title Scripture reserves for God, to describe the Spirit's identity and activity, Paul places the Spirit within the very identity of the one Lord of Israel's Scriptures.
elements.questionHint: What title does Paul use for the Spirit here, one Scripture normally reserves for God alone — what does applying it to the Spirit suggest about who he is?

elements.question: If someone said, ‘the Holy Spirit is just a feeling, or a kind of spiritual energy,‘ how would you use these verses to respond?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Write down your thoughts...

elements.text: 5. The Father, Son and Holy Spirit are distinct (i.e. not three terms for one person)

If Truths 1-4 stood alone, someone might try to solve the puzzle by saying that “Father,” “Son,” and “Spirit” are just three names or three roles that the one-person God takes on at different times – rather like an actor changing costume. This view has a name (modalism), and the church has always rejected it, because it doesn’t fit what the Bible actually shows us: Father, Son, and Spirit relating to one another, speaking to one another, and being present together, at the same moment.

elements.passageText: <sup>18</sup> Then Jesus came up and said to them, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. <sup>19</sup> Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, <sup>20</sup> teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you. And remember, I am with you always, to the end of the age.”

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are distinct (i.e. not three terms for one person)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus commands baptism "in the name" — singular — "of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit," listing three distinct persons under one shared name rather than three separate names. The grammar itself distinguishes them: each is named separately, connected by "and," which would make no sense if they were simply three labels for one individual. Yet all three share a single "name," indicating one identity held in common even while remaining three who can each be named and addressed distinctly — exactly the pattern of three distinct persons sharing one divine identity this study is tracing.
elements.questionHint: Jesus lists three parties joined by 'and' but places them under 'the name' — singular — why list them separately at all if they were just three words for the same person?

elements.passageText: <sup>16</sup> After Jesus was baptized, just as he was coming up out of the water, the heavens opened and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming on him. <sup>17</sup> And a voice from heaven said, “This is my one dear Son; in him I take great delight.”

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are distinct (i.e. not three terms for one person)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: All three are present and active at once, each doing something distinguishable from the others: Jesus stands in the water having just been baptized, the Spirit visibly descends "like a dove" onto him from above, and a voice speaks "from heaven," identifying Jesus as "my one dear Son." A single person cannot baptize himself, watch a dove descend onto himself, and simultaneously speak about himself from the sky in the third person. The scene only makes sense as three distinct persons interacting at the same moment — the Son in the river, the Spirit coming down, and the Father speaking from above.
elements.questionHint: In this one scene, how many separate locations are involved — the water, the sky, and the voice above — and could a single individual really occupy and act from all three at once?

elements.passageText: <sup>32</sup> This Jesus God raised up, and we are all witnesses of it. <sup>33</sup> So then, exalted to the right hand of God, and having received the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father, he has poured out what you both see and hear. <sup>34</sup> For David did not ascend into heaven, but he himself says, ‘The Lord said to my lord, “Sit at my right hand <sup>35</sup> until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.”’ <sup>36</sup> Therefore let all the house of Israel know beyond a doubt that God has made this Jesus whom you crucified both Lord and Christ.”

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are distinct (i.e. not three terms for one person)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter describes a sequence of distinct actions among distinct persons: "God raised up" Jesus, Jesus is "exalted to the right hand of God," and Jesus "received the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father" in order to pour it out. Three separate relationships are packed into these verses — God as the one who raises, Jesus as the one raised and exalted, and the Spirit as a promised gift passed from Father to Son and then poured out by the Son. None of these actions make sense if "God," "Jesus," and "the Spirit" were all the very same single person; the language requires them to be genuinely distinct.
elements.questionHint: Peter says Jesus received something 'from the Father' in order to pour it out — how many different parties does a transaction like that require: a giver, a receiver, and a gift?

elements.passageText: <sup>13</sup> The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are distinct (i.e. not three terms for one person)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's closing blessing names three distinct sources for three distinct gifts: "the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ," "the love of God," and "the fellowship of the Holy Spirit." Each phrase attaches a different gift to a different named person, and the three parallel clauses joined by "and" treat them as three who can each be invoked separately in prayer. If Father, Son, and Spirit were simply three names for one individual, this triple benediction would be needlessly repetitive; instead it reads naturally as an appeal to three distinct persons whose combined blessing Paul wants for his readers.
elements.questionHint: How many separate 'and's join the three phrases in this blessing, and what different gift is attached to each of the three names?

elements.passageText: <sup>16</sup> I pray that according to the wealth of his glory he may grant you to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person, <sup>17</sup> that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, so that, because you have been rooted and grounded in love, <sup>18</sup> you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, <sup>19</sup> and thus to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, so that you may be filled up to all the fullness of God.

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are distinct (i.e. not three terms for one person)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's prayer moves through a chain of distinct relationships: he petitions the Father, asking that believers "be strengthened... through his Spirit," so "that Christ may dwell in your hearts," resulting in being "filled up to all the fullness of God." Each person plays a different role within this single prayer — the Father is asked, the Spirit strengthens, Christ indwells — and these roles aren't interchangeable or collapsed into one actor performing everything under different names. The distinctions are essential to how the prayer actually works: one is asked, another empowers, another comes to dwell in the heart.
elements.questionHint: In this prayer, who is being asked, who does the strengthening, and who comes to 'dwell' in the heart — is that one action performed by one person, or three different actions?

elements.question: At Jesus’ baptism (Matthew 3:16-17), the Father, Son, and Spirit are all present and active at the same time. Why does this moment alone rule out the idea that Father, Son and Spirit are simply the same person under three different names?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Write down your thoughts...

elements.text: 6. The Father is personal
The Trinity is not “three forces” or “three functions.” Father, Son, and Spirit are persons – each one relates, speaks, loves, and can be related to. We begin with the Father.

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> “Just as the Father has loved me, I have also loved you; remain in my love.

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Father is personal?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus describes the Father's love for him with the same word he uses for his own love toward his disciples — a real, relational love passing between persons, not an abstract force or principle. Love in this sense requires a subject who loves and an object who is loved; the Father is presented as actively, personally loving the Son, engaging in the kind of relationship only a person can have. Jesus grounds his own love for his disciples directly in the pattern of the Father's love for him, treating the Father's love as a genuine, personal reality he himself has experienced and now passes on.
elements.questionHint: Can an impersonal force 'love' someone the way this verse says the Father loves the Son — what does love require of the one doing the loving?

elements.passageText: <sup>15</sup> For you did not receive the spirit of slavery leading again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba, Father.”

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Father is personal?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The Spirit of adoption doesn't just inform believers about God in the abstract; he prompts them to cry out "Abba, Father" — intimate, personal address, the kind a child uses with a parent they know and trust. This is relational language through and through: adoption implies a family, a father who receives, and children who can address him directly and personally. The verse assumes the Father is the kind of being who can be addressed, related to, and cried out to by name — not a distant force acted upon, but a person who receives the cry of his children as their own father.
elements.questionHint: What word does Paul say believers cry out to the Father — is that the kind of word you'd use for an impersonal power, or for someone you actually have a relationship with?

elements.text: 7. The Son is personal

elements.passageText: <sup>62</sup> “I am,” said Jesus, “and you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the Power and coming with the clouds of heaven .”

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Son is personal?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus speaks in the first person, directly answering the high priest's question about his identity with "I am," then describes himself in the third person as "the Son of Man" who will sit and come. This is self-aware, self-referential speech, the kind only a person can produce — someone with a will who chooses his own words and stakes his own claim about his own future. He isn't a description applied to him by others in this moment; he is actively speaking, answering, and asserting his own identity and destiny before the very people accusing him.
elements.questionHint: Jesus is answering a direct question in his own words here — what does the act of answering, rather than merely being described, tell you about whether he is a person?

elements.passageText: <sup>20</sup> For the Father loves the Son and shows him everything he does, and will show him greater deeds than these, so that you will be amazed. <sup>21</sup> For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes. <sup>22</sup> Furthermore, the Father does not judge anyone, but has assigned all judgment to the Son, <sup>23</sup> so that all people will honor the Son just as they honor the Father. The one who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Son is personal?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The Son is described doing things only a personal agent can do: he receives the Father's love, is shown things, exercises judgment that has been "assigned" to him, and gives life "to whomever he wishes" — an act of personal will and choice, not a mechanical function. He is also the object of honor, someone people either honor or fail to honor, which requires him to be a someone rather than a something. The reciprocal relationship described — Father loving Son, Son doing what he sees, both being honored together — is a relationship between persons, not between a person and an impersonal extension of himself.
elements.questionHint: The verse says the Son gives life 'to whomever he wishes' — what does having a 'wish' and choosing who receives it say about whether the Son is a person?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> He fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” <sup>5</sup> So he said, “Who are you, Lord?” He replied, “I am Jesus whom you are persecuting!

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Son is personal?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The risen Jesus speaks directly to Saul by name, asks him a personal question about his own actions ("why are you persecuting me?"), and answers Saul's question in return with a clear self-identification: "I am Jesus." This is a real conversation between two persons — one asking, one answering, each using personal pronouns. Notably, Jesus identifies Saul's persecution of the church as persecution of himself personally, showing he considers himself so united with his people that harming them means confronting him directly, exactly as one person confronts another.
elements.questionHint: Who asks the question and who answers it in this exchange — and what does having a real back-and-forth conversation require about the one speaking from heaven?

elements.text: 8. The Holy Spirit is personal

Because the Spirit isn’t seen or pictured the way the Father and the Son are, it’s easy to slip into thinking of Him as an “it” – a wind, a power, an atmosphere – rather than a “He.” These verses show that that’s a mistake.

elements.passageText: <sup>26</sup> In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness, for we do not know how we should pray, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings.

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Holy Spirit is personal?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The Spirit does things that require a will and an inner life: he "helps," he "intercedes," and he does so "himself" — the reflexive pronoun underlining that this is the Spirit's own personal action, not a byproduct or an impersonal influence flowing through us. Interceding on someone's behalf is a personal act, the kind a friend or advocate does for another, requiring understanding, care, and initiative. The "inexpressible groanings" describe something happening in the Spirit's own engagement with our weakness, not a mechanical process — this is a person entering sympathetically into human need on our behalf.
elements.questionHint: Paul says 'the Spirit ___ intercedes' using a reflexive word — what does interceding for someone, done by the intercessor 'himself,' require of the one doing it?

elements.passageText: <sup>30</sup> And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Holy Spirit is personal?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Grief is an emotional response, something only a person with feelings can experience; you cannot grieve a force, a power, or an impersonal influence any more than you could offend the wind. Paul's command assumes the Spirit has an emotional capacity that can be wounded by the believer's sin, which only makes sense if the Spirit is a personal being capable of being hurt by how his people live. The verse also ties this to being "sealed" by the Spirit "for the day of redemption," reinforcing that this grievable Spirit is personally invested in believers' ultimate salvation, not detached from it.
elements.questionHint: Can you 'grieve' a force or a power the way you can grieve a person — what emotional capacity does the command not to grieve the Spirit assume he has?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> But Peter said, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and keep back for yourself part of the proceeds from the sale of the land?

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Holy Spirit is personal?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter charges Ananias with lying "to the Holy Spirit," and lying is something you do to a person capable of being deceived, not to an impersonal principle or force. The accusation assumes the Spirit could have known the truth and been misled by Ananias's deceit, which requires the Spirit to have the kind of mind and awareness a person has. Peter frames it as an offense committed against someone — an interpersonal wrong — exactly the way you would describe deceiving another person, rather than the way you would describe misusing or wasting a resource.
elements.questionHint: What does it mean to 'lie' to someone — can you lie to a force, or only to someone capable of being told a truth or a falsehood?

elements.question: Does it change anything for you, practically, to think of the Holy Spirit as a person you can grieve, resist, or walk closely with – rather than as an impersonal force?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Write down your thoughts...

elements.text: 9. The Father, Son and Holy Spirit are not separate but one

Truths 6-8 showed three distinct persons. This truth balances that: those three persons are not three separate beings running their own agendas. They are perfectly united – one in essence, one in purpose, one in will.

elements.passageText: <sup>18</sup> Then Jesus came up and said to them, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. <sup>19</sup> Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, <sup>20</sup> teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you. And remember, I am with you always, to the end of the age.”

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are not separate but one?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The wording is precise: Jesus says "in the name" — one name, singular — even though three persons are listed afterward. If Father, Son, and Spirit were simply three separate beings with no underlying unity, the natural wording would be "in the names," plural, one for each. Instead, the single "name" shared by all three signals one identity, one divine reality, that the three equally bear even as they remain distinguishable persons. The threeness of the persons named and the oneness of the name they share sit together in the very grammar of Jesus's own command.
elements.questionHint: Jesus says 'the name' rather than 'the names,' even while listing three parties — what does that singular word suggest about how united they are?

elements.passageText: <sup>13</sup> The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are not separate but one?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Even as Paul names three distinct sources of blessing, he asks for all three — grace, love, fellowship — to be "with you all" as a single combined benediction, not three separate blessings to be received one at a time or weighed against each other. The three phrases function as facets of one act of blessing rather than competing gifts from three unrelated powers. Paul can move fluidly between Lord Jesus Christ, God, and the Holy Spirit within one sentence precisely because he assumes their unity; nothing here suggests he is invoking three independent deities.
elements.questionHint: Paul asks for grace, love, and fellowship to be with the readers together in one sentence — does that read as three separate blessings, or one blessing with three sources?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> There is one body and one Spirit, just as you too were called to the one hope of your calling, <sup>5</sup> one Lord, one faith, one baptism, <sup>6</sup> one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are not separate but one?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul stacks up a sevenfold list of unity — one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father — and the repetition of "one" is the entire point. Spirit, Lord, and God and Father are each named individually within this same insistent list of oneness, meaning naming them as distinct doesn't fracture the unity Paul is building; rather, each is affirmed to be one, and together they anchor the "one body" believers share. The passage that most emphatically names Father, Son, and Spirit separately is also the passage most emphatically insisting on oneness at every point.
elements.questionHint: Paul repeats the word 'one' seven times in three verses, applying it to Spirit, Lord, and God and Father alike — what does that repetition suggest about whether they are competing powers or a single reality?

elements.text: 10. The Father, Son and Holy Spirit indwell one-another

This is sometimes called perichoresis – the ancient word the church used to describe how each person of the Trinity is fully present within the others, without being confused or merged into one another. It’s one of the hardest ideas in this whole study to imagine, and perhaps that’s appropriate: we are creatures trying to describe the inner life of the eternal, uncreated God.

elements.passageText: <sup>18</sup> No one has ever seen God. The only one, himself God, who is in closest fellowship with the Father, has made God known.

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit indwell one-another?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The phrase "closest fellowship" describes an intimacy of position beyond ordinary closeness — the Son is pictured as residing within the Father's own innermost presence. This isn't proximity like two people standing near each other; it is a mutual indwelling so complete that the Son's very location is described in terms of the Father's own being. That this closeness is precisely what qualifies the Son to make the unseen God known shows how their mutual indwelling isn't incidental to who they are but constitutive of it, the very ground on which revelation of the Father becomes possible.
elements.questionHint: The phrase describing the Son's position with the Father is stronger than simply 'near' him — what does 'closest fellowship' suggest about where the Son actually is in relation to the Father's own being?

elements.passageText: <sup>30</sup> The Father and I are one.”

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit indwell one-another?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus doesn't say "the Father and I agree" or "work together" — he says "we are one," a statement of shared being rather than mere cooperation. The plural verb ("are") paired with the singular predicate ("one") captures exactly what this claims: two distinct persons, the Father and the Son, sharing one undivided reality so completely that Jesus can describe their union with a single word. This is the language of mutual indwelling, not two allies standing side by side, but two who are, in the deepest sense that being can be shared, one.
elements.questionHint: Jesus uses a plural verb ('we are') but a singular predicate ('one') in the same short sentence — what does combining those two forms tell you about the relationship he's describing?

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> Do you not believe that I am in the Father, and the Father is in me? The words that I say to you, I do not speak on my own initiative, but the Father residing in me performs his miraculous deeds. <sup>11</sup> Believe me that I am in the Father, and the Father is in me, but if you do not believe me, believe because of the miraculous deeds themselves.

elements.question: How does this verse show that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit indwell one-another?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus states the mutual indwelling twice, almost word for word, so it can't be missed: "I am in the Father, and the Father is in me." This is reciprocal, not one residing in the other while that one stands apart, but each dwelling within the other simultaneously. He grounds his own words and works in this mutual indwelling, explaining that his speech isn't self-generated but comes from "the Father residing in me" performing "his miraculous deeds" through him. The double repetition and the concrete evidence of the miracles are Jesus's own proof that this indwelling is real, not merely figurative language.
elements.questionHint: Jesus says this same thing twice, in both directions, within two verses — why would he need to state the indwelling both ways instead of just once?

elements.question: Which of the ten truths above did you find hardest to hold onto at the same time as the others? Why?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Write down your thoughts...

elements.text: Overview: God acting Triunely

Doctrine is not meant to stay on paper. The Trinity is not only a truth to be understood; it’s the shape of how God actually works in the world and in your life. In salvation, the Father plans, the Son accomplishes, and the Spirit applies – three persons, one saving work. The verses below show the Trinity in action: creating, saving, sealing, and sending.

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> Now in those days Jesus came from Nazareth in Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan River. <sup>10</sup> And just as Jesus was coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens splitting apart and the Spirit descending on him like a dove. <sup>11</sup> And a voice came from heaven: “You are my one dear Son; in you I take great delight.”

elements.question: How does this verse show God acting Triunely?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: In a single event, all three act together in distinguishable ways: Jesus is baptized in the water, the Spirit descends on him "like a dove," and the Father's voice speaks from heaven, declaring the Son's identity and his pleasure in him. None of the three substitutes for another — the Son doesn't speak from heaven about himself, and the Spirit doesn't verbally identify Jesus. Instead each does his own distinct part within one coordinated moment, launching Jesus's public ministry through the simultaneous involvement of Father, Son, and Spirit acting together.
elements.questionHint: List what each of the three does in this scene — who is in the water, who descends from above, and who speaks — are these overlapping actions or three separate ones?

elements.passageText: <sup>16</sup> Then I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate to be with you forever – <sup>17</sup> the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot accept, because it does not see him or know him. But you know him, because he resides with you and will be in you. <sup>18</sup> “I will not abandon you as orphans, I will come to you. <sup>19</sup> In a little while the world will not see me any longer, but you will see me; because I live, you will live too. <sup>20</sup> You will know at that time that I am in my Father and you are in me and I am in you. <sup>21</sup> The person who has my commandments and obeys them is the one who loves me. The one who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and will reveal myself to him.” <sup>22</sup> “Lord,” Judas (not Judas Iscariot) said, “what has happened that you are going to reveal yourself to us and not to the world?” <sup>23</sup> Jesus replied, “If anyone loves me, he will obey my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and take up residence with him. <sup>24</sup> The person who does not love me does not obey my words. And the word you hear is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me. <sup>25</sup> “I have spoken these things while staying with you. <sup>26</sup> But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you everything, and will cause you to remember everything I said to you.

elements.question: How does this verse show God acting Triunely?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus describes an interlocking operation: he will ask the Father, the Father will give another Advocate, the Spirit will reside in believers, and Jesus himself will come to them so they aren't left as orphans — three persons cooperating toward one goal of ongoing divine presence with the disciples. Later in the passage the Father and Son together "come" and "take up residence" with the one who loves Jesus, while the Spirit teaches and reminds believers of Christ's words on behalf of the Father who sent him. The roles differ — asking, giving, sending, residing, teaching — yet all serve the single outcome of God remaining with his people.
elements.questionHint: Trace the chain: Jesus asks someone, that someone sends someone else to the disciples — how many distinct actors and actions can you count across this one passage?

elements.passageText: <sup>26</sup> When the Advocate comes, whom I will send you from the Father – the Spirit of truth who goes out from the Father – he will testify about me,

elements.question: How does this verse show God acting Triunely?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The verse packs three persons into one coordinated act of testimony: the Son sends the Advocate, the Advocate comes "from the Father," and once he arrives, he "will testify about" the Son. Sending, originating, and testifying are three distinguishable roles carried out by three distinguishable persons working toward the single purpose of bearing witness to Christ. The Spirit's testimony isn't self-generated or independent of the other two; it flows directly out of his relationship to both the Father he comes from and the Son he testifies about.
elements.questionHint: Who does the sending, who does the coming, and who is being testified about in this one verse — can you match all three roles to Father, Son, and Spirit?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> But now I am going to the one who sent me, and not one of you is asking me, ‘Where are you going?’ <sup>6</sup> Instead your hearts are filled with sadness because I have said these things to you. <sup>7</sup> But I tell you the truth, it is to your advantage that I am going away. For if I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you, but if I go, I will send him to you. <sup>8</sup> And when he comes, he will prove the world wrong concerning sin and righteousness and judgment – <sup>9</sup> concerning sin, because they do not believe in me; <sup>10</sup> concerning righteousness, because I am going to the Father and you will see me no longer; <sup>11</sup> and concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world has been condemned. <sup>12</sup> “I have many more things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. <sup>13</sup> But when he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will guide you into all truth. For he will not speak on his own authority, but will speak whatever he hears, and will tell you what is to come. <sup>14</sup> He will glorify me, because he will receive from me what is mine and will tell it to you. <sup>15</sup> Everything that the Father has is mine; that is why I said the Spirit will receive from me what is mine and will tell it to you.

elements.question: How does this verse show God acting Triunely?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus lays out a division of labor among the three: he is "going to the one who sent me" (the Father), his departure clears the way for the Advocate to come, and the Advocate's ministry is entirely relational to the other two — he will "not speak on his own authority" but tell disciples "whatever he hears," and will "glorify" Jesus by taking "what is mine" and declaring it. Everything the Father has, Jesus says, is his, and the Spirit communicates from that same shared reservoir. Three distinct persons, each with a specific role, work through one seamless movement of revelation from the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit.
elements.questionHint: The Spirit takes from what belongs to Jesus, and everything Jesus has belongs to the Father — can you trace that chain of 'belonging' through all three persons in this passage?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. <sup>2</sup> For the law of the life-giving Spirit in Christ Jesus has set you free from the law of sin and death. <sup>3</sup> For God achieved what the law could not do because it was weakened through the flesh. By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and concerning sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, <sup>4</sup> so that the righteous requirement of the law may be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. <sup>5</sup> For those who live according to the flesh have their outlook shaped by the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit have their outlook shaped by the things of the Spirit. <sup>6</sup> For the outlook of the flesh is death, but the outlook of the Spirit is life and peace, <sup>7</sup> because the outlook of the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to the law of God, nor is it able to do so. <sup>8</sup> Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. <sup>9</sup> You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God lives in you. Now if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, this person does not belong to him. <sup>10</sup> But if Christ is in you, your body is dead because of sin, but the Spirit is your life because of righteousness. <sup>11</sup> Moreover if the Spirit of the one who raised Jesus from the dead lives in you, the one who raised Christ from the dead will also make your mortal bodies alive through his Spirit who lives in you.

elements.question: How does this verse show God acting Triunely?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul weaves the three together as jointly responsible for the believer's freedom from sin and death: "the law of the life-giving Spirit in Christ Jesus" sets us free, accomplished because "God" sent "his own Son" to deal with sin in the flesh. Later Paul calls the same indwelling reality "the Spirit of God," "the Spirit of Christ," and simply "his Spirit," moving between these descriptions as though naming one shared work carried out by Father, Son, and Spirit together. The chapter's logic — condemnation removed, righteousness fulfilled, mortal bodies to be made alive — depends at every step on the coordinated action of all three.
elements.questionHint: Paul uses three different phrases for the same indwelling reality — 'Spirit of God,' 'Spirit of Christ,' and 'his Spirit' — what does moving between those without explanation suggest about how closely Father, Son, and Spirit are joined?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> So I want you to understand that no one speaking by the Spirit of God says, “Jesus is cursed,” and no one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” except by the Holy Spirit. <sup>4</sup> Now there are different gifts, but the same Spirit. <sup>5</sup> And there are different ministries, but the same Lord. <sup>6</sup> And there are different results, but the same God who produces all of them in everyone.

elements.question: How does this verse show God acting Triunely?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul structures three parallel statements — "the same Spirit," "the same Lord," "the same God" — each governing a different category (gifts, ministries, results), showing all three persons actively at work in the diversity of the church's life. He opens by noting that confessing "Jesus is Lord" is only possible "by the Holy Spirit," linking the Spirit's own activity directly to right confession of the Son. The threefold "same" running through the passage insists that behind the different gifts, ministries, and results stands one coordinated divine activity, distributed across Spirit, Lord, and God without any one of them working in isolation.
elements.questionHint: Paul repeats 'the same' three times, once each for Spirit, Lord, and God — what does that repeated word suggest about the source behind all the different gifts, ministries, and results?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> But when the appropriate time had come, God sent out his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, <sup>5</sup> to redeem those who were under the law, so that we may be adopted as sons with full rights. <sup>6</sup> And because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, who calls “ Abba! Father!”

elements.question: How does this verse show God acting Triunely?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The two verses describe a matched pair of sendings: God sends "his Son" to accomplish redemption under the law, and then, once believers are adopted as sons, God sends "the Spirit of his Son" into their hearts. The Spirit doesn't operate independently of the Son but is identified as belonging specifically to him — "the Spirit of his Son" — and his work is to produce the same intimate cry, "Abba, Father," that marks a child's relationship to the Father. Father, Son, and Spirit act in sequence toward a single outcome: adoption into the family and the Spirit's own testimony to that new relationship.
elements.questionHint: God sends two things in these verses, his Son and then a Spirit described as belonging to whom — what does that description say about how the Spirit's mission relates to the Son's?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> Blessed is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms in Christ. <sup>4</sup> For he chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world that we may be holy and unblemished in his sight in love. <sup>5</sup> He did this by predestining us to adoption as his sons through Jesus Christ, according to the pleasure of his will – <sup>6</sup> to the praise of the glory of his grace that he has freely bestowed on us in his dearly loved Son. <sup>7</sup> In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace <sup>8</sup> that he lavished on us in all wisdom and insight. <sup>9</sup> He did this when he revealed to us the secret of his will, according to his good pleasure that he set forth in Christ, <sup>10</sup> toward the administration of the fullness of the times, to head up all things in Christ – the things in heaven and the things on earth. <sup>11</sup> In Christ we too have been claimed as God’s own possession, since we were predestined according to the one purpose of him who accomplishes all things according to the counsel of his will <sup>12</sup> so that we, who were the first to set our hope on Christ, would be to the praise of his glory. <sup>13</sup> And when you heard the word of truth (the gospel of your salvation) – when you believed in Christ – you were marked with the seal of the promised Holy Spirit, <sup>14</sup> who is the down payment of our inheritance, until the redemption of God’s own possession, to the praise of his glory.

elements.question: How does this verse show God acting Triunely?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This long passage traces blessing flowing from the Father, "who has blessed us... in Christ," through the Son in whom believers are chosen and redeemed, and finally sealed by "the promised Holy Spirit" as "the down payment of our inheritance." Each person has a distinguishable role in a single unfolding plan: the Father plans and predestines, the Son accomplishes redemption "through his blood," and the Spirit seals and guarantees what has been secured. The passage never treats this as three separate plans running side by side — it is one plan of salvation, executed by the Father's will, achieved in the Son, and confirmed by the Spirit.
elements.questionHint: This passage moves through three stages — being chosen, being redeemed, and being sealed — which divine person is credited with which stage?

elements.passageText: <sup>18</sup> so that through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.

elements.question: How does this verse show God acting Triunely?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: In a single short sentence, Paul routes access to God through all three persons at once: access is "through him" (Christ), "in one Spirit," and directed "to the Father." Each preposition marks a distinct role — Christ as the means, the Spirit as the sphere enabling the approach, the Father as the one being approached — compressed into a single act of coming near to God. The verse shows that ordinary Christian access to God is not a simple, undifferentiated event but one involving the coordinated work of Father, Son, and Spirit every single time it happens.
elements.questionHint: Three prepositions do the work in this verse — 'through,' 'in,' and 'to' — which person is attached to each one, and what role does that suggest for them?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> There is one body and one Spirit, just as you too were called to the one hope of your calling, <sup>5</sup> one Lord, one faith, one baptism, <sup>6</sup> one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.

elements.question: How does this verse show God acting Triunely?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Even in a passage built around unity, Paul distributes distinct roles across the three: "one Spirit" corresponds to the "one hope" believers share, "one Lord" corresponds to "one faith" and "one baptism," and "one God and Father" is described as "over all and through all and in all." The threefold structure isn't decorative; each divine person is tied to a specific aspect of the church's shared life — the Spirit to hope, the Lord to faith and baptism, the Father to all-encompassing presence. This is God acting in three distinguishable ways to produce the single unified body Paul describes at the start of the list.
elements.questionHint: Match each 'one' in this list to a person — which goes with the Spirit, which with the Lord, and which with the Father — and what different aspect of church life is each tied to?

elements.passageText: <sup>13</sup> But we ought to thank God always for you, brothers and sisters loved by the Lord, because God chose you from the beginning for salvation through sanctification by the Spirit and faith in the truth. <sup>14</sup> He called you to this salvation through our gospel, so that you may possess the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.

elements.question: How does this verse show God acting Triunely?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul thanks God for a salvation that involves all three at different stages: "God chose you... for salvation through sanctification by the Spirit and faith in the truth," a calling that comes "through our gospel" so believers "may possess the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ." The Father's choosing, the Spirit's sanctifying work, and the goal of sharing Christ's own glory are laid out as one continuous process rather than three unrelated activities. Each contribution is necessary to the whole: without the Father's choice there is no calling, without the Spirit's sanctification there is no holiness, and without Christ there is no glory to be possessed.
elements.questionHint: This passage names a distinct action for each divine person — choosing, sanctifying, and possessing glory — which action belongs to which person?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> But “when the kindness of God our Savior and his love for mankind appeared, <sup>5</sup> he saved us not by works of righteousness that we have done but on the basis of his mercy, through the washing of the new birth and the renewing of the Holy Spirit, <sup>6</sup> whom he poured out on us in full measure through Jesus Christ our Savior.

elements.question: How does this verse show God acting Triunely?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The passage credits salvation to "the kindness of God our Savior," accomplished "through the washing of the new birth and the renewing of the Holy Spirit," which God poured out "through Jesus Christ our Savior." Three distinct roles converge in one saving act: God's kindness as the motive, the Spirit's renewing work as the means applied to the believer, and Jesus Christ as the one through whom this outpouring happens. The phrase "poured out... through Jesus Christ" links the Spirit's work directly to Christ's mediating role, showing all three cooperating in a single act of mercy rather than three separate saving acts.
elements.questionHint: The word 'through' appears twice in these verses — what is accomplished 'through' the renewing of the Spirit, and what is that renewal itself poured out 'through'?

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup> according to the foreknowledge of God the Father by being set apart by the Spirit for obedience and for sprinkling with Jesus Christ’s blood. May grace and peace be yours in full measure!

elements.question: How does this verse show God acting Triunely?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter opens with a tightly compressed formula naming all three: believers are chosen "according to the foreknowledge of God the Father," "by being set apart by the Spirit," "for obedience and for sprinkling with Jesus Christ's blood."
