Each person contributes something no other provides — the Father's foreknowledge initiates the choosing, the Spirit's sanctifying work sets the person apart, and the Son's blood accomplishes the cleansing that makes obedience possible. It is a single act of salvation described from three angles at once, each necessary and none of them redundant.
elements.questionHint: This verse has three phrases in a row, each starting with a different word ('according to,' 'by,' 'for') — which divine person is tied to each phrase, and what distinct contribution does each make?

elements.passageText: <sup>20</sup> But you, dear friends, by building yourselves up in your most holy faith, by praying in the Holy Spirit, <sup>21</sup> maintain yourselves in the love of God, while anticipating the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that brings eternal life.

elements.question: How does this verse show God acting Triunely?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jude instructs believers toward a threefold posture: "praying in the Holy Spirit," maintaining themselves "in the love of God," while "anticipating the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ." Each preposition attaches to a different person and a different aspect of Christian life — prayer happens in the Spirit's sphere, present security rests in the Father's love, and future hope waits on the Son's mercy. The three aren't interchangeable; Jude structures spiritual life itself around distinct, ongoing relationships with all three persons operating at once.
elements.questionHint: Jude names three activities — praying, staying in love, anticipating mercy — is each one connected to the same divine person, or three different ones?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> From John, to the seven churches that are in the province of Asia: Grace and peace to you from “he who is,” and who was, and who is still to come, and from the seven spirits who are before his throne,

elements.question: How does this verse show God acting Triunely?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John's greeting names two sources of grace and peace in this verse — "he who is, and who was, and who is still to come" (the eternal Father) and "the seven spirits... before his throne," a symbolic description of the Holy Spirit in his fullness before God. Though this excerpt stops before naming Jesus Christ, John's greeting in Revelation continues immediately afterward with a third source, following the same triadic pattern found in other New Testament greetings. Even within this verse alone, God is described in two distinguishable but related ways — his eternal, unchanging existence and the sevenfold Spirit active before his throne — setting up the fuller Trinitarian greeting that follows.
elements.questionHint: John names grace and peace as coming from two different sources in this verse — the eternal 'he who is... and who was... and who is still to come' and something else 'before his throne' — what is that second source, and what number is attached to it?

elements.text:
Amina eventually described it this way to a friend:

  • “I used to think I believed in one God who sometimes showed up as Jesus and sometimes as the Spirit. Now I know I believe in one God who is, eternally, Father, Son, and Spirit, loving each other before the world even began – and who invited me into that love.”
Whatever words you find, the aim of this study isn’t a tidier diagram of God. It’s a deeper trust in the God who has always been, and always will be, exactly who He has revealed Himself to be.

chapters.chapterTitle: Christology: False Teaching & the Chalcedonian Definition

elements.text:
“If Christ is not fully God, He cannot pay for our sin. If Christ is not fully man, He should not pay for our sin.”
Anon.

elements.question: What do you think of this quotation? (Do you like it or not, and why?)
elements.answerPlaceholder: Write down your thoughts...

elements.text: Tanko had grown up hearing two very different pictures of Jesus. From one direction came friends who told him Jesus was really just a great prophet, a good man, a wise teacher – someone to admire, but not to worship. From another direction came a group at his workplace who spoke of Jesus almost like a spirit gliding through the Gospels: divine, powerful, but not really human in the way Tanko was human – never truly hungry, never truly afraid, never truly suffering as people suffer. Tanko found himself unsettled. If Jesus wasn’t fully God, could He really forgive sins and defeat death? If Jesus wasn’t fully human, could He really stand in Tanko’s place, tempted as Tanko is tempted, and understand what Tanko goes through? He needed to know: who exactly is Jesus?

elements.question: What would you say to Tanko?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Write down your thoughts...

elements.text: Tanko’s confusion is not new. In the fifth century there were many arguments and mistaken views about the person and nature of Jesus Christ. A Church Council was called, at Chalcedon in Asia Minor, in 451, to provide clarity on these debates. The Council produced a statement, the ‘Chalcedonian Definition’ which laid out some boundaries within which any biblically faithful doctrine would need to remain. This is not just ancient history – every mistaken view the Council responded to still has a modern descendant, whether in a cult, a casual assumption, or a well-meaning but confused Christian friend. Getting the answer right is not a matter of winning an academic argument; it is a matter of knowing whether the Jesus you trust can actually save you.
Wrong views of Christ

elements.question: Fully divine, not human.
elements.answer:
Docetism (from dokeo, to seem) taught that Jesus’ physical body was an illusion and that He only appeared to suffer and die. This view denied the reality of Christ’s human nature and His suffering.

  • Chalcedonian response: Jesus is truly human, with a real body and soul.

elements.question: Fully human, not divine.
elements.answer:
Ebionism (from ʾEẇyōnīm meaning the poor/lowly) was an early Jewish-Christian sect. It taught that Jesus was a human who was adopted as the Son of God at His baptism, thus denying His pre-existence and full divinity.

  • Chalcedonian response: Jesus is ‘begotten before all ages of the Father according to the Godhead,’ which clearly affirms His eternal divinity.

elements.question: Not fully God.
elements.answer:
Arianism (originated by Arius of Alexandria) taught that Jesus was a created being and not co-eternal or consubstantial with the Father, i.e. that the Son was subordinate to the Father and not fully divine.

  • Chalcedonian response: Arianism was primarily addressed by the Council of Nicaea (AD 325), but the Chalcedonian Definition also indirectly responds by affirming Christ’s full divinity and consubstantiality with the Father.

elements.question:
Not fully human.
(Human body & soul, divine mind)
elements.answer:
Apollinarianism (originated by Apollinaris of Laodicea) taught that Jesus had a human body and a human soul, but not a human mind. Instead, the divine Logos took the place of the human mind in Christ. Apollinarianism wanted to safeguard the unity of Christ’s person – but it did so at the unacceptable cost of denying His full humanity.

  • Chalcedonian response: Jesus is ‘perfect in Godhead and also perfect in manhood; truly God and truly man, of a reasonable soul and body.’

elements.question: Two persons, two natures.
elements.answer:
Nestorianism (originated by Nestorius of Constantinople) separated the human and the divine in Christ. It essentially taught that there were two separate persons in Christ – one divine and one human. Nestorius argued against using the title Theotokos (“God-bearer”) for Mary. He preferred Christotokos (“Christ-bearer”), implying that Mary gave birth to the human Jesus but not the divine Logos.

  • Chalcedonian response: Jesus is one person with two natures, fully united without division.

elements.question: One person, one nature.
elements.answer:
Eutychianism (originated by Eutyches of Constantinople) taught that Christ had only one nature, and that his nature was a mixture of human and divine. Eutychianism is also known as monophysitism, from monos (single) and physis (nature).

  • Chalcedonian response: Jesus exists in two natures, ‘without confusion, without change, without division, without separation.’ This maintains the full integrity and distinctiveness of both the divine and human natures.

elements.text:
Notice how each error, in trying to solve one puzzle about Jesus, ends up breaking something essential about the good news.

  • Deny His full humanity (like Docetism or Apollinarianism) and the cross becomes theatre, not a real death for real sin.
  • Deny His full deity (like Arianism or Ebionism) and you’re left with a wonderful man who simply isn’t strong enough to save you.
  • Split Him into two separate persons (like Nestorianism) and you lose the wonder of God Himself entering our suffering.
  • Blend His natures into one confused mixture (like Eutychianism) and He ends up neither fully God nor fully man – a third, unrecognisable thing.

elements.question: Which of these mistaken views do you recognise – even in a vague or unnamed form – from something you’ve heard before, whether from another religion, a cult, or simply a casual assumption among Christians?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Write down your thoughts...

elements.text: Summary of the Chalcedonian Definition
Having named the errors, the Council then stated, positively and carefully, what the Bible actually teaches about who Jesus is. Read the summary slowly. Each line was fought for.

• Jesus Christ is perfect in both His divinity and His humanity.
  • He is truly God and truly man, with a rational soul and human body.
  • He is of the same substance (‘consubstantial’) with the Father in His divinity.
  • He is consubstantial with us in His humanity, in all things like us except sin.
  • He was begotten of the Father before all ages according to His divinity.
  • He was born of the Virgin Mary, the mother of God, according to His humanity.
  • He is recognised in two natures: both divine and human.
  • These two natures co-exist in him, the one person, without confusion, change, division, or separation.
  • The distinction of natures is not abolished by their union.
  • Instead, the properties of each nature are preserved.
  • Both natures concur in one Person and one Subsistence (being).
  • Jesus Christ is not divided into two persons but is one.

elements.question: Read through that summary again. Which line did you find hardest to picture or explain in your own words?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Write down your thoughts...

elements.text: Full Text of the Chalcedonian Definition

elements.question: The summary above is drawn from this fuller, historic statement of the Council. It is dense, careful, ancient language – read it slowly, more than once if needed.
elements.answer:
Therefore, following the holy fathers, we all with one accord teach men to acknowledge one and the same Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, at once complete in Godhead and complete in manhood, truly God and truly man, consisting also of a reasonable soul and body; of one substance with the Father as regards his Godhead, and at the same time of one substance with us as regards his manhood; like us in all respects, apart from sin; as regards his Godhead, begotten of the Father before the ages, but yet as regards his manhood begotten, for us men and for our salvation, of Mary the Virgin, the God-bearer; one and the same Christ, Son, Lord, Only-begotten, recognised in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation; the distinction of natures being in no way annulled by the union, but rather the characteristics of each nature being preserved and coming together to form one person and subsistence, not as parted or separated into two persons, but one and the same Son and Only-begotten God the Word, Lord Jesus Christ; even as the prophets from earliest times spoke of him, and our Lord Jesus Christ himself taught us, and the creed of the fathers has handed down to us.


(source ↗)

elements.text: Before Tanko could trust the church fathers’ careful wording, he needed to see it for himself in Scripture. That’s the aim of the next section – not to accept the doctrine because a council said so, but because the Bible itself teaches it.
Biblical Background to the Chalcedonian Definition

Here are a series of statements from the Chalcedonian Definition, coupled with a list of Bible verses. Look up each verse and see what you can learn from it about Christology. To what extent does each verse support the Chalcedonian understanding of Christology?
1. Jesus is ’perfect in Godhead’ and ’truly God’?

elements.passageText:
6 For a child has been born to us,
a son has been given to us.
He shoulders responsibility
and is called:
Extraordinary Strategist,
Mighty God,
Everlasting Father,
Prince of Peace.

elements.question: How does this verse support that point that Jesus is ’perfect in Godhead’ and ’truly God’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Isaiah names this coming child, this "son... given to us," with titles that no mere human ruler could bear — "Mighty God" applies the very word for God directly to him, not as a comparison but as a title of identity. "Everlasting Father" adds an eternal quality no created being possesses. The prophecy describes a human birth ("a child has been born") while simultaneously ascribing divine names to that child, which is exactly the paradox Chalcedon later insisted on holding together: this is a real human birth, yet the one born already bears titles proper to God alone. The text does not soften "Mighty God" into a lesser sense; it stands alongside "Prince of Peace" as one of his given names.
elements.questionHint: What kind of being is normally addressed by the title "Mighty God" — and what does it mean that this title is given to a child who has just been "born"?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was fully God. ... <sup>14</sup> Now the Word became flesh and took up residence among us. We saw his glory – the glory of the one and only, full of grace and truth, who came from the Father.

elements.question: How do these verses support that point that Jesus is ’perfect in Godhead’ and ’truly God’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John does not say the Word was merely "godly" or "like God" — he was "fully God," even while existing distinctly "with God." That phrase holds together both identity and personal distinction from the Father in a single verse. Verse 14 then reports that this same Word, without ceasing to be who he was, "became flesh" — the eternal, fully divine Word entered human existence and could be seen: "we saw his glory." The glory John describes is not a borrowed or reflected glory but "the glory of the one and only," which only makes sense if the one who became flesh was truly God to begin with.
elements.questionHint: John says the Word "was with God" and also "was fully God" in the same sentence — what does holding both together rule out?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> who though he existed in the form of God did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, <sup>7</sup> but emptied himself by taking on the form of a slave, by looking like other men, and by sharing in human nature.

elements.question: How do these verses support that point that Jesus is ’perfect in Godhead’ and ’truly God’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's starting point is that Christ already "existed in the form of God" before anything else described in the passage happens — his deity is the given, not the achieved. "Equality with God" is treated as something already his by nature, something he did not need to "grasp" or seize because it was already true of him; this is the opposite of someone striving upward toward divinity. What follows — he "emptied himself," taking "the form of a slave" — is described as a movement from an already-possessed divine status, not the promotion of a human being into deity. The passage only makes sense as a real self-emptying if what was there beforehand was full deity.
elements.questionHint: Paul says Christ did not need to "grasp" at equality with God — what does that imply about whether he already possessed it?

elements.passageText: 15 He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation, 16 for all things in heaven and on earth were created by him – all things, whether visible or invisible, whether thrones or dominions, whether principalities or powers – all things were created through him and for him.

elements.question: How does this verse support that point that Jesus is ’perfect in Godhead’ and ’truly God’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul piles up universal language here — "all things," "whether visible or invisible," thrones, dominions, powers — to make clear there is no category of created reality that falls outside what Christ made. The passage says these things "were created through him and for him," placing Christ on the giving side of creation rather than the receiving side; he is the reason things exist, not one more thing that exists. Since Scripture elsewhere insists only God creates, a being who is himself the agent and the goal of "all things" cannot belong to the class of things he made — he stands on the Creator's side of the Creator/creature line, which is exactly what it means to be truly God.
elements.questionHint: The verse says all things were made "through him and for him" — can the one who is the reason all things exist also be one of the things that exists?

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> For in him all the fullness of deity lives in bodily form,

elements.question: How does this verse support that point that Jesus is ’perfect in Godhead’ and ’truly God’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This is about as direct a statement as Scripture makes: not a portion, spark, or reflection of God dwells in Christ, but "all the fullness of deity" — the complete divine nature, without remainder. Paul insists this fullness lives "in bodily form," meaning it is not held at a distance from the man Jesus but actually resident in a real human body. The verse resists two errors at once: it will not let Jesus be merely divine-adjacent, and it will not let his deity be diluted or partial because it is housed in flesh. Whatever "bodily form" means for how deity and humanity relate, the deity itself is described as complete.
elements.questionHint: Paul doesn't say "some" or "a measure of" deity dwells in Christ — what does the word "fullness" rule out?

elements.passageText: <sup>13</sup> as we wait for the happy fulfillment of our hope in the glorious appearing of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ.

elements.question: How does this verse support that point that Jesus is ’perfect in Godhead’ and ’truly God’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The grammar of the verse joins "our great God" and "Savior" under a single reference to one person, Jesus Christ — it is not describing the appearing of God the Father and, separately, the Savior Jesus, but a single "glorious appearing" of one who is called both. Paul is comfortable calling the very person Christians hope to see returning "God" without qualification, "great God" no less, in the same breath as "Savior." The verse gives no indication that "God" here is a lesser or figurative title; it is bound to the same referent as Savior, Jesus Christ.
elements.questionHint: Look at how "our great God" and "Savior" are connected to a single name, "Jesus Christ" — are these two different persons appearing, or one?

elements.passageText:
8 but of the Son he says,
“Your throne, O God, is forever and ever,
and a righteous scepter is the scepter of your kingdom.

elements.question: How does this verse support that point that Jesus is ’perfect in Godhead’ and ’truly God’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: What makes this verse remarkable is who is speaking to whom: the passage has the Father himself addressing the Son directly with the word "God" — "of the Son he says, 'Your throne, O God...'" This is not the church or an apostle calling Jesus God; it is God the Father applying that title to the Son. And the throne described is eternal, "forever and ever," matching a kingdom that never ends rather than a temporary or delegated rule. If the Father can rightly call the Son "God" and ascribe to him an everlasting throne, the Son shares the divine nature and rule that belongs to God alone.
elements.questionHint: Notice who is doing the speaking in this verse — whose words are these, and to whom are they addressed as "God"?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> From Simeon Peter, a slave and apostle of Jesus Christ, to those who through the righteousness of our God and Savior, Jesus Christ, have been granted a faith just as precious as ours.

elements.question: How does this verse support that point that Jesus is ’perfect in Godhead’ and ’truly God’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: As in Titus, the phrase "our God and Savior, Jesus Christ" links two titles to one name in a single construction, so the sentence is naming one person, not two. Peter is writing to those who received their faith "through the righteousness of our God and Savior, Jesus Christ" — the righteousness in view is Christ's own righteousness, credited to a person Peter does not hesitate to call "God" in the same phrase. Peter, a Jewish apostle steeped in strict monotheism, uses this language for Jesus without any sense that he is compromising the oneness of God, which only works if Jesus truly shares the divine identity.
elements.questionHint: The phrase "our God and Savior, Jesus Christ" names one person with two titles — what would it mean if Peter thought Jesus were only the second one?

elements.text: 2. Jesus is ’perfect in manhood’ and ’truly man’?

Some of the most moving evidence for Christ’s real, full humanity is found not in grand theological statements, but in small, ordinary human details: Jesus grows tired, grieves, gets hungry, weeps at a friend’s grave. These are not embarrassing details for Christian faith to explain away – they are essential to it.

elements.passageText: <sup>52</sup> And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature, and in favor with God and with people.

elements.question: How does this verse support that point that Jesus is ’perfect in manhood’ and ’truly man’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Growth is exactly what this verse describes — Jesus "increased" over time, in wisdom, in physical stature, and even "in favor with God and with people." An unchanging divine nature does not increase in wisdom or grow taller; growth belongs to finite, developing creatures. Luke is reporting ordinary human development: a mind that learned and matured, a body that grew from childhood toward adulthood, exactly as any real child does. The verse doesn't hint that this growth was staged or apparent — it simply narrates the normal course of human maturing, which is only possible if Jesus possessed an actual human nature that developed the way human natures do.
elements.questionHint: What does the word "increased" tell you about the kind of nature that experiences growth over time — is that true of unchanging deity?

elements.passageText: <sup>24</sup> And a great storm developed on the sea so that the waves began to swamp the boat. But he was asleep.

elements.question: How does this verse support that point that Jesus is ’perfect in manhood’ and ’truly man’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: A raging storm was swamping the boat, yet Jesus "was asleep" through it — a small detail, but a telling one. Sleep is not something deity experiences; it belongs to a body that gets tired and a mind that needs rest, the ordinary limitations of a physical human nature. Matthew doesn't explain this away or suggest it was feigned; he simply records it alongside the danger of the storm as a plain fact about Jesus in that moment. That he could be genuinely, deeply asleep in the middle of a life-threatening storm shows a real human body subject to real human fatigue.
elements.questionHint: What basic human need does sleep meet, and what does it say about Jesus that he needed it badly enough to sleep through a storm?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> Jacob’s well was there, so Jesus, since he was tired from the journey, sat right down beside the well. It was about noon.

elements.question: How does this verse support that point that Jesus is ’perfect in manhood’ and ’truly man’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John notes the ordinary cause and effect of a long walk: Jesus was "tired from the journey," and so he "sat right down beside the well." This is not symbolic language; it's the same fatigue anyone would feel after traveling on foot, and it produced the same response anyone would have — needing to sit and rest. The detail "it was about noon" even situates the tiredness in the heat of the day, reinforcing that this is a physically embodied person affected by real conditions like sun, distance, and time. A nature that cannot tire would have no need to sit down.
elements.questionHint: What everyday physical cause does John give for Jesus needing to sit down, and what kind of nature is subject to that cause?

elements.passageText: <sup>35</sup> Jesus wept.

elements.question: How does this verse support that point that Jesus is ’perfect in manhood’ and ’truly man’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This is the shortest sentence in the passage for a reason — it states a single, unadorned fact: Jesus wept. Not that he appeared to weep, or performed grief for the crowd's benefit, but that real tears came, in response to real loss, at the tomb of a friend he loved. Weeping is a human emotional and physical response tied to grief and a body capable of crying. The brevity of the statement makes it hard to explain away as theater; it reads as the plain, raw reaction of someone who genuinely grieved.
elements.questionHint: What does actual weeping require — both emotionally and physically — that mere appearance or performance would not?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James, Joses, Judas, and Simon? And aren’t his sisters here with us?” And so they took offense at him.

elements.question: How does this verse support that point that Jesus is ’perfect in manhood’ and ’truly man’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The whole force of this verse comes from the townspeople's familiarity with Jesus as an ordinary man: they know him as "the carpenter," they can name his mother and his brothers and sisters by name, and it is precisely this ordinariness that causes them to "take offense" at him. Nobody stumbles over someone they've never met claiming greatness; they stumble over the neighbor whose family, trade, and upbringing they've watched firsthand. The verse assumes Jesus grew up in a real household, learned a real trade, and had real siblings — an entirely unremarkable human biography that made his later claims hard for his hometown to accept.
elements.questionHint: Why would people who know Jesus's trade and his family by name be the ones most likely to "take offense" — what does their familiarity assume about his upbringing?

elements.passageText: <sup>12</sup> Now the next day, as they went out from Bethany, he was hungry.

elements.question: How does this verse support that point that Jesus is ’perfect in manhood’ and ’truly man’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The verse offers no elaborate theology here, just a simple physical fact recorded in passing: as Jesus and the disciples left Bethany, "he was hungry." Hunger is the body's ordinary signal that it needs food to keep functioning, and Mark reports it the same way he would report it of any of the disciples walking beside him. There is nothing in the text suggesting this hunger was symbolic or staged for effect; it is presented as the plain reason he then goes looking for fruit on the fig tree in the following verses. A nature immune to physical need would have no reason to feel hunger at all.
elements.questionHint: What bodily need is Mark describing, and what does needing food say about the kind of nature Jesus had at that moment?

elements.passageText: <sup>26:38</sup> Then he said to them, “My soul is deeply grieved, even to the point of death. Remain here and stay awake with me.” ... <sup>22:44</sup> And in his anguish he prayed more earnestly, and his sweat was like drops of blood falling to the ground.

elements.question: How do these verses support that point that Jesus is ’perfect in manhood’ and ’truly man’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: These two verses together describe an anguish that is both emotional and physical. Matthew has Jesus say his "soul is deeply grieved, even to the point of death" — language of overwhelming inner sorrow, not mild discomfort. Luke then describes the bodily toll of that anguish: praying "more earnestly," with sweat falling "like drops of blood." Whether or not this was literal blood, the image is of a body under such intense strain that it produced something resembling blood loss. Together the verses show a real human psyche capable of being crushed by dread and a real human body that manifested that dread physically — not a mere show of suffering, but suffering that reached soul and skin alike.
elements.questionHint: Luke doesn't just describe emotional distress in words — what physical detail does he add about Jesus's sweat, and what does that suggest about the intensity of the anguish?

elements.question: Why does it matter for your own faith that Jesus grew tired, felt hunger, and wept – rather than simply appearing to?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Write down your thoughts...

elements.text: 3. Jesus has ’a reasonable soul and body’?

elements.passageText: <sup>38</sup> Then he said to them, “My soul is deeply grieved, even to the point of death. Remain here and stay awake with me.”

elements.question: How does this verse support the point about Jesus having ’a reasonable soul and body’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The key word here is "soul" — Jesus does not simply say his body is in pain, he says his soul is "deeply grieved, even to the point of death." This locates the anguish in an inner, rational, human faculty of thought and feeling, not merely in physical nerves. Against any view that Christ was simply a divine mind operating a human body like a shell, this verse shows an actual human soul experiencing grief so real it is described as death-level. A body alone cannot be "grieved" in this sense — grief belongs to a thinking, feeling soul, which is exactly the human faculty some early heresies denied Christ possessed.
elements.questionHint: What part of a person is doing the grieving here — the body, or something else the verse specifically names?

elements.passageText: <sup>39</sup> Look at my hands and my feet; it’s me! Touch me and see; a ghost does not have flesh and bones like you see I have.” <sup>40</sup> When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet.

elements.question: How do these verses support the point about Jesus having ’a reasonable soul and body’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus is explicitly ruling out the idea that he is a spirit or apparition: "a ghost does not have flesh and bones like you see I have." He invites the disciples to verify this with touch — "touch me and see" — appealing to the most basic physical test available, tangible bone and flesh under their hands. He then backs the words with action, showing them "his hands and his feet." The passage is aimed directly at any suggestion that what they were seeing was an illusion or a purely spiritual appearance; it insists on a real, physical, touchable body as part of who the risen Jesus is.
elements.questionHint: What test does Jesus offer the disciples to prove he isn't a ghost, and why would a ghost fail that test but a real body pass it?

elements.passageText: <sup>27</sup> “Now my soul is greatly distressed. And what should I say? ‘Father, deliver me from this hour’? No, but for this very reason I have come to this hour.

elements.question: How does this verse support the point about Jesus having ’a reasonable soul and body’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus names the seat of his turmoil precisely: "my soul is greatly distressed." He then voices, as a real question he considers and sets aside, whether to ask the Father to "deliver me from this hour" — that back-and-forth of considering an appeal and then refusing it ("but for this very reason I have come to this hour") is the activity of a genuinely deliberating human mind and will, wrestling with what lies ahead and choosing to press on anyway. This is not the operation of a divine nature merely inhabiting flesh; it is the sound of an actual human soul working through dread toward resolve.
elements.questionHint: Jesus considers asking to be delivered and then decides against it — what kind of internal process is that "considering," and what part of him does he say is doing it?

elements.passageText: 14 Therefore, since the children share in flesh and blood, he likewise shared in their humanity, so that through death he could destroy the one who holds the power of death (that is, the devil), 15 and set free those who were held in slavery all their lives by their fear of death.

elements.question: How does this verse support the point about Jesus having ’a reasonable soul and body’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The writer's logic depends entirely on Jesus possessing a genuine human nature: "since the children share in flesh and blood, he likewise shared in their humanity." The word "likewise" insists his humanity matches theirs in kind, not in appearance only. And the reason given is functional — it was precisely by sharing real human flesh and blood that he "could... destroy" the devil "through death," since only a nature capable of dying could undergo death for others. If Jesus's humanity were only apparent, he could not truly die, and the whole purpose described here — breaking the devil's power over death and freeing those enslaved by fear of it — would collapse.
elements.questionHint: The verse says Jesus shared humanity so that "through death" he could accomplish something — what does that require him to be actually capable of doing?

elements.text: 4. Jesus is ’consubstantial with the Father according to the Godhead’?

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup> So he told them, “My Father is working until now, and I too am working.” <sup>18</sup> For this reason the Jewish leaders were trying even harder to kill him, because not only was he breaking the Sabbath, but he was also calling God his own Father, thus making himself equal with God.

elements.question: How do these verses support the point about Jesus being ’consubstantial with the Father according to the Godhead’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The verse tells us exactly how Jesus's original audience understood his words, and it wasn't a misunderstanding the text corrects. Jesus says simply, "My Father is working until now, and I too am working," but John explains the leaders' furious reaction: they saw him "calling God his own Father, thus making himself equal with God." The claim to a unique, personal sonship — "his own Father," not merely a general fatherhood over all people — was heard as a direct claim to divine equality, and John records that reaction without correcting it as a misreading. That is significant testimony to what Jesus's language actually implied.
elements.questionHint: John explains why the leaders wanted him dead — what specific claim did they hear in Jesus calling God "his own Father"?

elements.passageText: <sup>30</sup> The Father and I are one.”

elements.question: How does this verse support the point about Jesus being ’consubstantial with the Father according to the Godhead’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: In just five words, Jesus asserts a oneness with the Father that goes beyond mere agreement or shared purpose — in context he has just spoken of no one being able to snatch his sheep from the Father's hand, and now his own, treating his hand and the Father's hand as effectively the same protecting power. "One" here functions as a claim to shared identity and authority, which is why, in the verses immediately following, his hearers pick up stones, understanding him to be "making yourself God." The verse itself doesn't qualify "one" as merely relational; it stands as a bare statement of unity between Father and Son.
elements.questionHint: Given how the crowd reacts right after this statement (attempting to stone him), what kind of "oneness" did they understand Jesus to be claiming — unity of will, or something more?

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> Jesus replied, “Have I been with you for so long, and you have not known me, Philip? The person who has seen me has seen the Father! How can you say, ‘Show us the Father’? <sup>10</sup> Do you not believe that I am in the Father, and the Father is in me? The words that I say to you, I do not speak on my own initiative, but the Father residing in me performs his miraculous deeds.

elements.question: How do these verses support the point about Jesus being ’consubstantial with the Father according to the Godhead’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus's answer to Philip is startlingly direct: "The person who has seen me has seen the Father!" He is not saying he resembles the Father or represents him well, but that seeing him is, in effect, seeing the Father — a claim that only works if Father and Son share one divine nature. He grounds this in mutual indwelling, "I am in the Father, and the Father is in me," and even attributes his own works to the Father acting through him: "the Father residing in me performs his miraculous deeds." The unity described is not cooperation between two separate beings but an interpenetration proper to persons who share the same essence.
elements.questionHint: Jesus says seeing him is the same as seeing the Father — what would have to be true about their natures for that claim to be more than a figure of speech?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> The Son is the radiance of his glory and the representation of his essence, and he sustains all things by his powerful word, and so when he had accomplished cleansing for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high .

elements.question: How does this verse support the point about Jesus being ’consubstantial with the Father according to the Godhead’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The phrase "representation of his essence" is doing heavy theological work — the underlying term means something like an exact imprint, the way a seal leaves its precise shape in wax. The Son is not a symbol pointing to God's essence from outside it; he bears that essence stamped through, sharing the very substance the image represents. Paired with "radiance of his glory," which pictures light streaming from its source while remaining of one nature with it, the verse describes a Son who is not a lesser or derivative being but one who possesses, unaltered, the same essence as the Father he radiates from.
elements.questionHint: Think about what a "representation" or exact imprint of something's essence would have to share with the original — a resemblance, or the substance itself?

elements.passageText: <sup>20</sup> And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us insight to know him who is true, and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. This one is the true God and eternal life.

elements.question: How does this verse support the point about Jesus being ’consubstantial with the Father according to the Godhead’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John traces a careful chain in this verse — the Son of God has come, has given "insight to know him who is true," and believers are "in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ" — and then closes with a statement whose most natural referent is Jesus himself: "This one is the true God and eternal life." John, writing to guard against teaching that diminished who Jesus was, does not hesitate to apply the title "the true God" directly to the Son, alongside calling him "eternal life" itself, not merely the giver of it. The verse identifies Jesus's very being with the true God the Father has revealed.
elements.questionHint: Trace the pronoun "this one" back through the sentence — whom does it most naturally refer to, and what title does it then apply to him?

elements.passageText: <sup>1:8</sup> “I am the Alpha and the Omega,” says the Lord God – the one who is, and who was, and who is still to come – the All-Powerful! ... <sup>22:12</sup> (Look! I am coming soon, and my reward is with me to pay each one according to what he has done! <sup>13</sup> I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end!) <sup>14</sup> Blessed are those who wash their robes so they can have access to the tree of life and can enter into the city by the gates. <sup>15</sup> Outside are the dogs and the sorcerers and the sexually immoral, and the murderers, and the idolaters and everyone who loves and practices falsehood! <sup>16</sup> “I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify to you about these things for the churches. I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star!”

elements.question: How do these verses support the point about Jesus being ’consubstantial with the Father according to the Godhead’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Revelation 1:8 puts the title "Alpha and Omega... the All-Powerful" in the mouth of "the Lord God" — language of absolute, eternal sovereignty over all history, beginning to end. Then in chapter 22, the speaker who says "I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end" identifies himself two verses later by name: "I, Jesus... I am the root and the descendant of David." The same exalted divine title given to "the Lord God" in chapter 1 is claimed by Jesus himself in chapter 22, with no sense that he is borrowing or diminishing it. Jesus applies to himself the identity marker Revelation reserves for God alone.
elements.questionHint: Compare who is speaking in 1:8 ("the Lord God") with who says almost the identical words in 22:13 and then names himself in 22:16 — what does that overlap tell you?

elements.text: 5. Jesus is ’consubstantial with us according to the manhood; in all things like unto us, without sin’?

elements.passageText: <sup>14</sup> Therefore, since the children share in flesh and blood, he likewise shared in their humanity, so that through death he could destroy the one who holds the power of death (that is, the devil) ... <sup>17</sup> Therefore he had to be made like his brothers and sisters in every respect, so that he could become a merciful and faithful high priest in things relating to God, to make atonement for the sins of the people.

elements.question: How do these verses support the point about Jesus being ’consubstantial with us according to the manhood; in all things like unto us, without sin’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The phrase "in every respect" is the crucial one — the writer does not qualify or limit how far Jesus's likeness to us goes. He "shared in flesh and blood" just as "the children" do, and he "had to be made like his brothers and sisters in every respect" in order to function as "a merciful and faithful high priest." The purpose clause matters: his qualification to represent humanity before God, to "make atonement for the sins of the people," depends on genuinely sharing our nature, not approximating it. A partial or merely apparent humanity could not do the priestly work this passage describes.
elements.questionHint: The verse says Jesus was made like us "in every respect" — what job requires that completeness, and why would a partial likeness fail to qualify him for it?

elements.passageText: <sup>15</sup> For we do not have a high priest incapable of sympathizing with our weaknesses, but one who has been tempted in every way just as we are, yet without sin.

elements.question: How does this verse support the point about Jesus being ’consubstantial with us according to the manhood; in all things like unto us, without sin’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This verse holds two things together without letting either erode the other. Jesus was "tempted in every way just as we are" — real, full-strength temptation, matching human experience exactly, not a watered-down version he could easily brush off. And yet he was "without sin" — the temptation never once produced the fall it aims at. The verse's whole comfort ("sympathizing with our weaknesses") depends on both halves being true: if the temptation weren't real, he couldn't sympathize with us; if it had ever succeeded, he couldn't save us. He is like us in the trial, unlike us in the outcome.
elements.questionHint: The verse says Jesus was tempted "just as we are" and yet without sin — why does his sympathy for us depend on the temptation being real rather than just for show?

elements.passageText: ... <sup>1:19</sup> but by precious blood like that of an unblemished and spotless lamb, namely Christ. ... <sup>2:22</sup> He committed no sin nor was deceit found in his mouth.

elements.question: How do these verses support the point about Jesus being ’consubstantial with us according to the manhood; in all things like unto us, without sin’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter uses sacrificial language to describe Christ's moral purity — "an unblemished and spotless lamb" echoes the Old Testament requirement that offerings be physically without defect, applied here to Jesus's moral condition. That qualifies him as an acceptable, valid sacrifice; a flawed lamb could not be offered. The second verse makes the same point in plain moral terms: "He committed no sin nor was deceit found in his mouth" — not only no sinful act, but not even hidden deceit in his speech. Together the verses describe someone who was, in actual conduct and character, exactly what humanity was supposed to be but consistently fails to be.
elements.questionHint: Why would an "unblemished and spotless" lamb be required for a sacrifice to work, and what does applying that image to Jesus say about the completeness of his sinlessness?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> And you know that Jesus was revealed to take away sins, and in him there is no sin.

elements.question: How does this verse support the point about Jesus being ’consubstantial with us according to the manhood; in all things like unto us, without sin’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John ties Jesus's mission directly to his moral condition: he "was revealed to take away sins," and the reason that mission works is stated immediately after — "in him there is no sin." Someone who needed his own sins dealt with could not simultaneously take away the sins of others; the verse's logic requires that the one doing the removing stand entirely outside the problem he's removing. John states this as a flat fact about Jesus's character, not an ideal he approximated — "in him there is no sin," present and total, which is what makes him able to accomplish what he came to do.
elements.questionHint: Why would Jesus need to have "no sin" himself in order to be the one who "takes away sins" for others?

elements.question: Hebrews 4:15 says Jesus can sympathise with our weaknesses because He was tempted in every way, yet without sin. Where in your life right now do you most need a Saviour who understands, from the inside, what you’re facing?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Write down your thoughts...

elements.text: 6. Jesus was ’begotten before all ages of the Father according to the Godhead’?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was fully God. <sup>2</sup> The Word was with God in the beginning.

elements.question: How do these verses support the point about Jesus being ’begotten before all ages of the Father according to the Godhead’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John pushes the Word's existence back before any starting point we could name: "in the beginning was the Word" — not "in the beginning God made the Word," but the Word already existing when "the beginning" occurred. Verse 2 repeats it for emphasis: "The Word was with God in the beginning," underscoring that there was no point at which the Word came into being alongside the created order. This is what "begotten before all ages" means — not a birth within time, like the incarnation later in the chapter, but an eternal relationship that has no beginning at all, since the Word already was when time itself began.
elements.questionHint: John says the Word already "was" when "the beginning" happened — does that leave room for a moment when the Word did not yet exist?

elements.passageText: <sup>58</sup> Jesus said to them, “I tell you the solemn truth, before Abraham came into existence, I am!”

elements.question: How does this verse support the point about Jesus being ’begotten before all ages of the Father according to the Godhead’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus's grammar here is deliberately jarring: he doesn't say "before Abraham was, I was," matching tense for tense, but "before Abraham came into existence, I am" — a timeless present set against a datable past event. That phrasing echoes God's self-identification to Moses, "I AM," and Jesus applies it to his own existence relative to a man who lived centuries earlier. The claim is not merely that he existed before Abraham chronologically, but that he exists in a manner that doesn't fit ordinary sequence at all — a mode of being appropriate to the eternal Son, "begotten... before all ages," rather than to any creature born in time.
elements.questionHint: Why does Jesus say "I am" instead of "I was" when comparing himself to a man who lived long before him — what does the tense itself suggest about his existence?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> And now, Father, glorify me at your side with the glory I had with you before the world was created.

elements.question: How does this verse support the point about Jesus being ’begotten before all ages of the Father according to the Godhead’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus asks to be restored to something he already possessed, not something new — "the glory I had with you before the world was created." That phrase places his glory, shared personally with the Father ("with you"), at a point prior to the existence of the created order itself. This is not language a creature could use of itself; no created being can speak of a glory it held "before the world was created," since creatures come into being along with or after the world. The prayer assumes an eternal, pre-creation relationship between the Son and the Father that the incarnation temporarily veiled and that Jesus now asks to have openly restored.
elements.questionHint: Jesus asks for glory he "had" before creation — what does that claim assume about his existence relative to the world's beginning?

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup> He himself is before all things and all things are held together in him.

elements.question: How does this verse support the point about Jesus being ’begotten before all ages of the Father according to the Godhead’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: "Before all things" is a claim of absolute priority — not merely earlier than other created things, but prior to "all things" as a category, which places Christ outside the created order entirely rather than merely first within it. The verse then adds a present, ongoing role: "all things are held together in him," meaning creation's continued coherence depends on him right now, not just at its origin. A being who precedes everything and currently sustains everything cannot himself be one of the "things" he precedes and sustains — this is exactly the eternal, uncreated priority meant by his being begotten of the Father before all ages.
elements.questionHint: The verse says Christ is "before all things" — can something that exists before everything also be counted as one of the things that came into existence?

elements.text: 7. Jesus was ’born of the Virgin Mary, the mother of God, according to the manhood’?

elements.passageText: <sup>18</sup> Now the birth of Jesus Christ happened this way. While his mother Mary was engaged to Joseph, but before they came together, she was found to be pregnant through the Holy Spirit. <sup>19</sup> Because Joseph, her husband to be, was a righteous man, and because he did not want to disgrace her, he intended to divorce her privately. <sup>20</sup> When he had contemplated this, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream and said, “Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife, because the child conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. <sup>21</sup> She will give birth to a son and you will name him Jesus, because he will save his people from their sins.” <sup>22</sup> This all happened so that what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet would be fulfilled: <sup>23</sup> “ Look! The virgin will conceive and bear a son, and they will call him Emmanuel ,” which means “ God with us .” <sup>24</sup> When Joseph awoke from sleep he did what the angel of the Lord told him. He took his wife, <sup>25</sup> but did not have marital relations with her until she gave birth to a son, whom he named Jesus.

elements.question: How do these verses support the point about Jesus being ’born of the Virgin Mary, the mother of God, according to the manhood’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This passage narrates an actual, real birth with real historical particulars — an engagement, a pregnancy discovered before marriage, a troubled fiancé considering a quiet divorce, an angel's intervention. It states plainly that Mary "was found to be pregnant through the Holy Spirit," meaning the conception had a divine origin even though the birth itself, and Mary's motherhood, were entirely real and human. The passage explicitly ties this event to the prophecy that "the virgin will conceive and bear a son... Emmanuel... God with us," binding together a genuine human birth from a genuine human mother with the presence of God himself in the child born. Mary is truly the mother of the one who is "God with us" — the child she bore in the ordinary way mothers bear children was, in fact, God incarnate.
elements.questionHint: The angel names the child "Emmanuel," meaning "God with us" — what does that name claim about the identity of the baby Mary was carrying and gave birth to in the ordinary way?

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup> As they came into the house and saw the child with Mary his mother, they bowed down and worshiped him. They opened their treasure boxes and gave him gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh.

elements.question: How does this verse support the point about Jesus being ’born of the Virgin Mary, the mother of God, according to the manhood’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The wise men find exactly what you would expect to find visiting a newborn: "the child with Mary his mother" — an ordinary domestic scene of infant and mother. Yet their response to this scene is worship: they "bowed down and worshiped him," an act reserved for deity, not merely royalty. The passage places these two facts side by side without tension: a real infant with his real mother, and worship due to God. The Magi's action assumes that the child in Mary's arms, however ordinary the scene looked, was one who could rightly receive worship — God present in genuine human infancy, born of a genuine human mother.
elements.questionHint: The wise men see an ordinary scene — a child with his mother — but respond with worship rather than mere admiration. What does their response assume about who that child is?

elements.passageText: <sup>30</sup> So the angel said to her, “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God! <sup>31</sup> Listen: You will become pregnant and give birth to a son, and you will name him Jesus. <sup>32</sup> He will be great, and will be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give him the throne of his father David. <sup>33</sup> He will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and his kingdom will never end.” <sup>34</sup> Mary said to the angel, “How will this be, since I have not had sexual relations with a man?” <sup>35</sup> The angel replied, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the child to be born will be holy; he will be called the Son of God.

elements.question: How do these verses support the point about Jesus being ’born of the Virgin Mary, the mother of God, according to the manhood’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Gabriel's announcement joins a genuinely human process to a uniquely divine cause. Mary asks the entirely reasonable human question, "How will this be, since I have not had sexual relations with a man?" — assuming the pregnancy would otherwise require ordinary conception. Gabriel's answer supplies the exception: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you," so that the one born will be, from the very moment of conception, "the Son of God." Mary is not made pregnant with a mere human being who is later adopted into divine sonship; the child conceived in her by the Spirit's power is Son of God from the start, while still being the child she herself conceives and bears.
elements.questionHint: Mary asks how this is possible "since I have not had sexual relations with a man" — what answer does Gabriel give, and what title does he say the child born of that will hold from the start?

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup> Today your Savior is born in the city of David. He is Christ the Lord.

elements.question: How does this verse support the point about Jesus being ’born of the Virgin Mary, the mother of God, according to the manhood’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The angel announces an ordinary birth event, "your Savior is born," using the same verb you'd use of any child entering the world, in "the city of David" — a specific, real place. Yet in the very same breath, the child born is identified with three weighty titles: "Savior," "Christ" (the anointed one), and "Lord" — this last term used throughout Luke's Gospel as the equivalent of the divine name. A baby has been born, in the plain, historical sense, and that baby is simultaneously announced as one who bears the title reserved for Israel's God. The birth is real; so is the identity of the one born.
elements.questionHint: The title "Lord" in Luke's Gospel usually points to God himself — what does it mean that this title is applied to a baby who has just been "born"?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> But when the appropriate time had come, God sent out his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, <sup>5</sup> to redeem those who were under the law, so that we may be adopted as sons with full rights.

elements.question: How do these verses support the point about Jesus being ’born of the Virgin Mary, the mother of God, according to the manhood’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's sentence moves in a single breath from eternal sending to human birth: "God sent out his Son, born of a woman, born under the law." The one who is sent already exists as God's Son prior to the sending — you cannot send someone into existence, only into a situation — and yet the sending results in a real, ordinary human birth, "born of a woman," and a real submission to Israel's legal and covenantal obligations, "born under the law." The purpose clause that follows, "to redeem those who were under the law," depends on both halves: he had to be truly born under the law's demands in order to fulfill and redeem those under it, while remaining the Son who was sent.
elements.questionHint: Paul says the Son was "sent" and then "born of a woman" — what does the order of those two phrases tell you about whether his sonship began at birth or existed before it?

elements.text: 8. Jesus was ’acknowledged in two natures, inconfusedly, unchangeably, indivisibly, inseparably’?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was fully God. ... <sup>18</sup> No one has ever seen God. The only one, himself God, who is in closest fellowship with the Father, has made God known.

elements.question: How do these verses support the point about Jesus being ’acknowledged in two natures, inconfusedly, unchangeably, indivisibly, inseparably’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Verse 14 states the union without dissolving either side: "the Word became flesh" — the divine Word, already established in verse 1 as "fully God," now also takes on flesh, real human existence, without the text saying the Word stopped being the Word or the flesh became something other than flesh. Verse 18 then describes the result in a single figure: "the only one, himself God," who nonetheless is "in closest fellowship with the Father" and reveals him from within human history. This is one person who is "himself God" acting through flesh to make God known — divine and human held together, neither erased nor blended into some third thing, in the single act of revealing the Father.
elements.questionHint: Verse 14 says the Word "became flesh" — does becoming flesh mean the Word stopped being the fully divine Word described in verse 1?

elements.passageText: <sup>30</sup> The Father and I are one.

elements.question: How does this verse support the point about Jesus being ’acknowledged in two natures, inconfusedly, unchangeably, indivisibly, inseparably’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This same short statement, "The Father and I are one," also illustrates how thoroughly united Christ's divine nature is with the Father's, even while Jesus remains a distinct speaker addressing the Father as another. The oneness is real and unbroken — not occasional agreement that could come apart — yet it does not erase the "I" who says it, distinct from the "Father" he names. That is the pattern later councils described for the incarnate Christ generally: real, indivisible, inseparable unity that never collapses the distinctness of what is united. Here the distinctness is of persons within the Godhead; the verse shows unity so complete it can be called "one" without either party ceasing to be who they are.
elements.questionHint: Jesus says "we are one," using both a singular claim of unity and a plural reference that keeps two speakers distinct — what does that combination suggest about unity without collapsing distinction?

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> For in him all the fullness of deity lives in bodily form,

elements.question: How does this verse support the point about Jesus being ’acknowledged in two natures, inconfusedly, unchangeably, indivisibly, inseparably’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The verse names two distinct realities and refuses to let either one absorb the other: "the fullness of deity" on one side, "bodily form" on the other, joined by the simple word "in." The deity is not diminished or changed by residing in a body — it remains "all the fullness" — and the bodily form is not swallowed up or dissolved by housing deity; it remains a real body. Yet the verse describes no gap between them either: the fullness of deity presently "lives," continuously, "in bodily form." Full deity and real bodily humanity, together in one subject, neither mixed into something else nor separated from each other.
elements.questionHint: The verse keeps two things distinct — "fullness of deity" and "bodily form" — but joins them with the word "in." What does that wording avoid: either erasing one of them, or keeping them apart?

elements.passageText: <sup>8</sup> Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever!

elements.question: How does this verse support the point about Jesus being ’acknowledged in two natures, inconfusedly, unchangeably, indivisibly, inseparably’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: "The same yesterday and today and forever" asserts an identity that spans every possible division of time without alteration. Whatever changed about Christ's circumstances — pre-incarnate glory, humble birth, earthly ministry, death, resurrection, heavenly exaltation — the writer insists the person himself has not changed across any of it. This is the heart of "unchangeably" applied to the union of his two natures: taking on a human nature did not alter or diminish his divine nature, and his identity as one Christ has remained constant through every stage of that history. He is not a different Christ "today" than "yesterday," nor will he be a different one "forever."
elements.questionHint: The verse spans "yesterday," "today," and "forever" — across all the changes in Christ's circumstances over that span, what does the verse say stayed exactly the same?

elements.text: 9. In Jesus ’the distinction of natures being by no means taken away by the union, but rather the property of each nature being preserved, and concurring in one Person and one Subsistence’?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> And now, Father, glorify me at your side with the glory I had with you before the world was created.

elements.question: How does this verse support the point about ’the distinction of natures being by no means taken away by the union, but rather the property of each nature being preserved, and concurring in one Person and one Subsistence’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Notice who is speaking and how: this is a prayer, an act of dependent asking directed to the Father — a distinctly human posture, since deity as such has no need to request anything. Yet what is being asked for is "the glory I had with you before the world was created" — a claim belonging to his eternal divine nature. In one verse, the properties of both natures show up without being merged: the humbling, petitioning voice belongs to the nature that can pray and wait, while the eternal pre-creation glory belongs to the nature that never lacked it. One person is speaking, but the "I" who prays and the "I" who once held pre-creation glory are the same subject holding two distinct sets of properties together.
elements.questionHint: A prayer is something a dependent person does — but what does Jesus ask the Father for that only an eternal divine nature could have possessed "before the world was created"?

elements.passageText: <sup>2:5</sup> For there is one God and one intermediary between God and humanity, Christ Jesus, himself human ... <sup>3:16</sup> And we all agree, our religion contains amazing revelation: He was revealed in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among Gentiles, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.

elements.question: How do these verses support the point about ’the distinction of natures being by no means taken away by the union, but rather the property of each nature being preserved, and concurring in one Person and one Subsistence’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul calls the one mediator "Christ Jesus, himself human" — his qualification to stand between God and humanity depends on genuinely belonging to the human side, sharing our nature so he can represent us. But the hymn-like statement in 3:16 immediately surrounds that humanity with things no mere human undergoes: "revealed in the flesh" (implying a prior, non-fleshly existence to be revealed from), "seen by angels," "taken up in glory." The same one subject is "himself human" and also the object of a revelation and exaltation that spans heaven and earth. Each nature keeps its own properties — real human mediation, real angelic and heavenly acknowledgment — yet both are said of the single person, Christ Jesus.
elements.questionHint: 3:16 says Christ was "revealed in the flesh" — what does the word "revealed" imply about what existed before it took on flesh, compared to the plain statement in 2:5 that he is "himself human"?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> The Son is the radiance of his glory and the representation of his essence, and he sustains all things by his powerful word, and so when he had accomplished cleansing for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high.

elements.question: How does this verse support the point about ’the distinction of natures being by no means taken away by the union, but rather the property of each nature being preserved, and concurring in one Person and one Subsistence’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This single verse moves fluidly between properties and actions of each nature without confusing them, all said of one subject. "The radiance of his glory and the representation of his essence" describes what belongs to him as fully divine; "sustains all things by his powerful word" is an act of divine, universal power. Then the verse pivots to something only the incarnate mediator could do: "accomplished cleansing for sins," an act tied to his atoning work in human history, after which "he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty" — the language of a completed mission and a granted position. Divine radiance and priestly, historical accomplishment are both true of the very same "he," each property intact, both concurring in one person.
elements.questionHint: The verse moves from "sustains all things" (an act of cosmic power) to "accomplished cleansing for sins" and "sat down" (a completed historical act) — are these two different actors, or one person doing both kinds of things?

elements.text: 10. Jesus is ’not parted or divided into two persons, but one and the same Son, and only begotten, God the Word, the Lord Jesus Christ’?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was fully God. ... <sup>14</sup> Now the Word became flesh and took up residence among us. We saw his glory – the glory of the one and only, full of grace and truth, who came from the Father.

elements.question: How do these verses support the point about Jesus being ’not parted or divided into two persons, but one and the same Son, and only begotten, God the Word, the Lord Jesus Christ’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The grammatical subject never changes across these verses — it is "the Word" in verse 1 who "was God," and it is the very same "the Word" in verse 14 who "became flesh." John does not introduce a second character partway through, as if a human person were joined to or replaced by the divine Word; one continuous subject undergoes the transition described. "We saw his glory" in verse 14 refers back to that same Word now dwelling among us. This is exactly what it means for Christ to be "one and the same Son," not two persons operating side by side but a single divine person who took on human flesh while remaining who he already was.
elements.questionHint: Track the subject "the Word" from verse 1 to verse 14 — does John ever switch to describing a second, separate person, or is it the same subject throughout?

elements.passageText: ... <sup>3</sup> concerning his Son who was a descendant of David with reference to the flesh, <sup>4</sup> who was appointed the Son-of-God-in-power according to the Holy Spirit by the resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord.

elements.question: How do these verses support the point about Jesus being ’not parted or divided into two persons, but one and the same Son, and only begotten, God the Word, the Lord Jesus Christ’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul describes one person, "his Son," under two aspects joined by contrast markers — "with reference to the flesh" he is David's descendant, a real, traceable human lineage; "according to the Holy Spirit" he was "appointed the Son-of-God-in-power" through the resurrection. These are not two different sons or two different individuals, one human and one divine, but a single sentence about a single Son named at the end: "Jesus Christ our Lord." The resurrection did not create a new person or promote a mere man into deity; it powerfully vindicated and displayed the Sonship of the very one who was, all along, also David's human descendant.
elements.questionHint: Paul names one Son twice, "with reference to the flesh" and "according to the Holy Spirit" — is he describing two different sons, or two aspects of the same one, named together as "Jesus Christ our Lord" at the end?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we live, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we live.

elements.question: How does this verse support the point about Jesus being ’not parted or divided into two persons, but one and the same Son, and only begotten, God the Word, the Lord Jesus Christ’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's confession here is carefully numbered: "one God, the Father... and one Lord, Jesus Christ." Jesus is not a lesser, secondary "lord" tacked onto the true God; he is named with the exact same exclusive, singular language — "one" — that monotheistic Judaism reserved for God alone. And the description of his role, "through whom are all things and through whom we live," attributes to this one Lord the same creative and sustaining activity Scripture elsewhere assigns to God. There is a distinction of persons named here — Father and Son are not identical — but no division into rival or competing gods; one Lord, undivided in himself, is confessed alongside one God the Father.
elements.questionHint: Paul uses "one" for both the Father and Jesus Christ — what does applying that same exclusive word to both suggest about dividing Jesus into someone less than fully, singularly Lord?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> one Lord, one faith, one baptism, <sup>6</sup> one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.

elements.question: How do these verses support the point about Jesus being ’not parted or divided into two persons, but one and the same Son, and only begotten, God the Word, the Lord Jesus Christ’?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's rhythm of "one... one... one..." is a confession of undivided unity at every level of Christian faith and worship: one body, one Spirit, one hope, "one Lord" (Christ), "one faith, one baptism," and "one God and Father of all." Placing "one Lord" in the middle of this string, distinct from "one God and Father" yet described with the identical numerical singularity, keeps Christ's Lordship from being fragmented or treated as one option among several. He is not divided into a partial lord alongside other lords; he is confessed as singularly, wholly "one Lord," in the same breath as the oneness of God the Father and the oneness of the church's faith and baptism.
elements.questionHint: Paul lists several things as singularly "one," including "one Lord" — what does using that same word "one" for Christ's Lordship rule out about splitting him into parts or persons?

elements.text: Trusting the God-Man

Doctrine like this is easy to treat as a puzzle for scholars, far from ordinary life. But think again about Tanko. He needed to know that Jesus was fully God, so that His death could actually deal with sin and His resurrection could actually defeat death. And he needed to know that Jesus was fully man, so that Jesus could genuinely stand in his place, be tempted as he is tempted, and sympathise with him as only one who has truly suffered can. Take away either truth, and the good news collapses. Hold both together, as the Bible does and as Chalcedon carefully guarded, and you have a Saviour big enough to save you and close enough to understand you.

Tanko eventually found his answer, not in a clever argument, but in sitting with these very verses. He put it simply: “I don’t need a Jesus who only seems human, and I don’t need a Jesus who is merely a great man. I need the one the Bible actually gives me – truly God, truly man, one Person, my Saviour.”

elements.question: What would it look like for you to bring that same confidence into how you trust Christ this week?
