elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter describes salvation as one work carried out by three distinct persons: the Father who foreknows and chooses, the Spirit who sets apart, and Jesus Christ whose blood accomplishes the sprinkling that seals the covenant. Each phrase assigns an essential, distinct role in redemption to a different person, yet all three are folded into a single sentence describing a single saving act. This isn't one God wearing three titles for the same action; it's one God existing as three persons cooperating, with foreknowledge, sanctification, and atonement belonging properly to Father, Spirit, and Son respectively.
elements.questionHint: Look at the three different verbs attached to each name -- foreknowing, setting apart, sprinkling with blood -- why would Peter divide one act of salvation across three persons instead of just crediting it to "God"?

elements.text:
“In the unity of the Godhead there are three persons, of one substance, power, and eternity: God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Ghost. The Father is of none, neither begotten nor proceeding; the Son is eternally begotten of the Father; the Holy Ghost eternally proceeding from the Father and the Son.”
1647 Westminster Confession of Faith, 2:3
2. Self-existent (‘Aseity’) – God is independent and self-sufficient. He exists by His own power, uncaused by anything else outside of Him.

elements.passageText: <sup>14</sup> God said to Moses, “ I am that I am .” And he said, “You must say this to the Israelites, ‘ I am has sent me to you.’”

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is self-existent?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: When Moses asks for God's name, God doesn't answer with something borrowed from outside himself -- he says simply "I am that I am," meaning his existence is self-defined and depends on nothing beyond himself for its explanation. Every creature can be traced back to some cause outside itself, but this answer refuses that structure entirely: God is what he is, purely and underived. That this becomes his actual name -- "I am has sent me to you" -- makes self-existence the very name by which the covenant people will call on him, not a description theologians later added.
elements.questionHint: Try to name anything else that could honestly answer "what are you?" by simply saying "I am what I am" -- what makes the way everything else exists different from that?

elements.passageText:
28 Do you not know?
Have you not heard?
The Lord is an eternal God,
the creator of the whole earth.
He does not get tired or weary;
there is no limit to his wisdom.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is self-existent?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Isaiah links God's status as "creator of the whole earth" directly to the claim that he "does not get tired or weary" -- everything else that exists was made and therefore runs down, but the maker himself draws on no outside source of energy that could be depleted. Weariness happens to beings spending a limited reserve they didn't generate themselves; God has no such reserve to exhaust because his life isn't derived from anything outside himself. The closing line, "there is no limit to his wisdom," makes the same point from another angle -- his capacities aren't allotted the way a creature's are, because his existence was never given to him by something else.
elements.questionHint: Why does needing rest depend on having a limited supply of energy that came from somewhere outside you -- and what does it mean that Isaiah says God has no such limit at all?

elements.passageText:
10 You are my witnesses,” says the Lord,
“my servant whom I have chosen,
so that you may consider and believe in me,
and understand that I am he.
No god was formed before me,
and none will outlive me.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is self-existent?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God states plainly that "no god was formed before me" -- every rival god people worship was made, brought into being at some point, but God denies having any such origin. The companion line, "none will outlive me," rules out the opposite end too: nothing will survive past him either. Between those two claims there's no point of origin and no point of termination to God's existence -- he simply is, self-existent, while every so-called god people can name was formed at some point and will eventually be outlasted. His being doesn't sit on the same timeline that formed and finite things occupy.
elements.questionHint: The verse rules out gods being "formed" before God and rules out anything "outliving" him -- what kind of existence is left over once both of those are excluded?

elements.passageText: <sup>26</sup> For just as the Father has life in himself, thus he has granted the Son to have life in himself,

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is self-existent?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The phrase "life in himself" is doing precise work -- it isn't merely saying the Father is alive, but that his life originates from nothing outside himself; it's intrinsic to who he is rather than received from another source. What's striking is that the Father "granted" the Son this same kind of underived life, meaning the Son doesn't receive existence the way a creature receives it from a cause outside itself -- he receives, from eternity, the very self-existence proper to God. This is one of the few places Scripture explicitly names self-existence and shows it belonging fully to both Father and Son.
elements.questionHint: What's the difference between simply "being alive" and having "life in yourself" -- and why would it matter that the Father grants the Son that exact kind of life rather than a lesser copy of it?

elements.passageText: <sup>8</sup> “I am the Alpha and the Omega,” says the Lord God – the one who is, and who was, and who is still to come – the All-Powerful!

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is self-existent?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: "Alpha and Omega" -- the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet -- frames God as encompassing the entire span in which everything else exists, with nothing before him and nothing after him to bound him. The threefold description "who is, and who was, and who is still to come" refuses to locate God's existence inside a sequence of past, present, and future the way a creature's life only ever occupies one point in that sequence; he simply possesses being in every direction without change. Being called "All-Powerful" caps the description -- his existence isn't sustained by drawing strength from somewhere else, since the strength originates with him.
elements.questionHint: An alphabet's first and last letters contain every letter that could fall between them -- what is this verse saying about God's relationship to everything that exists between his own "beginning" and "end"?

elements.text:
“God exists of himself; he is neither from another, nor of another, nor by another, nor for another. The sufficiency of God [means] he himself is sufficient in himself for himself, and for us; hence he is also called All-sufficient. He is said to live in himself, because he receives neither being nor life from any other, in any part.”
William Ames, The Marrow of Theology, 1:4:36
3. Eternal – God exists outside of time and has no beginning or end.

elements.passageText: <sup>18</sup> The Lord will reign forever and ever!

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is eternal?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This is the victory song sung after the Red Sea, and it ends by projecting God's kingship into unending future time -- not "for a long reign" or "for generations," but "forever and ever," a phrase that refuses to name any endpoint at all. Earthly kings rise and are eventually replaced or die, but the song declares that God's rule has no such expiration built into it. It's more doxology than philosophy, but it still commits to the specific claim that time itself will never catch up to God's throne.
elements.questionHint: Every human king's reign eventually ends in something -- what does the song's choice of "forever and ever," instead of naming any specific limit, tell you about how the Israelites understood God's rule to be different?

elements.passageText: <sup>27</sup> The everlasting God is a refuge,

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is eternal?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Moses calls God "the everlasting God" in the very same breath as calling him "a refuge" -- the comfort of fleeing to God for shelter depends specifically on his lasting without end. A refuge that might itself eventually give out wouldn't offer much comfort over the long run, so the phrase ties God's usefulness as a shelter directly to his being outside of time's wearing-down process. Even in this short line, eternity isn't an abstract attribute tacked onto God -- it's the very thing that makes fleeing to him for safety make sense.
elements.questionHint: Why would calling God "everlasting" matter to someone who is using him specifically as "a refuge" -- what would be lost if the refuge could someday run out?

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup> Even before the mountains came into existence,

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is eternal?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This line reaches back before the point most ancient people treated as the outer edge of permanence -- the mountains, the standing symbol of what looked unshakable -- and places God there already, prior to their existence. If the mountains themselves had a beginning and God preceded even that beginning, then God's existence isn't just very long; it doesn't start on the same timeline the created world starts on. The psalm measures God's eternity by comparing him to the oldest, most fixed thing people could point to, and puts him before it.
elements.questionHint: Ancient people treated mountains as about as permanent as anything gets -- what does it mean that this line places God's existence even earlier than that?

elements.passageText: <sup>25</sup> In earlier times you established the earth; <sup>26</sup> They will perish, <sup>27</sup> But you remain;

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is eternal?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The contrast across these three short lines is deliberate: the earth, which God himself "established," is still described as something that "will perish" -- even his own handiwork wears out and comes to an end. Set against that, "but you remain" is a plain, unadorned claim that God's existence doesn't share the fate of the created order he set in motion. Everything with a starting point in this passage, the earth included, also has an ending point, except God, who simply persists through and beyond it.
elements.questionHint: The earth was "established" by God, yet the psalm still says it "will perish" -- why does that make "but you remain" such a strong claim to make about God specifically?

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup> Now to the eternal king, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever! Amen.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is eternal?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul stacks up four descriptions in a row -- eternal, immortal, invisible, the only God -- and each one rules out something a mortal king could never claim for himself. "Eternal" removes any beginning or end to his reign; "immortal" removes the possibility of his kingship ending in death, the way every human king's eventually does. The doxology's own closing words, "forever and ever," aren't merely a customary way to end a prayer -- they match the content of what's being praised, since a king who is genuinely eternal deserves praise that likewise never runs out.
elements.questionHint: Paul lists "eternal," "immortal," and "invisible" back to back -- what specific limitation of a human king does each of those three words rule out?

elements.text:
“The infinity of God in relation to time is called His eternity. The form in which the Bible represents God’s eternity is simply that of duration through endless ages.”
Louis Berkhof, Systematic Theology, 61

“The fact that God is not bound by time does not mean that he is not conscious of the succession of points of time. He knows what is now occurring in human experience. He is aware that events occur in a particular order, and in the biblical accounts, he knows what has already transpired, what is now the case, and what is yet in the future.”
Millard Erickson, Christian Theology, ch 11
4. Unchangeable (Immutable) – God’s nature, character & purposes don’t change.

elements.passageText: <sup>19</sup> God is not a man, that he should lie,

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is unchangeable?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Balaam's oracle draws a hard line between God and human beings on exactly the point of reliability over time: people change their minds, but "God is not a man" who does that. The logic runs from character to action -- because God doesn't shift in his intentions the way people do, whatever he has "said" he will in fact "make happen." His unchangeableness here isn't cold or static; it's precisely what guarantees his spoken promises and warnings actually land as declared, unlike a human's word, which can quietly get revised.
elements.questionHint: The verse links "not lying" and "not changing his mind" to the guarantee that "he will make it happen" -- why would a God capable of changing his mind be one whose promises you couldn't fully trust?

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup> The Lord ’s decisions stand forever;

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is unchangeable?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The verb here is worth sitting with -- God's decisions don't merely get renewed or reaffirmed over time, they "stand," as something already settled that needs no revision. "Forever" removes any future point at which those decisions might need updating or reversing. Human plans have to be constantly adjusted as circumstances shift and new information arrives, but the psalm credits God's plans with an immovability that outlasts every one of those shifting circumstances.
elements.questionHint: What does it mean for a decision to simply "stand forever," compared to a decision that has to be periodically reconsidered as things change?

elements.passageText:
8 The grass dries up,
the flowers wither,
but the decree of our God is forever reliable.”

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is unchangeable?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The prophet sets God's decree against the two most obvious pictures of impermanence available to him -- grass and flowers, things that flourish briefly and then dry up within a season. Against that backdrop, God's "decree" is called "forever reliable," meaning it doesn't share the fate of everything organic and temporary surrounding it. The point isn't abstract: whatever God has spoken keeps its force no matter how much time passes or how much of the created world withers away around it.
elements.questionHint: Why does Isaiah pick grass and flowers specifically -- things known for withering fast -- as the contrast to what he says about God's decree?

elements.passageText: <sup>15</sup> For this is what the high and exalted one says,

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is unchangeable?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Even in this brief introductory line, the title chosen -- "the high and exalted one" -- sets God apart from everything beneath him as occupying a fixed, supreme position rather than one that rises and falls. Things exalted by human standards can be brought low again; empires and rulers move up and down over time. But this title functions almost as a permanent designation for who God is, not a temporary status he currently holds, consistent with how the rest of this same verse in Isaiah goes on to describe him as the one who "lives forever."
elements.questionHint: A human ruler can be "exalted" one year and deposed the next -- what would it mean for someone to simply be called, as a fixed title, "the high and exalted one"?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> “Since, I, the Lord , do not go back on my promises, you, sons of Jacob, have not perished.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is unchangeable?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God ties the nation's very survival directly to his own unchanging character: because "I, the Lord, do not go back on my promises," Israel has "not perished." If God's commitments could shift the way a person's resolve shifts under pressure, Israel's covenant relationship with him would have collapsed long before this point, given how often the nation broke faith. Instead, the reason given for Israel still existing at all is God's own steadiness -- he doesn't revise his covenant promises just because their unfaithfulness might seem to justify it.
elements.questionHint: Malachi connects God "not going back on his promises" directly to Israel "not perishing" -- what does that connection suggest would have happened to Israel if God changed the way people do?

elements.passageText:
6:17 In the same way God wanted to demonstrate more clearly to the heirs of the promise that his purpose was unchangeable, and so he intervened with an oath, 18 so that we who have found refuge in him may find strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us through two unchangeable things, since it is impossible for God to lie.


13:8Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever!

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is unchangeable?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The writer piles up guarantees on top of each other -- God's purpose is unchangeable, he backs it with an oath, and it is flatly "impossible for God to lie" -- calling these "two unchangeable things" meant to give believers "strong encouragement." The redundancy is the point: God didn't need to add an oath to his word for his own sake, since his character alone already made it certain, but he did so to give doubting humans extra assurance. The paired line that Jesus Christ is "the same yesterday and today and forever" applies that same unchangeableness to the Son specifically, spanning all of time without variation.
elements.questionHint: Why would God add an oath to a promise that was already guaranteed just by his saying it -- what does that extra assurance tell you about how seriously Hebrews takes God's unchangeableness?

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup> All generous giving and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or the slightest hint of change.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is unchangeable?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: James borrows an image from the sky -- "the Father of lights" evokes sun, moon, and stars, whose light visibly varies with the time of day and the phases of the moon. Yet he insists that in God, the source of every good gift, there is "no variation or the slightest hint of change," not even the small, predictable shifting the heavenly lights themselves display. The contrast makes God's constancy more striking still: even the most reliable-looking things in creation still vary, but the character behind God's gifts does not waver at all.
elements.questionHint: The sun, moon, and stars ("lights") all shift and vary in a predictable way -- why would James specifically deny that God, "the Father of lights," has even that much variation?

elements.text:
“The Immutability of God is that perfection by which He is devoid of all change, not only in His Being, but also in His perfections, and in His purposes and promises. [Thus] He is exalted above all growth or decay in His Being or perfections.”
Louis Berkhof, Systematic Theology, 60
5. Omnipresent – God is present everywhere simultaneously.

elements.passageText: <sup>7</sup> Where can I go to escape your spirit? <sup>8</sup> If I were to ascend to heaven, you would be there. <sup>9</sup> If I were to fly away on the wings of the dawn, <sup>10</sup> even there your hand would guide me,

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is omnipresent?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalmist tests the two most extreme directions he can imagine -- straight up to "heaven" and clear across the earth on "the wings of the dawn," the far horizon -- and finds God present at both without having had to travel there himself. There is no gap he can put between himself and God by changing location, because God isn't confined to being in one place and absent from another the way a person is. The comfort of the passage rests entirely on this: wherever the psalmist could possibly go, God's "hand" is already there guiding him, not catching up after the fact.
elements.questionHint: The psalmist picks the two farthest-apart places he can imagine, heaven above and the far horizon below -- what does finding God already present in both, without traveling, say about how his presence differs from ours?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> The eyes of the Lord are in every place,

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is omnipresent?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The proverb doesn't say God's eyes reach into "many" places or only "important" ones -- it says "every place," a claim with no exception, and then immediately applies it to moral accountability by naming both "the evil and the good." Nothing is hidden from view because there is nowhere his attention doesn't already reach; presence and observation are fused into the single image of watching eyes. It's a practical, almost unsettling way to state omnipresence -- not abstract metaphysics but the reason no wrongdoing ever truly happens unseen.
elements.questionHint: The proverb specifically says God's eyes watch "those who are evil and those who are good" in "every place" -- why connect God's presence everywhere directly to moral accountability rather than describing it as a neutral fact?

elements.passageText: <sup>23</sup> “Do you people think that I am some local deity and not the transcendent God?” the Lord asks. <sup>24</sup> “Do you really think anyone can hide himself where I cannot see him?” the Lord asks. “Do you not know that I am everywhere?” the Lord asks.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is omnipresent?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God confronts a specific, cramped idea of himself here -- that he might be merely "some local deity," the kind ancient people imagined was tied to one region or shrine -- and rejects it outright by calling himself "the transcendent God." The rhetorical question "can anyone hide himself where I cannot see him?" assumes an obvious no, and God states the conclusion plainly himself: "I am everywhere." The passage is explicitly correcting a wrong, smaller view of God's presence, not just adding detail to a view people already had right.
elements.questionHint: God specifically denies being "some local deity" -- what wrong assumption about him is he correcting, and how does "I am everywhere" answer it directly?

elements.passageText: <sup>27</sup> so that they would search for God and perhaps grope around for him and find him, though he is not far from each one of us. <sup>28</sup> For in him we live and move about and exist, as even some of your own poets have said, ‘For we too are his offspring.’

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is omnipresent?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul tells the Athenians God is "not far from each one of us" -- not distant, the way an absent deity confined to a temple might be imagined, but near to every single person regardless of who or where they are. The phrase "in him we live and move about and exist" goes further than mere nearness, though -- it pictures human life itself as sustained within God's presence at every moment, the way a fish exists within water. Paul uses this closeness to argue that people don't need to "grope around" blindly for a distant God, since he is already present to the very act of their existing.
elements.questionHint: Paul says people "live and move about and exist" in God -- what's the difference between God simply being nearby and human existence itself happening within his presence?

elements.text:
“The infinity of God ... viewed with reference to space, [is] called His immensity. It may be defined as that perfection of the Divine Being by which He transcends all spatial limitations, and yet is present in every point of space with His whole Being.”
Louis Berkhof, Systematic Theology, 60
6. Omnipotent (Sovereign) – God is all-powerful & can do all things consistent with His nature. He has supreme authority & power over creation. His will is ultimately accomplished.

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup> “I know that you can do all things; no purpose of yours can be thwarted;

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is omnipotent?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: After God has spoken to him from the whirlwind, Job's response is a confession stated in the most absolute terms available -- "you can do all things" -- with no qualifier limiting it to great or important things. The second half draws out the practical implication: because God's power has no ceiling, "no purpose" of his "can be thwarted," meaning nothing in creation, including Job's own suffering and confusion, has been able to block whatever God intended. Job reaches this confession only after being confronted with something of that power directly, so it isn't detached theology but a direct response to it.
elements.questionHint: Job connects "you can do all things" directly to the claim that no purpose of God's can be "thwarted" -- why does unlimited power specifically guarantee that nothing can block what God intends?

elements.passageText:
115:3 Our God is in heaven!
He does whatever he pleases!


135:6 He does whatever he pleases
in heaven and on earth,
in the seas and all the ocean depths.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is omnipotent?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Both psalms use the same striking phrase -- God "does whatever he pleases" -- which locates the limit on his action nowhere but in his own will; there is no other force, obstacle, or permission he needs to secure first. Psalm 135 then extends that reach across every conceivable domain, "in heaven and on earth, in the seas and all the ocean depths," leaving no realm exempted from his freedom to act. Together the two lines describe a power bounded only by what God himself wills, never by any limit external to him.
elements.questionHint: The psalms say God does "whatever he pleases" -- what's the difference between a power limited by outside obstacles and one limited only by its own will?

elements.passageText: <sup>35</sup> All the inhabitants of the earth are regarded as nothing. He does as he wishes with the army of heaven and with those who inhabit the earth. No one slaps his hand and says to him, ‘What have you done?’

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is omnipotent?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This comes from Nebuchadnezzar's own confession after being humbled, and it's blunt: compared to God's power, "all the inhabitants of the earth are regarded as nothing" -- not merely diminished, but effectively weightless against what God can do. The image of no one being able to "slap his hand" pictures the most a subordinate might try in order to stop a superior's action, and denies that even this token resistance is possible against God. It's the testimony of a king who had just experienced firsthand what it meant to have his own power overridden completely.
elements.questionHint: The image of "slapping God's hand" pictures someone trying to physically stop him mid-action -- what is Nebuchadnezzar, having just lost and regained his own throne by God's decision, saying is even possible to try against God?

elements.passageText:
10 who announces the end from the beginning
and reveals beforehand what has not yet occurred;
who says, ‘My plan will be realized,
I will accomplish what I desire;’

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is omnipotent?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The verse links two things that might seem unrelated -- knowing the future, "the end from the beginning," and having the power to bring about whatever is desired, "my plan will be realized" -- and pairs them together rather than treating them separately. God doesn't merely predict correctly what will happen as an observer might; he "accomplishes" what he desires, meaning his announced plans and the actual outcome are guaranteed to match because his power secures them. Knowledge of the future here isn't detached foresight; it flows from his being the one who brings that future about.
elements.questionHint: Why does the verse pair "revealing beforehand what has not occurred" with "I will accomplish what I desire" -- what's the connection between God knowing the future and God having power to bring it about?

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup> ‘Oh, Lord God , you did indeed make heaven and earth by your mighty power and great strength. Nothing is too hard for you!

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is omnipotent?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jeremiah prays this in the middle of a desperate, humanly hopeless situation -- the city under siege -- and grounds his confidence in the single largest feat imaginable, that God "made heaven and earth" by nothing less than his "mighty power and great strength." From that he draws the flat conclusion "nothing is too hard for you," a claim with no exceptions listed. The logic moves from the biggest thing God has already done, creation, to the confidence that whatever smaller thing is needed now cannot possibly exceed his ability.
elements.questionHint: Jeremiah reasons from "you made heaven and earth" straight to "nothing is too hard for you" -- why would creating the universe be evidence strong enough to cover every other possible difficulty, including his present crisis?

elements.passageText: <sup>26</sup> Jesus looked at them and replied, “This is impossible for mere humans, but for God all things are possible.”

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is omnipotent?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This comes right after the disciples ask, stunned, "who then can be saved?" following Jesus' hard teaching about wealth, and his answer draws the exact line between human limitation and divine power. What is flatly "impossible for mere humans" -- including a rich person letting go of what holds them, or anyone earning their own salvation -- is "possible" for God, full stop. Jesus doesn't soften human impossibility into mere difficulty; he keeps the contrast sharp, so that salvation is credited entirely to what only God's power can accomplish.
elements.questionHint: Jesus doesn't say salvation is "hard" for people, he says it's "impossible" -- why does he need that strong a word before he can say "but for God all things are possible"?

elements.text:
“There are, however, certain qualifications of this all-powerful character of God. He cannot arbitrarily do anything whatsoever that we may conceive of. He can do only those things that are proper objects of his power. Thus, he cannot do the logically absurd or contradictory. He cannot make square circles or triangles with four corners. He cannot undo what happened in the past, although he may wipe out its effects or even the memory of it. He cannot act contrary to his nature – he cannot be cruel or unconcerned. He cannot fail to do what he has promised... All of these ‘inabilities’, however, are not weaknesses, but strengths. The inability to do evil or to lie or to fail is a mark of positive strength rather than of failure.”
Millard Erickson, Christian Theology, ch 11
7. Omniscient – God possesses complete and perfect knowledge of all things.

elements.passageText:
5 Our Lord is great and has awesome power;
there is no limit to his wisdom.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is omniscient?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalmist pairs God's "awesome power" with "no limit to his wisdom" in a single line, treating both as facets of the same greatness rather than separate topics. "No limit" is the operative phrase -- it isn't that God's wisdom is merely vast or greater than any human's, but that it has no boundary at all, in the same way his power has none. Knowledge that's merely very large would eventually meet some outer edge; the psalm specifically denies that God's understanding has one.
elements.questionHint: What's the difference between saying someone's wisdom is "very great" and saying, as the psalm does, that it has "no limit" at all?

elements.passageText:
3 The eyes of the Lord are in every place,
keeping watch on those who are evil and those who are good.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is omniscient?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The same image that shows God's presence everywhere also shows his knowledge reaching everywhere, since his "eyes" aren't merely located in every place but are actively "keeping watch" there -- seeing and knowing what happens, not just occupying space. The proverb singles out moral conduct specifically, "those who are evil and those who are good," which means this isn't generic omniscience about facts in the abstract; it's God's precise, ongoing awareness of every person's actions and character, with nothing screened from that watching.
elements.questionHint: The proverb says God's eyes are "keeping watch," not just present -- what's the difference between simply being everywhere and actually knowing everything that happens everywhere?

elements.passageText:
9 Remember what I accomplished in antiquity!
Truly I am God, I have no peer;
I am God, and there is none like me,10 who announces the end from the beginning
and reveals beforehand what has not yet occurred;
who says, ‘My plan will be realized,
I will accomplish what I desire;’

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is omniscient?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God grounds his uniqueness -- "I have no peer... none like me" -- specifically in his ability to announce "the end from the beginning," meaning what sets him apart from every rival isn't just power but total knowledge of history before it unfolds. No competing god, in the taunt running through this section of Isaiah, can do this, because true foreknowledge requires a vantage point outside time's passage that only God occupies. His plans being "realized" isn't a lucky guess repeated reliably; it's knowledge of the future so complete that his forecasts and outcomes never diverge.
elements.questionHint: Isaiah connects "none like me" directly to the ability to reveal "beforehand what has not yet occurred" -- why would that specific ability, rather than mere strength, prove God has no rival?

elements.passageText: <sup>13</sup> And no creature is hidden from God, but everything is naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must render an account.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is omniscient?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The writer piles up two vivid words -- "naked" and "exposed" -- to describe how thoroughly nothing can be concealed from God, language usually reserved for something stripped bare with no covering left at all. "No creature" leaves no exception; whatever exists is included in this total visibility. The final clause ties this directly to accountability, "him to whom we must render an account," meaning the point isn't abstract omniscience but the specific fact that every person will eventually answer to the one from whom nothing was ever actually hidden.
elements.questionHint: Why does the writer choose the specific images of being "naked" and "exposed," rather than simply saying God "knows everything," and how does that connect to rendering an account?

elements.passageText: 19 And by this we will know that we are of the truth and will convince our conscience in his presence, 20 that if our conscience condemns us, that God is greater than our conscience and knows all things.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is omniscient?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John's argument works by contrast: even our own conscience, which can accuse us fairly severely, is still smaller in its knowledge than God is -- "God is greater than our conscience and knows all things." The pastoral point is that God's knowledge isn't only a threat; because it's total, it also sees more than our guilty feelings can see, including facts about us our own conscience might miss or misjudge. "Knows all things" is stated without qualification, applied here to the deepest, most private terrain a person has -- their own inner sense of guilt.
elements.questionHint: Why would John comfort someone whose own conscience is condemning them by pointing out that God's knowledge is even greater than that condemning conscience?

elements.text:
“[God] knows every truth, even those not yet discovered by humankind, for it was he who built them into the creation. And he therefore knows every genuine possibility, even when the possibilities seem limitless in number. ... God also knows the future, as well as the past and present.”
Millard Erickson, Christian Theology, ch 11
8. Omnisapience – God has infinite wisdom.

elements.passageText:
19 By wisdom the Lord laid the foundation of the earth;
he established the heavens by understanding.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is infinitely wise?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The verse credits creation itself -- "the foundation of the earth" and "the heavens" -- to God's "wisdom" and "understanding" as the actual means by which they were made, not merely to raw power exercised apart from wisdom. This makes wisdom something demonstrated in the very structure and order of the physical world, not just an abstract trait God happens to possess; the intricacy and coherence of creation is the evidence. Where power answers whether God could make the world, this verse answers a different question -- that the way it was made, and the order it displays, came specifically from wisdom.
elements.questionHint: The verse doesn't say God made the world "by his power" but "by wisdom" and "understanding" -- what does crediting the world's foundation to wisdom, rather than only power, tell you about what wisdom is for?

elements.passageText:
29 This also comes from the Lord who commands armies,
who gives supernatural guidance and imparts great wisdom.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is infinitely wise?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This verse sits at the end of a parable about a farmer who knows exactly the right way and season to plow, plant, and thresh, ordinary agricultural skill that Isaiah then traces back to the Lord as its ultimate source, "who gives supernatural guidance and imparts great wisdom." The point is that even the practical competence people display in mundane tasks reflects wisdom that originates with God rather than being a purely human achievement. If the know-how needed to farm well comes from God's wisdom, that wisdom reaches into the smallest, most ordinary details of how the world actually works.
elements.questionHint: This verse follows an illustration about a farmer's practical skill -- why would Isaiah trace even that everyday competence back to God's own wisdom rather than crediting it purely to human learning?

elements.passageText: <sup>27</sup> to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, be glory forever! Amen.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is infinitely wise?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's phrase "the only wise God" functions the same way "the only true God" would -- it isn't saying God is the wisest among several wise beings, but that wisdom in the fullest sense belongs to God alone, with anything resembling wisdom elsewhere being derivative or partial by comparison. That this doxology closes out the entire letter to the Romans, after chapters of dense theological argument about God's plan of salvation, gives the phrase weight: Paul has just walked through God's redemptive wisdom in detail and lands on ascribing "glory forever" to the "only wise" one responsible for it.
elements.questionHint: Paul calls God "the only wise God" rather than "the wisest God" -- what's the difference between being the wisest among many wise beings and being the only one who is wise in that full sense?

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> The purpose of this enlightenment is that through the church the multifaceted wisdom of God should now be disclosed to the rulers and the authorities in the heavenly realms.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is infinitely wise?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's word for God's wisdom here is striking -- "multifaceted," picturing something like a many-sided jewel that shows a different color or angle depending on how it's turned, rather than a single simple idea. What makes this remarkable is the vehicle Paul names for displaying it: "through the church," an ordinary, often flawed community of believers, God puts his wisdom on display even before "the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms," spiritual powers who presumably already know a great deal. If the church becomes a display case for wisdom that impresses even angelic powers, that wisdom must run deeper than any single facet could capture.
elements.questionHint: Why would Paul choose the word "multifaceted" to describe God's wisdom being shown "through the church," rather than simply saying God is wise?

elements.text:
“God acts in the light of all of the facts and of correct values. Knowing all things, God knows what is good. He sees all things in their proper perspective.”
Millard Erickson, Christian Theology, ch 11

9. Unity (Simplicity) – God is wholly unified in His being, not composed of parts. His attributes cannot be separate from His essence & they include each other (e.g. His self-existence is eternal; and his eternality is unchangeable; etc.).

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> Listen, Israel: The Lord is our God, the Lord is one!

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is a unity, not composed of separate parts?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The Shema was Israel's foundational confession, recited daily, and it states God's oneness in the plainest terms right alongside the claim on Israel's exclusive worship: "the Lord is our God, the Lord is one." Surrounded by nations that worshiped whole pantheons of competing, specialized gods, Israel confessed instead a single, undivided God, not a deity assembled out of separate divine parts or rival powers sharing the job. This "oneness" grounds Israel's demand for undivided loyalty in worship precisely because God himself is undivided.
elements.questionHint: Israel's neighbors worshiped many gods, each handling a different part of life -- what does insisting God is simply "one," rather than a collection of specialized powers, rule out about how he could be structured?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we live, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we live.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is a unity, not composed of separate parts?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul restates Israel's confession of the "one God" while now including Jesus within it, "one God, the Father... and one Lord, Jesus Christ," without treating this as adding a second God alongside the first. Both are described using cosmic language, "from whom are all things," "through whom are all things," that only fits the one true God, yet Paul keeps the count strictly at "one" throughout. The unity he's defending isn't diluted by including the Son; Father and Son are both located within the single reality of the one God rather than treated as two beings that add up to more than one.
elements.questionHint: Paul uses the exact language of Israel's "one God" confession but now includes Jesus in describing that one God's work -- how does he do that without ending up with two Gods instead of one?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> There is one body and one Spirit, just as you too were called to the one hope of your calling, <sup>5</sup> one Lord, one faith, one baptism, <sup>6</sup> one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is a unity, not composed of separate parts?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul builds toward this list with a rhythm of repeated "ones" -- body, Spirit, hope, Lord, faith, baptism, God -- piling up sevenfold, and the church's whole unity is grounded in a single, undivided God standing behind all of it. The final phrase pushes further: God is "over all and through all and in all," a totalizing description leaving no room for God to be one power among several cooperating powers; he's the singular reality permeating everything at once. The unity believers are called to mirrors the very unity of the God they belong to.
elements.questionHint: Paul stacks seven different "ones" leading up to "one God" -- why would the church's own unity be grounded specifically in God being undivided rather than in God simply being powerful?

elements.text:
“God is a unitary, not a composite being; his nature is not something external to him or added to his being or substance; there is no fundamental tension among the attributes, and they are ultimately aspects of the one divine nature.”
Millard Erickson, Christian Theology, ch 11
10. Independent – God does not depend on anything or anyone outside of Himself for His existence or for His actions.

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup> O Lord , you are great, mighty, majestic, magnificent, glorious, and sovereign over all the sky and earth! You have dominion and exalt yourself as the ruler of all. <sup>12</sup> You are the source of wealth and honor; you rule over all. You possess strength and might to magnify and give strength to all.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is independent of His creation?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: David's prayer describes God as "the source of wealth and honor" rather than a recipient of it, meaning whatever value or greatness exists anywhere in creation flows out from God rather than being something he needed to acquire. Likewise he "possesses strength and might" as his own, giving it to others rather than drawing it from them. Every good thing David can name -- wealth, honor, strength -- traces back to God as its origin point, which is exactly why nothing outside of God could ever be the thing that supplies or completes him.
elements.questionHint: David calls God "the source of wealth and honor" instead of a recipient of it -- what does being the source of something, rather than needing to receive it, tell you about whether God depends on anyone else?

elements.passageText:
11 (Who has confronted me that I should repay?
Everything under heaven belongs to me!)

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is independent of His creation?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This line comes as God finishes his long response to Job, and the logic is direct: since "everything under heaven belongs" to God already, no one is in a position to hand him something and thereby put him in their debt. The rhetorical question "who has confronted me that I should repay?" assumes no transaction anyone could initiate with God would leave him owing them anything, because whatever they might offer was already his to begin with. God's independence here is framed almost economically -- he can't be indebted to his own creation, because creation has nothing to give him that isn't already his.
elements.questionHint: If everything that exists already belongs to God, what would it even mean for someone to try to put God in their debt by giving him something?

elements.passageText:
13 Who comprehends the mind of the Lord,
or gives him instruction as his counselor? 14 From whom does he receive directions? Who teaches him the correct way to do things,
or imparts knowledge to him,
or instructs him in skillful design?

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is independent of His creation?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Each rhetorical question here assumes an obvious "no one" as its answer -- no one instructs God, no one teaches him, no one imparts knowledge to him -- which rules out his depending on any outside counselor or source of information to do what he does. The picture being denied is of God as a ruler who consults advisors the way human kings do; instead, whatever wisdom and skillful design show up in his works originate entirely within himself. His plans and knowledge aren't the product of collaboration with anyone or anything he made.
elements.questionHint: Each question in this passage assumes an obvious "no one" as its answer -- what would it mean about God's independence if the honest answer to even one of these questions were actually "yes, someone"?

elements.passageText: <sup>24</sup> The God who made the world and everything in it, who is Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by human hands, <sup>25</sup> nor is he served by human hands, as if he needed anything, because he himself gives life and breath and everything to everyone.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is independent of His creation?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul directly confronts an assumption built into Athenian religion -- that gods need houses to live in and offerings to sustain them -- and denies both: God doesn't "live in temples made by human hands" and isn't "served... as if he needed anything." The reasoning Paul gives is that the relationship actually runs opposite to what pagan worship assumed: God "gives life and breath and everything to everyone," meaning he's the giver in every exchange between himself and his creatures, never the needy recipient. Total self-sufficiency, not need, is what makes worship of him appropriate in the first place.
elements.questionHint: Paul says God doesn't need to be "served... as if he needed anything" -- how does that directly contradict the whole logic behind building temples and bringing offerings to a god?

elements.text:
“He is, regardless of whether anything else is. Just as he existed before anything else came into being, so he also can continue to exist independent of everything else. While God is independent in the sense of not needing anything else for his existence, this is not to say that he is aloof, indifferent, or unconcerned. God relates to us, but by his choice, not because he is compelled by some need. That he does so relate to us is therefore an even greater cause for glorifying him.”
Millard Erickson, Christian Theology, ch 11
11. Impassible – God does not experience suffering or emotions in a way that changes His nature or divine essence.

elements.passageText:
19 God is not a man, that he should lie,
nor a human being, that he should change his mind.
Has he said, and will he not do it?
Or has he spoken, and will he not make it happen?

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is impassible?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Applied to impassibility, the key phrase is "nor a human being, that he should change his mind" -- human emotion often works by overwhelming or altering a person's prior resolve, so that what someone decided in a calm moment gets reversed under the pressure of feeling. Balaam denies this pattern applies to God at all: whatever he has determined to do, he does, without an inner emotional upheaval derailing or revising the plan partway through. This doesn't make God emotionless in the passage's own terms, but it does mean his settled purposes are never overturned by fluctuating inner states the way a human's resolve can be.
elements.questionHint: Human minds often get "changed" specifically because of a shift in feeling that overrides an earlier decision -- what is the verse denying happens to God when it says he doesn't change his mind "as a human being" would?

elements.passageText:
22 The Lord ’s loyal kindness never ceases;
his compassions never end.
23 They are fresh every morning;
your faithfulness is abundant!

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is impassible?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Written in the middle of a book grieving Jerusalem's destruction, this line insists God's "compassions" don't run dry even in the worst circumstances -- they are "fresh every morning," not a finite reserve being spent down by the disaster the author is lamenting. Rather than a God whose kindness gets knocked off course by circumstances the way a person's patience wears thin, this passage describes steady compassion that renews without fail, day after day, regardless of what's happening around it. The constancy of "never ceases" and "never end" is what makes hope possible even inside Lamentations' grief.
elements.questionHint: The author is describing a catastrophe when he writes these lines -- why would he insist God's compassions are "fresh every morning" and "never end" at that exact moment, rather than describing them as worn down by what's happening?

elements.passageText: <sup>14</sup> “‘I the Lord have spoken; judgment is coming and I will act! I will not relent, or show pity, or be sorry! I will judge you according to your conduct and your deeds, declares the sovereign Lord .’”

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is impassible?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This is a hard verse and needs to be read on its own terms: God announces he will "not relent, or show pity, or be sorry" about the coming judgment, meaning his resolve to act justly here won't be overturned by an emotional wave of regret partway through. It isn't a claim that God feels nothing about judgment; elsewhere Scripture shows him grieving over sin. Rather, in this specific case his settled decision to act on Judah's persistent, deliberate "conduct and deeds" will not be talked out of itself by a change of heart, and his justice proceeds according to what he has determined rather than a shifting mood.
elements.questionHint: God says he will "not... be sorry" about this specific judgment -- is this verse claiming God has no feelings at all, or that his settled decision here won't be reversed by a change of heart partway through?

elements.passageText: <sup>13</sup> If we are unfaithful, he remains faithful, since he cannot deny himself.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is impassible?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's logic runs from God's nature outward: God's faithfulness toward his people doesn't fluctuate with their behavior, "if we are unfaithful, he remains faithful," because the alternative would require God acting against his own unchanging character, "he cannot deny himself." Human faithfulness is often reactive, rising and falling depending on how we're treated; this verse denies that God's faithfulness works that way, tying it instead to something fixed in who he is rather than something that adjusts to our shifting behavior. Our unfaithfulness has no power to provoke a change in God's own settled disposition toward his promises.
elements.questionHint: Paul says God "cannot deny himself" -- why would God's faithfulness toward us have to hold steady even when ours doesn't, if faithfulness is part of his fixed nature rather than a reaction to how he's treated?

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup> All generous giving and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or the slightest hint of change.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is impassible?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Applied here to impassibility rather than unchangeableness in general, the phrase "no variation or the slightest hint of change" specifically covers God's disposition toward giving good gifts -- it isn't erratic or dependent on his mood, the way a person's generosity might depend on how they're feeling that day. Even the small, cyclical changes of light and shadow James may be alluding to with "Father of lights" don't apply to God's own character; his goodness toward those he gives to isn't subject to the emotional fluctuation that makes human generosity so inconsistent.
elements.questionHint: Why would James specifically deny "the slightest hint of change" in God's giving, when human generosity is so often affected by mood or circumstance?

elements.text:
“God has chosen to create a world that often grieves him. He is active rather than passive. [God is never] overcome by waves of passion. Impassibility should not be used to deny that God has emotions, or that God the Son suffers real injury and death on the cross. But God in his transcendent nature cannot be harmed in any way, nor can he suffer loss.”
John Frame, Systematic Theology, ch 19
12. Incomprehensible – God is beyond full human understanding, though we can know Him truly through His revelation.

elements.passageText: <sup>29</sup> Secret things belong to the Lord our God, but those that are revealed belong to us and our descendants forever, so that we might obey all the words of this law.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is incomprehensible?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Moses divides all truth into two categories -- "secret things" that stay with God alone, and "revealed things" given to Israel -- and the very existence of a category permanently belonging to God alone assumes there is more to know about him and his purposes than any person, or even the whole covenant community, can access. Notably, the verse doesn't treat this as a problem needing to be solved; the revealed portion is called sufficient for its purpose, "that we might obey," meaning incomprehensibility about the secret things isn't an obstacle to a right relationship with God, just a boundary on it.
elements.questionHint: Moses splits truth into "secret" things kept by God and "revealed" things given to Israel -- what does the existence of a permanently "secret" category tell you about the limits of what people can know about God?

elements.passageText:
3 The Lord is great and certainly worthy of praise!
No one can fathom his greatness.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is incomprehensible?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalm moves from praising God's greatness to a flat statement about its scale: "no one can fathom" it. "Fathom" is a word borrowed from measuring the depth of water, and the point is that God's greatness isn't merely very deep the way an unusually deep lake might be, but unmeasurable in principle, with no bottom a person could ever sound out. Worship, in this verse, is the appropriate response precisely to a greatness too vast to be fully grasped, not a substitute for understanding it.
elements.questionHint: "Fathom" originally meant measuring how deep water is -- what is the psalmist saying about the "depth" of God's greatness by using a word that normally applies to something with a measurable bottom?

elements.passageText:
11 God has made everything fit beautifully in its appropriate time,
but he has also placed ignorance in the human heart
so that people cannot discover what God has ordained,
from the beginning to the end of their lives.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is incomprehensible?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The Preacher makes an unusual claim -- that God himself "placed" a kind of built-in ignorance into the human heart, not as an accident of human limitation but as part of how he designed people. Even though God "made everything fit beautifully" and has a purpose running "from the beginning to the end" of a person's life, that very purpose is something people "cannot discover" on their own. Incomprehensibility here isn't just a gap waiting to be filled by more study; the text presents it as intentional on God's part, built into the human condition itself.
elements.questionHint: The verse says God himself "placed" ignorance in the human heart -- why would this be described as something God intentionally built in, rather than just a natural limit of the human mind?

elements.passageText:
8 “Indeed, my plans are not like your plans,
and my deeds are not like your deeds,” says the Lord,
9 for just as the sky is higher than the earth,
so my deeds are superior to your deeds
and my plans superior to your plans.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is incomprehensible?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God uses a spatial image to describe a conceptual gap -- the distance between his "plans" and ours is measured the way "the sky is higher than the earth," a comparison chosen for being vast and fixed rather than a gap that could gradually be closed through more careful human thinking. This isn't just saying God's plans are better than ours in degree; it's a difference in kind, two different domains rather than two points on the same scale. Human reasoning, however refined, operates on a different plane than God's, and the passage doesn't offer a technique for closing that gap.
elements.questionHint: Why does Isaiah compare the gap between God's plans and ours to the distance between "the sky" and "the earth," instead of just saying God's plans are "better" than ours?

elements.passageText: <sup>33</sup> Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how fathomless his ways!

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is incomprehensible?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul breaks into this exclamation right after several dense chapters reasoning carefully about God's plan for Israel and the nations, and even after all that argument he ends not with a tidy conclusion but with wonder at what remains beyond him, calling it "unsearchable" and "fathomless." Both words describe something that resists a search that would eventually succeed if pursued long enough; no amount of further inquiry would exhaust God's judgments and ways. That this comes from Paul after his most theologically rigorous letter shows incomprehensibility isn't a failure of effort but a real limit built into the difference between God's mind and ours.
elements.questionHint: Paul writes this right after several chapters of careful theological argument -- what does it say about the limits of even careful human reasoning that his conclusion is "unsearchable" and "fathomless" rather than a tidy resolution?

elements.text:
“We do not know God’s qualities or his nature completely. We know God only as he has revealed himself. While his self-revelation is undoubtedly consistent with his full nature and accurate, it is not an exhaustive revelation. Further, we do not totally understand or know comprehensively that which he has revealed to us of himself. Thus, there is, and always will be, an element of mystery regarding God.”
Millard Erickson, Christian Theology, ch 11
13. Spiritual – God is Spirit.

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup> Now the earth was without shape and empty, and darkness was over the surface of the watery deep, but the Spirit of God was moving over the surface of the water.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is spirit?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Before anything in the material world has taken shape, "the Spirit of God" is already present and active, "moving over the surface of the water" -- involvement that doesn't require, or wait for, a physical body or location within a material order that doesn't yet even exist. This is one of the earliest indications in Scripture that God's own being isn't made of the stuff he's about to shape into a world; he moves and acts over the material creation from a mode of existence that precedes and isn't dependent on matter at all.
elements.questionHint: At this point in Genesis, no physical world has been shaped yet -- how can "the Spirit of God" already be present and active "over the water" if his own being depended on having a physical body like the things about to be made?

elements.passageText:
3 You carefully observe me when I travel or when I lie down to rest;
you are aware of everything I do.
4 Certainly my tongue does not frame a word
without you, O Lord, being thoroughly aware of it.
5 You squeeze me in from behind and in front;
you place your hand on me.
6 Your knowledge is beyond my comprehension;
it is so far beyond me, I am unable to fathom it.
7 Where can I go to escape your spirit?
Where can I flee to escape your presence?
8 If I were to ascend to heaven, you would be there.
If I were to sprawl out in Sheol, there you would be.
9 If I were to fly away on the wings of the dawn,
and settle down on the other side of the sea,
10 even there your hand would guide me,
your right hand would grab hold of me.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is spirit?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalm describes God's awareness reaching into places no physical body could occupy at once -- knowing an unspoken word before it's even "framed" on the tongue, and being present whether the psalmist goes up to "heaven," down to "Sheol," or across the sea on "the wings of the dawn." A body, however powerful, can only be in one location doing one thing; but here God "squeezes" the psalmist front and back while also being ahead of him wherever he might travel, which is exactly why the psalm calls this trying "to escape your spirit" -- not a body to run from, but a presence not tied to physical location the way ours is.
elements.questionHint: The psalmist imagines going to the most opposite places possible -- heaven, Sheol, across the sea -- and finds God present at all of them without traveling; what kind of being could be "present" like that instead of moving from place to place the way a body does?

elements.passageText: <sup>24</sup> God is spirit, and the people who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.”

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is spirit?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus states this to the Samaritan woman in the middle of a debate about where God ought to be worshiped, on which mountain or in which temple, and his answer undercuts the whole premise of the debate: "God is spirit," meaning he isn't the kind of being confined to, or more present at, one physical location than another. Because worship is aimed at a being who is spirit, true worship must correspond to that reality, happening "in spirit and truth" rather than depending on geography, architecture, or ritual location as if God's presence were more concentrated in one physical place than another.
elements.questionHint: Jesus says this right after being asked which mountain is the correct place to worship -- how does the simple statement "God is spirit" make that whole location-based question the wrong kind of question to ask?

elements.text:
“God is spirit; he is not composed of matter and does not possess a physical nature. This is also implied in various references to his invisibility. He does not have the limitations involved with a physical body ... he is not limited to a particular geographical or spatial location [and] he is not destructible, as is material nature.”
Millard Erickson, Christian Theology, ch 11
14. Transcendent – God is exalted above, and independent of, His creation; He is not simply attached to it, nor confined within it.

elements.passageText:
9 For you, O Lord , are the sovereign king over the whole earth;
you are elevated high above all gods

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is transcendent?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalm doesn't just say God rules the earth; it adds that he is "elevated high above all gods," language that places him in an entirely different category from every other power people might worship or fear, not merely at the top of a list that includes them as lesser members of the same category. "Elevated" pictures a vertical distance separating God's throne from every rival, a gap of kind rather than of degree. Whatever authority other so-called gods might claim, this psalm locates them all beneath a God who stands in a class by himself, above the whole created order those "gods" belong to.
elements.questionHint: The psalm says God is "elevated high above all gods" rather than just "greater than" them -- what's the difference between being the greatest member of a category and being elevated entirely above it?

elements.passageText:
22 He is the one who sits on the earth’s horizon;
its inhabitants are like grasshoppers before him.
He is the one who stretches out the sky like a thin curtain,
and spreads it out like a pitched tent.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is transcendent?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Isaiah's picture is deliberately disorienting in scale: God sits above "the earth's horizon," the whole visible curve of the world beneath him, while its inhabitants, every person and nation on it, look from that vantage point like "grasshoppers," small and numerous rather than significant and imposing. The following image pushes the scale further: what looks to us like the vast, fixed expanse of the sky is, to God, something he "stretches out" and pitches "like a tent," an act of ordinary construction on his part. Both images use the same technique -- taking what looks enormous from a human vantage and showing it as small and manageable from God's.
elements.questionHint: From where God sits, whole nations of people look like "grasshoppers" and the vast sky is just a "tent" he pitches -- what does the size of these comparisons tell you about the difference between how big things look to us and how they actually compare to God?

elements.passageText:
48 Yet the Most High does not live in houses made by human hands, as the prophet says,
49 ‘Heaven is my throne,
and earth is the footstool for my feet.
What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord,
or what is my resting place?

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is transcendent?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Stephen quotes Isaiah to make a pointed argument to an audience who had come to treat the temple itself as God's proper dwelling: "the Most High does not live in houses made by human hands" at all, no matter how magnificent the structure. The rhetorical questions that follow, "what kind of house will you build for me... or what is my resting place?", expect the obvious answer that no human construction project could possibly be adequate, since God already has "heaven" itself as his throne and treats "the earth" merely as a "footstool." Any building people erect is, by comparison, laughably undersized for a God whose scale dwarfs the entire created order it sits within.
elements.questionHint: God calls heaven his "throne" and earth merely his "footstool" -- what does that scale comparison say about the adequacy of any human-built "house" meant to contain him?

elements.text:
“God is separate from and independent of nature and humanity. God is not simply attached to, or involved in, his creation. He is also superior to it.”
Millard Erickson, Christian Theology, ch 11

Daniel eventually stopped trying to shrink God down to a manageable size. He put it simply: “I don’t need a God who is merely bigger than me, still figuring things out, still stretched thin. I need the God the Bible actually gives me – self-existent, unchangeable, all-knowing, everywhere present, and beyond my full understanding, but still truly known through what He has revealed. That’s not a smaller comfort. It’s a far greater one.”

None of these attributes make God distant or cold. They make Him trustworthy. A God who changes His mind, or runs out of power, or is caught off guard by the news, could not be leaned on in a crisis. But the God who is truly self-sufficient, truly unchangeable, truly all-powerful and all-knowing – that God can actually be trusted with everything Daniel was afraid to hand over.
A Confidence in God’s Character Scale

elements.instruction: How much do these incommunicable attributes actually shape your day-to-day trust in God? Tick the box that best fits.

chapters.chapterTitle: Attributes of God part 2: Communicable Attributes

elements.text:
Case Study – Ifeoma (late 20s)

Ifeoma had spent months wrestling with just how other God is – eternal, unchangeable, all-powerful, beyond her full understanding. She had come to treasure those truths. But somewhere along the way, a new fear crept in. If God is really that vast, that transcendent, that different from her – could He actually be close? Could He actually love her the way her own mother loved her, or was ‘love’ just a word borrowed and stretched to cover something colder and more abstract?

She found herself praying less personally. Her prayers became formal, careful, almost like addressing a distant head of state rather than a Father. When a friend spoke about “feeling God’s kindness” during a hard week, Ifeoma felt a pang of envy she couldn’t quite explain. Did God actually have kindness, joy, patience, the way people did – or was she projecting human warmth onto something that had none of it?

She needed to know: is the God who is so far above her also, somehow, genuinely like her at His best moments of love and kindness – or has she simply been told a comforting story?
These attributes exist perfectly in God, and also are shared with (or ‘communicated to’) humans to some degree. Jot down how each verse supports each attribute.
1. Love – God is love. His nature is fundamentally loving, and He expresses this love through His relationship with creation.

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup> For as the skies are high above the earth, so his loyal love towers over his faithful followers.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is loving?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalmist reaches for the biggest visual measurement he can think of — the height of the sky over the earth — and says that's how far God's loyal love towers over those who fear him. It's not a small, occasional kindness; it's love on a cosmic scale, far exceeding anything we could measure or exhaust. The word 'loyal love' also carries the sense of covenant faithfulness, not just warm feeling — God's love is love he has committed himself to, not love that could run out or wear thin toward those who revere him.
elements.questionHint: Why does the psalmist compare God's love to the distance between the skies and the earth instead of using a smaller image?

elements.passageText:
Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good,
for his loyal love endures.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is loving?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This verse links two things together: God is good, and his loyal love 'endures.' That single word carries the weight of the whole psalm, which repeats it after every line as a refrain — no matter what is being described, God's love keeps going. It doesn't show up once and fade; it endures through creation, through the exodus, through the giving of the land, and presumably through whatever the reader is living through now.
