The verse grounds the appeal to 'give thanks' in the fact that his love has already proven durable over time, not merely in a promise about the future.
elements.questionHint: The psalm repeats the phrase 'his loyal love endures' after every single line — what does that repetition suggest about how long God's love lasts?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> In a far-off land the Lord will manifest himself to them. He will say to them, ‘I have loved you with an everlasting love. That is why I have continued to be faithful to you.’

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is loving?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God speaks directly to a people in exile — 'a far-off land' — and tells them the reason he has kept coming after them: he loved them with an 'everlasting love.' Notice the order of the sentence: love comes first, and faithfulness follows from it — 'that is why I have continued to be faithful.' His love isn't a reaction to their circumstances or their worthiness; it precedes and explains every faithful act that follows. Even displaced and seemingly cut off, they aren't outside the reach of a love God describes as having no end.
elements.questionHint: In the sentence 'I have loved you... that is why I have continued to be faithful,' which comes first — the love or the faithfulness — and what does that order tell you about which one causes the other?

elements.passageText:
17 The Lord your God is in your midst;
he is a warrior who can deliver.
He takes great delight in you;
he renews you by his love;
he shouts for joy over you.”

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is loving?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This isn't distant or dutiful love — the verse pictures God 'in your midst,' close by, actively delighting in his people rather than merely tolerating them. He 'renews' them by his love, meaning his love isn't just a feeling he has about them but something that acts on them, restoring what has worn down. And the final image — God shouting for joy over his people — pushes the point further than most readers expect: this love is exuberant, not restrained or begrudging. A warrior who delivers and a lover who sings are held together in the very same verse.
elements.questionHint: What does it mean that God doesn't just love his people quietly but 'renews' them by that love and 'shouts for joy' over them — what kind of love expresses itself that way?

elements.passageText: <sup>16</sup> For this is the way God loved the world: He gave his one and only Son, so that everyone who believes in him will not perish but have eternal life.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is loving?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John pins down exactly what form God's love for the world took: he 'gave his one and only Son.' This isn't love as sentiment but love as costly, concrete action — the gift is the most valuable thing God has to give. The purpose clause that follows, 'so that everyone who believes... will not perish but have eternal life,' shows the love was aimed at rescue, not merely feeling. It's also universal in scope ('the world') and personal in application ('everyone who believes'), which means this love isn't reserved for a deserving few but offered as wide as the need for it.
elements.questionHint: The verse defines God's love by a specific action — what did God actually give, and why does giving something that costly say more than just being told 'God loves you'?

elements.passageText: <sup>8</sup> But God demonstrates his own love for us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is loving?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul makes the timing the whole point: Christ died for us 'while we were still sinners' — not after we cleaned up, not in response to our repentance, but in the middle of our rebellion. That timing is what 'demonstrates' the love; anyone can claim to love people who deserve it, but God showed his love precisely where it wasn't earned. The verse also roots love in an event, not just a feeling — Christ's death is the demonstration, the proof offered instead of a mere claim.
elements.questionHint: Paul says God demonstrated his love 'while we were still sinners' — why does the timing (before we changed, not after) matter to what kind of love this is?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> But God, being rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, <sup>5</sup> even though we were dead in transgressions, made us alive together with Christ – by grace you are saved!

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is loving?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul stacks up the reasons this love is remarkable: God is 'rich in mercy,' his love is 'great,' and it reached people who were not merely weak or struggling but 'dead in transgressions' — spiritually incapable of responding on their own. Love, here, isn't drawn out by anything attractive in its object; it moves toward the dead and makes them alive. The parenthetical outburst — 'by grace you are saved!' — shows Paul can barely contain himself describing it; this love results in an entirely new condition, not just a better outlook on the old one.
elements.questionHint: The passage says God loved us 'even though we were dead in transgressions' — what does loving someone who is spiritually dead, rather than merely weak, say about where this love originates?

elements.passageText: <sup>8</sup> The person who does not love does not know God, because God is love.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is loving?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John doesn't just say God loves — he says God 'is love,' making love part of God's very identity rather than one activity among others. That's why John can reason backward from a person's behavior to their knowledge of God: someone who doesn't love 'does not know God,' because knowing a being who is essentially loving should show up as love in the one who knows him. This is a strong claim — it means love isn't optional or occasional for God, and encountering him genuinely should reshape how a person loves others.
elements.questionHint: John doesn't say God 'loves' — he says God 'is love.' What's the difference between a being who performs loving acts and a being whose very nature is love?

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> By this the love of God is revealed in us: that God has sent his one and only Son into the world so that we may live through him. <sup>10</sup> In this is love: not that we have loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the atoning sacrifice for our sins.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is loving?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John defines love almost like a formula: 'not that we have loved God, but that he loved us.' The initiative is entirely God's — his love isn't a response to ours, it's the origin of ours. And the content of that love is specific: sending his Son 'to be the atoning sacrifice for our sins,' meaning the love wasn't just a rescue from misfortune but a dealing with guilt, so that we could 'live through him.' Love, for John, is measured by the cost God was willing to bear and the purpose he accomplished, not by our prior affection for him.
elements.questionHint: John says love is 'not that we loved God, but that he loved us' — whose love comes first in this verse, and what does that order rule out about earning God's love?

elements.text: 2. Holiness – God is separated from sin and His honour is above all else.

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup> Who is like you, O Lord, among the gods? Who is like you – majestic in holiness, fearful in praises, working wonders?

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is holy?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This is the song Israel sang right after the Red Sea crossing, and the question 'who is like you' is rhetorical — the obvious answer is no one. God's holiness here is bound up with his uniqueness: he is set apart from every rival 'god' precisely because of how 'majestic' that holiness is. It's also paired with fearsome praise and wonder-working power, which shows holiness isn't a quiet, private purity but something that provokes awe when it acts in the world — in this case, in the very deliverance the Israelites had just witnessed.
elements.questionHint: The verse asks 'who is like you... majestic in holiness' as a question with an obvious answer — what does comparing God to 'the gods' and finding none like him tell you about what holiness means here?

elements.passageText: <sup>44</sup> for I am the Lord your God and you are to sanctify yourselves and be holy because I am holy. You must not defile yourselves by any of the swarming things that creep on the ground,

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is holy?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The command to 'be holy' is grounded directly in God's own character — 'because I am holy' — not in abstract morality or social convention. Holiness is first a fact about God, and only secondarily a command to his people, who are told to reflect what he already is. The very practical, almost mundane instruction that follows, about not defiling themselves with creeping things, shows that this holiness isn't confined to worship rituals; it's meant to reach into ordinary details of life, marking Israel out as belonging to a God who is himself set apart from everything common or unclean.
elements.questionHint: The command 'be holy' is followed immediately by 'because I am holy' — whose holiness comes first in that sentence, God's or Israel's, and what does that order mean for why they're being asked to change?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> They called out to one another, “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord who commands armies! His majestic splendor fills the entire earth!”

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is holy?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The seraphim don't just call God holy once — they triple it, a Hebrew way of expressing the superlative, as if ordinary repetition can't capture how thoroughly set apart God is. And the declaration doesn't stay abstract: 'his majestic splendor fills the entire earth,' meaning holiness isn't a trait hidden away in heaven but something with reach and visible weight in creation. This is the vision that immediately undoes Isaiah, who responds by crying out about his own uncleanness — holiness, seen clearly, exposes everything that isn't holy by comparison.
elements.questionHint: Why do the seraphim say 'holy' three times instead of once — what is a threefold repetition doing that a single statement couldn't?

elements.passageText: <sup>15</sup> but, like the Holy One who called you, become holy yourselves in all of your conduct, <sup>16</sup> for it is written, “ You shall be holy , because I am holy .”

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is holy?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter calls God 'the Holy One' as a title, then applies it as the pattern believers are called to imitate — 'like the Holy One who called you, become holy yourselves.' Notice the phrase 'in all of your conduct': this holiness isn't limited to sacred moments or religious activities but is meant to characterize the whole of a person's behavior. Peter is quoting the same command from Leviticus, which shows this isn't a New Testament innovation — God's holiness has always been both the standard and the reason his people are called to be different from those around them.
elements.questionHint: Peter says to be holy 'in all of your conduct' — what does adding 'all' rule out about which parts of life holiness is supposed to touch?

elements.passageText: <sup>8</sup> Each one of the four living creatures had six wings and was full of eyes all around and inside. They never rest day or night, saying: “Holy Holy Holy is the Lord God, the All-Powerful, Who was and who is, and who is still to come!”

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is holy?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Like Isaiah's vision, the cry here is threefold — 'Holy Holy Holy' — and it comes from creatures covered in eyes who never stop watching and never stop declaring it, 'day or night.' Their eyes suggest unceasing, comprehensive perception of who God is, and what they see leads to endless worship rather than boredom or familiarity. The titles piled on afterward — 'All-Powerful,' 'who was and who is and who is still to come' — link holiness to God's power and his existence across all time, as though holiness is the fitting response to seeing God fully, from every angle, forever.
elements.questionHint: Why would creatures covered in eyes, watching from every angle, be the ones who never stop repeating 'Holy Holy Holy' — what does their unceasing vigilance suggest about what they keep seeing?

elements.text: 3. Beauty – God is Himself beautiful and is the source of beauty.

elements.passageText:
4 I have asked the Lord for one thing –
this is what I desire!
I want to live in the Lord’s house all the days of my life,
so I can gaze at the splendor of the Lord
and contemplate in his temple.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is beautiful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: David narrows his whole life down to 'one thing' he desires, and it isn't safety or provision — it's proximity to God so he can 'gaze at the splendor of the Lord.' The verb 'gaze' suggests sustained, attentive looking, the way you'd look at something beautiful rather than glance at something merely useful. Pairing that with 'contemplate in his temple' shows this isn't a passing aesthetic experience; David wants to keep looking and keep thinking about what he sees for as long as he lives. Beauty, here, is something worth reorganizing an entire life around.
elements.questionHint: David says gazing at God's splendor is the 'one thing' he wants for 'all the days of my life' — what kind of object is worth building an entire life's desire around like that?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> El, God, the Lord speaks, <sup>2</sup> From Zion, the most beautiful of all places,

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is beautiful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This fragment ties God's speaking to a specific location, Zion, which it calls 'the most beautiful of all places.' The beauty of Zion isn't incidental scenery; it's the fitting stage from which God himself speaks, as though the loveliest place in creation is the appropriate setting for his voice. Even in this short line, beauty and God's self-revelation are linked together — where God is present and speaking, beauty follows, or perhaps beauty marks out where he has chosen to dwell.
elements.questionHint: The verse calls Zion 'the most beautiful of all places' right before saying God speaks from there — what does pairing those two ideas suggest about the connection between beauty and God's presence?

elements.passageText:
May our sovereign God extend his favor to us!
Make our endeavors successful!
Yes, make them successful!


NIV footnote version:

May the beauty of the Lord our God rest on us;
establish the work of our hands for us –
yes, establish the work of our hands.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is beautiful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalmist prays that the 'beauty of the Lord' would 'rest on us' — as if beauty is something that can be transferred, settling on people the way light settles on a surface. It's requested alongside a prayer that God would 'establish the work of our hands,' repeated twice for emphasis, which connects divine beauty to everyday, practical labor. This isn't beauty admired from a distance; it's beauty asked to come rest on ordinary people and make their work meaningful and lasting.
elements.questionHint: The psalmist asks for God's beauty to 'rest on us' rather than just be admired from far away — what does it mean for beauty to settle on a person rather than stay at a distance?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> Majestic splendor emanates from him;

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is beautiful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The verb 'emanates' pictures splendor radiating outward from God the way light radiates from its source — it isn't attached to him from outside or borrowed from somewhere else, it flows out of who he is. 'Majestic splendor' combines grandeur with beauty, suggesting God's beauty isn't merely pretty but overwhelming and dignified, the kind that commands attention rather than simply pleasing the eye.
elements.questionHint: The verse says splendor 'emanates from him' rather than being placed on him — what's the difference between beauty that radiates out of someone and beauty that's added to them from outside?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> At that time the Lord who commands armies will become a beautiful crown

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is beautiful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The image is striking: God himself 'will become a beautiful crown' for his people, not merely give them a crown or wear one himself. A crown marks honor, royalty, and glory, so this pictures God as the very source and substance of his people's honor — their beauty and dignity will come from him personally, not from their own achievements. Even the title used, 'the Lord who commands armies,' pairs power with beauty in the same figure, so that strength and splendor aren't opposites in God but come together.
elements.questionHint: The verse says God himself will 'become' a crown, not that he'll give one — what does it mean for God to be the source of his people's beauty rather than just a giver of it?

elements.text: 4. Righteousness & Justice – God is perfect and impartial; His justice is rooted in His righteousness.

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> As for the Rock, his work is perfect,

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is righteous and just?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Calling God 'the Rock' evokes stability and reliability, and pairing that title with 'his work is perfect' ties God's justice to the flawlessness of what he does, not merely what he says. Even from this short line, the logic is that a being as solid and unshifting as a rock does work that matches — nothing careless, arbitrary, or unfinished. Justice, on this reading, is simply what perfect work looks like when it touches how God treats people.
elements.questionHint: Why call God 'the Rock' right before describing his work as 'perfect' — what does the image of an unmovable rock suggest about how reliably just that work will be?

elements.passageText: <sup>7</sup> But the Lord rules forever; <sup>8</sup> He judges the world fairly;

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is righteous and just?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The two clauses here are linked: because the Lord 'rules forever,' his judgment of the world is 'fairly' administered — his justice isn't a temporary policy that could later change or be revoked, it's backed by an eternal reign. An earthly judge's fairness can be undone by death, corruption, or a change in power; this verse roots the fairness of God's judgment in the permanence of his rule, which never ends and is never handed off to someone less trustworthy.
elements.questionHint: The verse connects God's eternal rule with judging 'fairly' — why would a judgeship that never ends be more trustworthy than one that could someday change hands?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> To do righteousness and justice

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is righteous and just?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Even in this short phrase, righteousness and justice are named as things to be 'done' — active, practiced realities, not just abstract qualities to admire. Proverbs consistently treats wisdom as behavior rather than mere belief, and grouping 'righteousness and justice' together as a pair to actually do suggests these aren't separate ideas but two sides of the same practical commitment: doing right by God and doing right by other people at the same time.
elements.questionHint: The phrase pairs 'righteousness and justice' together as things 'to do' — what does putting them side by side, as a single pair of actions, suggest about how closely related they are?

elements.passageText: <sup>24</sup> If people want to boast, they should boast about this:

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is righteous and just?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This line is only the setup for what follows in the passage — Jeremiah is about to say what's actually worth boasting in, as opposed to wisdom, strength, or wealth. Even in this introductory clause, the implication is that whatever ground is legitimate for human boasting must come from outside ourselves, from knowing something true about God rather than admiring our own qualities. It reframes justice, alongside righteousness and covenant love, as the kind of knowledge so significant that grasping it becomes the one thing genuinely worth being proud of.
elements.questionHint: This verse is only the introduction — it says people 'should boast about this' but doesn't yet say what 'this' is. Based on the chapter's theme, what about God's justice do you think Jeremiah is about to say makes it worth boasting about instead of wisdom or wealth?

elements.passageText: <sup>25</sup> God publicly displayed him at his death as the mercy seat accessible through faith. This was to demonstrate his righteousness, because God in his forbearance had passed over the sins previously committed. <sup>26</sup> This was also to demonstrate his righteousness in the present time, so that he would be just and the justifier of the one who lives because of Jesus’ faithfulness.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is righteous and just?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul is solving a problem: how could God have 'passed over' sins committed before Christ without compromising his own righteousness? The answer is the cross — God 'publicly displayed' Christ as the mercy seat so that his righteousness would be demonstrated, not set aside, when he forgives. The striking phrase is 'just and the justifier' — God doesn't overlook sin to be merciful, and he doesn't punish sin at the expense of mercy; the death of Christ lets him do both at once, remaining fully just while still declaring sinners righteous through faith.
elements.questionHint: Paul says God had to demonstrate his righteousness so that he could be both 'just and the justifier' at the same time — why would forgiving sin threaten God's justice unless something like the cross accounted for it?

elements.text: 5. Truthfulness – God’s words are true, and God Himself is the final standard of truth.

elements.passageText: <sup>19</sup> God is not a man, that he should lie,

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is truthful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Balaam states the contrast directly: God is 'not a man,' and lying is treated as a characteristically human failure that simply doesn't apply to God's nature. The comparison implies that human speech is unreliable enough that we build in the expectation people might lie, but that expectation has no basis when it comes to God — his difference from humanity isn't just in power but in the trustworthiness of his word.
elements.questionHint: The verse grounds God's truthfulness in the fact that he is 'not a man' — what is it about being human that makes lying possible, and why would God's difference from that rule it out?

elements.passageText:
119:160 Your instructions are totally reliable;
all your just regulations endure.


17:17 Set them apart in the truth; your word is truth.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is truthful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalmist says God's instructions are 'totally reliable' and his regulations 'endure' — meaning their truthfulness isn't just accurate at the moment they were given, it holds up over time without needing revision or retraction. Jesus' prayer takes this even further: he doesn't just say God's word is true, he says it 'is truth,' making truth practically identical with what God has spoken. Put together, these verses show truthfulness isn't one quality among many in God's word — it's what makes it capable of setting people apart, since something less than fully true couldn't be trusted to do that.
elements.questionHint: The psalm says God's regulations 'endure' and Jesus says God's word 'is truth' rather than merely 'contains' truth — what's the difference between a word that is true and one that simply is truth itself?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> Jesus replied, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is truthful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus doesn't say he teaches the truth or points toward it — he says 'I am... the truth,' identifying himself personally with it. That's a much larger claim than being a reliable source of information; it means truth about God and reality is ultimately found in a person, not just a set of accurate statements. The exclusive claim that follows, 'no one comes to the Father except through me,' only makes sense if he really is what he claims — an untrue mediator couldn't guarantee anyone's access to God.
elements.questionHint: Jesus says 'I am... the truth' rather than 'I speak the truth' — what's the difference between someone who tells the truth and someone who claims to be it?

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup> in hope of eternal life, which God, who does not lie, promised before the ages began.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is truthful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul grounds the hope of eternal life in a specific description of God: he is the one 'who does not lie.' That phrase is doing real work — the reliability of the promise depends entirely on the reliability of the promiser, and Paul reminds readers that this promise was made 'before the ages began,' long before there was any way to verify it in the moment. Trusting a promise made that far in advance, about something as significant as eternal life, only makes sense if the one who made it is incapable of deception.
elements.questionHint: Why does Paul specifically mention that God 'does not lie' right before talking about a promise made 'before the ages began' — what would be at stake if a promise that old came from someone untrustworthy?

elements.passageText: <sup>18</sup> so that we who have found refuge in him may find strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us through two unchangeable things, since it is impossible for God to lie.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is truthful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The author doesn't say it's simply unlikely for God to lie — he says it's 'impossible.' That's a claim about God's nature, not just his track record or good intentions; lying is something God cannot do, the way a shadow cannot exist without light being blocked. Because of that impossibility, the 'two unchangeable things' — God's promise and his oath — give 'strong encouragement' to hold on to hope. The confidence isn't in our own grip on the hope but in the fact that what we're holding onto cannot be false.
elements.questionHint: The verse says it's 'impossible' for God to lie, not just unlikely — what's the difference between someone who tends to be honest and someone for whom lying is simply not possible?

elements.text: 6. Faithfulness – God is always faithful to His promises and His own character.

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> So realize that the Lord your God is the true God, the faithful God who keeps covenant faithfully with those who love him and keep his commandments, to a thousand generations,

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is faithful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Moses ties God's faithfulness directly to the covenant — he 'keeps covenant faithfully,' meaning his reliability isn't abstract but shows up concretely in keeping the specific commitments he has made. The phrase 'to a thousand generations' pushes the timescale far beyond anything one person could witness, meaning faithfulness for God isn't measured verse by verse or year by year but across a span longer than any human family could track on its own. It's also worth noticing the command to 'realize' this — Israel's confidence is meant to rest on knowing this fact, not on guessing at his intentions.
elements.questionHint: The verse specifies God's faithfulness lasts 'to a thousand generations' — why use a number that far exceeds any single lifetime to describe how long his covenant faithfulness holds?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> For the Lord ’s decrees are just,

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is faithful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Even this short fragment ties God's faithfulness to something concrete and examinable: his 'decrees,' his actual spoken commands. Calling them 'just' means they can be trusted to reflect what is actually right, not just what happens to be convenient or arbitrary. A faithful God is one whose words match reality and whose commands don't have to be second-guessed for hidden unfairness.
elements.questionHint: The verse calls God's decrees 'just' — what does the justice of what God actually commands or decrees have to do with whether he can be counted on to be faithful?

elements.passageText:
5 For the Lord is good.
His loyal love endures,
and he is faithful through all generations.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is faithful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This is a bare, simple declaration with no qualification or exception attached: 'the Lord is good.' Its simplicity is part of the point — the psalmist doesn't need to build an elaborate case, because this is meant to be a settled, foundational truth that everything else about trusting and thanking God rests on. A faithfulness that flows from genuine goodness isn't reluctant or forced; it's the natural expression of who God already is, which is exactly why the rest of the psalm can call people to thanksgiving without hesitation.
elements.questionHint: The verse states plainly that God 'is good' with no conditions attached — why might a simple, unqualified statement like this be a more solid foundation for trusting his faithfulness than a longer argument would be?

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> God is faithful, by whom you were called into fellowship with his son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is faithful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul connects God's faithfulness directly to an action he has already taken: calling believers 'into fellowship with his Son.' The faithfulness isn't abstract or merely a character trait admired from a distance — it's the reason a specific relationship now exists between believers and Christ. Because God is the one who called them, and God is faithful, the relationship he initiated can be trusted to hold; it doesn't depend on the shifting reliability of the people who were called into it.
elements.questionHint: Paul says 'God is faithful' right after mentioning that he 'called you into fellowship with his Son' — whose reliability is this fellowship resting on, God's or ours?

elements.passageText: <sup>23</sup> And let us hold unwaveringly to the hope that we confess, for the one who made the promise is trustworthy.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is faithful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The instruction to 'hold unwaveringly' is grounded entirely in a reason given at the end: 'the one who made the promise is trustworthy.' The steadiness asked of believers is meant to mirror the steadiness of the one they're trusting — an unwavering grip makes sense only because the promise-maker himself doesn't waver. This flips the usual logic: instead of hope needing to be strong enough on its own to hold up under pressure, the verse locates the strength in God's trustworthiness, which the believer simply relies on.
elements.questionHint: The verse gives a reason for holding on 'unwaveringly' — is the reason something about the believer's own strength, or something about the character of the one who made the promise?

elements.text: 7. Self-control – God acts according to His will, not swayed by external circumstance.

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> The Lord passed by before him and proclaimed: “The Lord , the Lord , the compassionate and gracious God, slow to anger, and abounding in loyal love and faithfulness,

elements.question: How does this verse show that God exercises self-control?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This is God's own self-description, given directly to Moses, and the phrase 'slow to anger' is essentially a statement about self-control: God is not quick-tempered or reactive despite having every right to be, given what Israel had just done with the golden calf. Being 'slow' to anger implies restraint that could be exercised otherwise — anger is a real and legitimate response available to God, but he governs its release rather than being driven by it. That restraint is paired with, not opposed to, being 'abounding in loyal love,' showing that self-control here serves love rather than suppressing it.
elements.questionHint: God describes himself as 'slow to anger' rather than 'never angry' — what's the difference between someone who has no anger and someone who has anger but exercises restraint over it?

elements.passageText:
38 Yet he is compassionate.
He forgives sin and does not destroy.
He often holds back his anger,
and does not stir up his fury.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God exercises self-control?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalm has just finished cataloging Israel's repeated rebellion, which makes the word 'yet' carry real weight — despite ample provocation, God 'often holds back his anger.' That phrase pictures anger as a real force being actively restrained, not absent altogether; God 'does not stir up his fury,' as though he could easily provoke it further in himself but deliberately chooses not to. Self-control, in this verse, isn't the absence of a reaction God could justly have, but the deliberate holding back of a reaction that would otherwise be entirely warranted.
elements.questionHint: The verse says God 'often holds back his anger' rather than saying he has no anger to hold back — what does 'holds back' suggest about anger being present but restrained rather than simply missing?

elements.passageText:
8 The Lord is compassionate and merciful;
he is patient and demonstrates great loyal love.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God exercises self-control?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The word translated 'patient' here carries the idea of being 'long-tempered' rather than quick-tempered, the opposite image of someone who flares up easily. Pairing patience with compassion and mercy in the same breath shows that God's self-control isn't cold restraint for its own sake; it exists in the same character as warmth and loyal love. He isn't patient because he's indifferent to sin, but because compassion and mercy shape how he chooses to respond to it.
elements.questionHint: The verse lists 'patient' right alongside 'compassionate' and 'merciful' — what does grouping patience together with those warmer qualities suggest about why God restrains himself rather than simply not caring?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> Or do you have contempt for the wealth of his kindness, forbearance, and patience, and yet do not know that God’s kindness leads you to repentance?

elements.question: How does this verse show that God exercises self-control?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul calls God's kindness, forbearance, and patience a 'wealth' — an abundance, not a thin or grudging reserve of restraint. And he makes clear this self-control has a purpose: it 'leads you to repentance,' meaning God's holding back isn't passive tolerance of sin but an active strategy aimed at bringing people to change. Paul's rebuke — that some show 'contempt' for this — implies that mistaking patience for indifference or weakness is a serious misreading of what God is actually doing by not immediately acting in judgment.
elements.questionHint: Paul says God's patience is meant to 'lead you to repentance' — what does that purpose tell you about whether God's self-control is passive indifference or an active, purposeful choice?

elements.passageText: <sup>13</sup> Let no one say when he is tempted, “I am tempted by God,” for God cannot be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God exercises self-control?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: James rules out two things at once: God 'cannot be tempted by evil,' and he 'tempts no one.' The first is a statement about God's own internal constitution — evil has no pull on him whatsoever, unlike humans who can be drawn toward wrongdoing. The second follows from the first: because evil holds no attraction for God, he has no motive to draw others toward it either. This is self-control taken to its logical limit — not simply resisting temptation but existing in a state where temptation gets no traction at all.
elements.questionHint: James says God 'cannot' be tempted by evil, not that he simply resists it — what's the difference between successfully resisting temptation and being a being that temptation has no power over in the first place?

elements.text: 8. Goodness – God is Himself good and is the standard and source of goodness.

elements.passageText: <sup>8</sup> Taste and see that the Lord is good! How blessed is the one who takes shelter in him!

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is good?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalmist invites experience, not just assent — 'taste and see,' as if God's goodness is meant to be personally sampled rather than merely affirmed as doctrine. That verb choice suggests a kind of knowledge you can only get by direct contact, the way you can't fully understand a flavor from a description alone. The second line ties this tasting to refuge: the 'blessed' person is the one who 'takes shelter in him,' meaning experiencing God's goodness happens specifically through trusting him for protection, not from a safe distance.
elements.questionHint: The psalmist says 'taste and see' rather than 'believe' or 'consider' — what kind of knowledge do you get from tasting something that you can't get just from being told about it?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> For the Lord is good.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is good?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The declaration stands on its own, unqualified by circumstance: 'the Lord is good.' It doesn't say God is good when things go well or good by comparison to something worse — it's stated as a plain, unconditional fact about his character. Coming in a psalm devoted to thanksgiving and worship, this simple statement functions as the reason for everything else the psalm calls people to do: entering God's gates with thanksgiving only makes sense as a response to a God whose goodness is this straightforward and certain.
elements.questionHint: This same phrase is used elsewhere for God's faithfulness — what does the word 'good' add here, specifically about his basic character, beyond just being reliable?

elements.passageText: <sup>7</sup> The Lord is good –

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is good?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Even the punctuation matters here — the sentence trails off with a dash, as if goodness is about to be explained further by what God does for those in trouble. Nahum is otherwise a book largely about God's judgment on Nineveh, so this declaration of goodness stands out: even a prophet focused on pronouncing coming judgment pauses to affirm, without qualification, that the Lord is good. Goodness and justice toward the wicked aren't presented as competing ideas in this book — they belong to the same God.
elements.questionHint: This line appears in a book largely about God's judgment on a wicked nation — why would the prophet still pause to declare, without qualification, that 'the Lord is good'?

elements.passageText: <sup>18</sup> Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is good?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus doesn't deny being good; he questions the rich man's casual use of the word, pointing out that goodness in the fullest sense belongs to God 'alone.' This sets an extremely high bar for what genuine goodness actually requires — not the relative decency we apply to people who are kind or well-behaved, but an absolute standard that only God meets. Read alongside the rest of the New Testament's claims about Jesus' identity, the question actually presses the man to consider what he's implying about Jesus by calling him good so easily — is he prepared to say Jesus is God?
elements.questionHint: Jesus questions why the man called him 'good' and says only God is good in that ultimate sense — what does that response actually invite the man to consider about who Jesus is?

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup> All generous giving and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or the slightest hint of change.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is good?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: James traces every truly good thing back to a single source: 'the Father of lights,' from whom 'all generous giving and every perfect gift' descends. The phrase 'no variation or the slightest hint of change' is the key to his point — unlike the sun or moon, the 'lights' in view, which cast shifting shadows and cycle through phases, God's goodness never flickers, dims, or turns to something else. That consistency is what makes every gift from him reliably 'good' and 'perfect,' not just occasionally so.
elements.questionHint: James contrasts God with the 'lights' in the sky, which change and cast shifting shadows — what does saying there is 'no variation' in God tell you about how consistent his goodness is compared to those lights?

elements.text: 9. Kindness – God’s kindness reflects His boundless love for all creation.

elements.passageText:
20:14While I am still alive, extend to me the loyalty of the Lord, or else I will die!


22:51 He gives his chosen king magnificent victories;
he is faithful to his chosen ruler,
to David and to his descendants forever!”


3:6 Solomon replied, “You demonstrated great loyalty to your servant, my father David, as he served you faithfully, properly, and sincerely. You have maintained this great loyalty to this day by allowing his son to sit on his throne.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is kind?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: These three moments trace kindness across generations of one family's story. Jonathan asks David to show him 'the loyalty of the Lord,' treating God's own kindness as the model and standard for how people should treat each other. David later testifies that God was faithful and kind 'to David and to his descendants forever,' and Solomon, inheriting the throne, recognizes that God 'maintained this great loyalty' by letting him sit on his father's throne. Read together, God's kindness isn't a single event but a thread that holds steady across an entire family line, outlasting each individual person in the story.
elements.questionHint: Notice these three passages span three generations of one family — what does it mean that the 'loyalty' or kindness described keeps showing up long after the original recipient, David, is gone?

elements.passageText: <sup>7</sup> Our ancestors in Egypt failed to appreciate your miraculous deeds, they failed to remember your many acts of loyal love, and they rebelled at the sea, by the Red Sea.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is kind?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This verse is actually a confession of failure, not praise — Israel's ancestors 'failed to appreciate' and 'failed to remember' God's kindness even while it was actively being shown to them at the Red Sea. That failure highlights the kindness by contrast: God's 'many acts of loyal love' were real and repeated, even though the people receiving them were too focused on their fear to notice or be grateful. Kindness given doesn't depend on being properly recognized by its recipients to remain real.
elements.questionHint: This verse describes people failing to notice God's kindness right as it was happening — what does that failure to appreciate it tell you about whether the kindness itself was still genuinely there?

elements.passageText: <sup>8</sup> In a burst of anger I rejected you momentarily, but with lasting devotion I will have compassion on you,” says your protector, the Lord.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is kind?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God contrasts two timeframes directly: anger that lasted only 'momentarily' against 'lasting devotion' that produces compassion. The imbalance is the point — whatever discipline or rejection Israel experienced was brief and temporary, while the kindness that follows is described as enduring. God doesn't deny the anger happened, but he refuses to let it define the relationship the way his lasting devotion does; the momentary and the lasting aren't given equal weight.
elements.questionHint: The verse contrasts anger that was only 'momentary' with devotion that is 'lasting' — why does God specifically point out how brief the anger was compared to how long the kindness lasts?

elements.passageText: <sup>7</sup> I will tell of the faithful acts of the Lord, of the Lord’s praiseworthy deeds. I will tell about all the Lord did for us, the many good things he did for the family of Israel, because of his compassion and great faithfulness.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is kind?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The prophet commits himself to telling this story — repeating 'I will tell' — because the kindness in view isn't a single act but 'many good things' accumulated over Israel's history. He specifies the source of all these deeds at the end: 'because of his compassion and great faithfulness,' tracing every good thing God did back to something in God's own character rather than anything Israel had done to deserve it. Kindness like this, recounted deed after deed, becomes something worth retelling rather than a fact simply stated once.
elements.questionHint: The prophet repeats 'I will tell' multiple times about God's deeds — why might rehearsing many specific acts, rather than one, be the fitting response to the kind of kindness described here?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> But “when the kindness of God our Savior and his love for mankind appeared, <sup>5</sup> he saved us not by works of righteousness that we have done but on the basis of his mercy, through the washing of the new birth and the renewing of the Holy Spirit,

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is kind?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says God's kindness 'appeared' — as if it had a moment of arrival, presumably referring to the coming of Christ, giving kindness a concrete, historical anchor rather than leaving it a vague attribute. And he's careful to specify what this kindness did not do: it didn't save 'by works of righteousness that we have done.' Kindness that operated on the basis of merit would stop being kindness; instead it acted 'on the basis of his mercy,' producing what Paul calls 'new birth,' a total renewal rather than a reward for good behavior.
elements.questionHint: Paul specifically says salvation came 'not by works of righteousness that we have done' — why would kindness that depended on our own good works stop being kindness at all?

elements.text: 10. Patience – God is long-suffering, slow to wrath, willing to forgive.

elements.passageText: <sup>18</sup> ‘The Lord is slow to anger and abounding in loyal love, forgiving iniquity and transgression, but by no means clearing the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children until the third and fourth generations.’

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is patient?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Moses quotes God's own self-revelation back to him after Israel's rebellion, and the verse holds two things together that might seem to be in tension: God is 'slow to anger' and forgiving, yet he 'by no means' clears the guilty. Patience, in other words, isn't the same as permissiveness — God can delay judgment and forgive freely without pretending guilt doesn't matter or simply ignoring it. This is patience with real moral seriousness attached, not patience because sin doesn't ultimately count.
elements.questionHint: The verse says God forgives, yet 'by no means' clears the guilty, in the same breath — how can patience and forgiveness coexist with a refusal to just overlook guilt entirely?

elements.passageText: <sup>15</sup> But you, O Lord, are a compassionate and merciful God. You are patient and demonstrate great loyal love and faithfulness.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is patient?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: David lists patience alongside compassion, mercy, loyal love, and faithfulness as though they're all facets of the same character rather than separate virtues. The word order matters a little: compassion and mercy come first, then patience follows as almost their natural outworking, because God is compassionate, he is willing to wait rather than react immediately. This is a psalm of personal appeal, so this list functions as the ground for David's confidence that God will actually respond to him.
elements.questionHint: Patience is listed right alongside compassion and mercy here — what does grouping it with those qualities suggest about why God is willing to wait rather than react right away?

elements.passageText:
18 There is no other God like you!
You forgive sin
and pardon the rebellion
of those who remain among your people.
You do not remain angry forever,
but delight in showing loyal love.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is patient?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Micah frames God's patience as part of what makes him unique — 'there is no other God like you' — specifically because he 'does not remain angry forever.' The contrast implied is with an anger, human or otherwise, that once provoked simply doesn't let up; God's anger has a limit, but his loyal love does not. And that limit isn't grudging — Micah says God 'delights' in showing loyal love, meaning the patience that lets his anger subside flows from something he actually takes pleasure in doing, not reluctant restraint.
elements.questionHint: Micah says God's uniqueness is partly that he 'does not remain angry forever' — what would it mean for anger to have no limit, and why does God's patience matter as part of what sets him apart from that?

elements.passageText: <sup>16</sup> But here is why I was treated with mercy: so that in me as the worst, Christ Jesus could demonstrate his utmost patience, as an example for those who are going to believe in him for eternal life.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is patient?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul calls himself 'the worst' of sinners and says that's exactly the point — God chose the most extreme case available to display Christ's 'utmost patience.' If patience could hold out even for someone like Paul, a persecutor of the church by his own account, then no later believer needs to wonder whether they're too far gone to be received. Paul's own life becomes evidence, an 'example,' meant to reassure future believers that this patience isn't rationed out to easy cases only.
elements.questionHint: Paul specifically calls himself the 'worst' case as a deliberate 'example' for others — why would demonstrating patience toward the worst case, rather than an easy one, be more convincing evidence of just how patient Christ is?

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some regard slowness, but is being patient toward you, because he does not wish for any to perish but for all to come to repentance.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is patient?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter directly reinterprets what looks like delay: what some call 'slowness' is actually God 'being patient.' The distinction matters — slowness implies a failure to act on time, while patience implies a deliberate choice to wait for a good reason. Peter gives that reason explicitly: God 'does not wish for any to perish but for all to come to repentance.' The apparent delay in judgment isn't inaction; it's time being extended on purpose so more people have the chance to respond.
elements.questionHint: Peter distinguishes between 'slowness' and being 'patient' — what's the difference between a delay caused by inability and a delay chosen on purpose for a stated reason?

elements.text: 11. Joy – God is Himself joyful and is the source of joy.

elements.passageText:
27 Majestic splendor emanates from him,
he is the source of strength and joy.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is joyful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This verse calls God 'the source of... joy' — not merely someone who experiences joy or occasionally grants it, but the wellspring joy actually comes from. Pairing joy with 'strength' in the very same phrase suggests the two aren't unrelated for God: strength and gladness belong together rather than joy being a soft or fragile thing set against sturdier qualities like power. If God himself is the fountainhead of joy, then any joy anywhere ultimately traces back to him.
elements.questionHint: The verse calls God the 'source' of joy rather than someone who merely feels or gives it occasionally — what's the difference between a source of something and just a place where it sometimes shows up?

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> He said to them, “Go and eat delicacies and drink sweet drinks and send portions to those for whom nothing is prepared. For this day is holy to our Lord. Do not grieve, for the joy of the lord is your strength.”

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is joyful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Nehemiah tells the people not to weep, since they had just heard the Law read and were convicted, but to celebrate instead, because 'the joy of the Lord is your strength.' That phrase can be read as God's own joy becoming the people's source of strength, not their own manufactured happiness, but a joy that originates with him and gets shared with those who belong to him. It's telling that this joy is commanded in response to a holy day and is meant to be generous, extending even to those who have nothing prepared, rather than kept for those who can afford a feast.
elements.questionHint: The phrase is 'the joy of the Lord is your strength' — whose joy is described as the source of the people's strength, theirs or God's?

elements.passageText:
17 The Lord your God is in your midst;
he is a warrior who can deliver.
He takes great delight in you;
he renews you by his love;
he shouts for joy over you.”

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is joyful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The final image of this verse is unexpected: God doesn't just approve of his people or forgive them quietly, he 'shouts for joy over you,' language usually reserved for celebration and festival, now applied to God's own reaction to his people. Combined with 'he takes great delight in you,' this shows God's joy isn't distant satisfaction but something exuberant and vocal, directed personally at the very people he is also described as delivering like a warrior. Rescue and celebration happen together in the same verse.
elements.questionHint: The verse says God 'shouts for joy' over his people, the kind of expression used at a celebration — what does using festival language for God's own reaction tell you about how restrained or exuberant his joy is?

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> In the same way, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of God’s angels over one sinner who repents.”

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is joyful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus specifies the trigger for this joy precisely: 'one sinner who repents,' not a crowd, not a nation, just a single person turning back. That specificity, at the end of a chapter built around parables of a lost sheep and a lost coin, shows that heaven's celebration doesn't wait for large-scale results; the return of even one person is enough to set off real joy 'in the presence of God's angels,' implying this is joy that happens around God himself, not merely joy angels feel independently.
elements.questionHint: Jesus says there is joy over 'one sinner' who repents, not over large numbers — why would the return of just a single person be enough to trigger this kind of celebration?

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup> I have told you these things so that my joy may be in you, and your joy may be complete.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is joyful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus states his purpose directly: he has been teaching, about the vine and branches, just before this, so that 'my joy' would be 'in you.' The joy being offered isn't a generic emotion generated by circumstances; it's specifically Jesus' own joy, transferred into his disciples so that theirs becomes 'complete.' That word 'complete' suggests that without this transferred joy, something would be missing or unfinished; joy for the disciple isn't self-generated but received from staying connected to Jesus, as the vine imagery just before this verse implies.
elements.questionHint: Jesus says he wants 'my joy' to be in the disciples so their joy becomes 'complete' — whose joy is the source here, and what does 'complete' suggest was missing before?

elements.text: 12. Grace – God gives us blessings we do not deserve.

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> But he said to me, “My grace is enough for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” So then, I will boast most gladly about my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may reside in me.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is gracious?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God's answer to Paul's request for relief isn't removal of the problem but a statement about grace: 'my grace is enough for you.' The word 'enough' matters — grace isn't offered as one resource among several Paul might need, it's declared sufficient on its own, even while the weakness remains unresolved. The paradox that follows, power 'made perfect in weakness,' turns the normal expectation upside down: grace doesn't merely help despite weakness, it actually operates through it, which is why Paul can respond by boasting in the very thing he originally wanted taken away.
elements.questionHint: God says his grace is 'enough' rather than removing Paul's weakness — what does it mean for grace to be sufficient in a hard situation instead of just eliminating the hardship?

elements.passageText: and he raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus, 7 to demonstrate in the coming ages the surpassing wealth of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus. 8 For by grace you are saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God; 9 it is not from works, so that no one can boast.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is gracious?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul says God's purpose in raising and seating believers with Christ is 'to demonstrate... the surpassing wealth of his grace' — meaning grace isn't just the means of salvation but something God intends to put on permanent display 'in the coming ages,' as though eternity itself will keep unfolding just how much grace was involved. The famous line that follows nails down where this grace originates: salvation is 'not from yourselves,' it's 'the gift of God,' explicitly not from works, 'so that no one can boast.' Grace, by definition here, excludes any contribution that could become a basis for self-credit.
elements.questionHint: Paul says salvation is 'the gift of God... not from works, so that no one can boast' — what would change about grace if there were even a small contribution from us that we could take credit for?

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> He is the one who saved us and called us with a holy calling, not based on our works but on his own purpose and grace, granted to us in Christ Jesus before time began,

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is gracious?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul locates the origin of grace before any of us existed to earn or forfeit it: it was 'granted to us in Christ Jesus before time began.' That timing rules out the possibility that grace was a response to anything we did, since we hadn't done anything yet, it flows entirely from God's 'own purpose,' not ours. Calling and salvation are explicitly separated from 'our works,' which means the whole relationship rests on a decision God made about his own purposes long before there was a person around to deserve or reject it.
elements.questionHint: Paul says this grace was granted 'before time began' — why does timing something before we even existed rule out the idea that it was a response to anything we had done?

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup> For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all people.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is gracious?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The verse pictures grace almost like a person or a light source that has 'appeared,' entering history at a definite point rather than being a timeless abstract principle. And its scope is stated broadly: it brings salvation 'to all people,' not a narrow class defined by ethnicity, status, or achievement. Grace here is something that showed up, visibly and historically, almost certainly referring to the coming of Christ, and its arrival is itself described as good news reaching everyone within its scope.
elements.questionHint: The verse says grace 'has appeared,' as if pointing to a specific moment in history — what does describing grace this way, rather than as a timeless idea, suggest about how concretely it entered the world?

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> And, after you have suffered for a little while, the God of all grace who called you to his eternal glory in Christ will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is gracious?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter calls God 'the God of all grace,' a title that ties grace directly to what God is about to do next in the sentence: personally restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish suffering believers. The four verbs piled up show grace isn't a single gesture but a sustained, thorough work, grace that responds to genuine suffering, 'after you have suffered,' by rebuilding what the suffering wore down, rather than simply excusing believers from hardship in the first place.
elements.questionHint: Peter stacks up four verbs — restore, confirm, strengthen, establish — to describe what grace does after suffering, rather than saying grace prevents suffering. What does that stacking of verbs suggest about how thoroughly grace works?

elements.text: 13. Mercy – God refrains from giving us the condemnation we do deserve.

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> Have mercy on me, O God, because of your loyal love! Because of your great compassion, wipe away my rebellious acts!

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is merciful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: David's appeal for mercy is explicitly grounded not in anything about himself but in God's own character: 'because of your loyal love' and 'because of your great compassion.' He isn't arguing that he deserves mercy or minimizing what he's done; the psalm's context, written after his sin with Bathsheba, makes clear he calls his acts 'rebellious.' The basis for mercy is entirely on God's side of the equation, which is exactly why someone as guilty as David can still ask for it with real hope of being heard.
elements.questionHint: David asks for mercy 'because of your loyal love,' not because of anything about himself — whose character is the basis for this request, David's or God's?

elements.passageText: <sup>22</sup> The Lord’s loyal kindness never ceases; his compassions never end. <sup>23</sup> They are fresh every morning; your faithfulness is abundant!

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is merciful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Written in the middle of a book mourning Jerusalem's destruction, this verse insists that God's compassions 'never end' even as the writer surveys genuine devastation. The image of mercy being 'fresh every morning' is striking; it isn't a single reservoir being slowly used up but something renewed daily, so that no matter how bad yesterday was, today's mercy hasn't been depleted by it. Mercy here isn't a static fact but a daily, ongoing supply, matched by faithfulness the writer calls 'abundant.'
elements.questionHint: The verse says God's compassions are 'fresh every morning' rather than a single fixed supply — what does daily renewal suggest about whether yesterday's troubles could use up today's mercy?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> Blessed is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort,

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is merciful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's title for God here is worth pausing on: not simply 'merciful,' but 'the Father of mercies,' as if mercy is something that originates from him the way children come from a parent, he is its source and progenitor. Pairing that with 'God of all comfort' links mercy to comfort directly: the mercy Paul has in mind isn't abstract forgiveness alone but a mercy that produces real comfort for people in real distress, which is exactly the theme Paul develops in the verses that immediately follow.
elements.questionHint: Paul calls God 'the Father of mercies' rather than just 'merciful' — what does describing God as the source or parent of mercies suggest about where all mercy ultimately comes from?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> But God, being rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, <sup>5</sup> even though we were dead in transgressions, made us alive together with Christ – by grace you are saved!

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is merciful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul opens with mercy as the starting point of the whole sentence: 'God, being rich in mercy.' The word 'rich' suggests abundance rather than a bare minimum; this isn't mercy doled out sparingly but overflowing. And the object of that mercy is specified precisely: people who 'were dead in transgressions,' not merely struggling or imperfect. Mercy shown to the spiritually dead has nowhere else to originate except in God himself, since the dead can't do anything to prompt or deserve it.
elements.questionHint: Paul says God is 'rich in mercy' toward people who were 'dead in transgressions' — what does showing mercy to someone who is dead, rather than merely struggling, tell you about what could have prompted that mercy?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> he saved us not by works of righteousness that we have done but on the basis of his mercy, through the washing of the new birth and the renewing of the Holy Spirit,

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is merciful?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul draws a clean line: salvation came 'not by works of righteousness that we have done but on the basis of his mercy.' Mercy, by its nature, responds to need rather than merit; it's the opposite of a reward system, which is why Paul is so careful to rule out 'works' as the basis. And the result of this mercy isn't just pardon; it's 'the washing of the new birth and the renewing of the Holy Spirit,' meaning mercy here doesn't just excuse the past, it produces a genuinely new beginning.
elements.questionHint: Paul says salvation rests 'on the basis of his mercy,' explicitly not on 'works of righteousness that we have done' — what would happen to the meaning of 'mercy' if it were actually earned by our works?

elements.text: 14. Personhood – God is relational, communicative, and interactive.

elements.passageText: <sup>26</sup> Then God said, “Let us make humankind in our image, after our likeness, so they may rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air, over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over all the creatures that move on the earth.”

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is personal?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The plural language, 'let us make... in our image,' along with the deliberate, first-person planning of 'let us,' shows God engaging in something like personal deliberation before he acts, not merely issuing an impersonal decree the way he does for the rest of creation with 'let there be light.' Making humanity 'in our image' establishes a relationship unlike anything else in creation: humans are made to resemble and relate to God in a way fish, birds, and cattle are not, which is exactly why they're given rule over those other creatures rather than being classed alongside them.
elements.questionHint: Notice God says 'let us make' here, unlike the simple commands, 'let there be...', used for the rest of creation — what does that shift in language suggest about how personally involved God is in making humanity specifically?

elements.passageText:
1 The Lord is my shepherd,
I lack nothing.
2 He takes me to lush pastures,
he leads me to refreshing water.
3 He restores my strength.
He leads me down the right paths
for the sake of his reputation.
4 Even when I must walk through the darkest valley,
I fear no danger,
for you are with me;
your rod and your staff reassure me.


1 O Lord, you examine me and know.
2 You know when I sit down and when I get up;
even from far away you understand my motives.
3 You carefully observe me when I travel or when I lie down to rest;
you are aware of everything I do.
4 Certainly my tongue does not frame a word
without you, O Lord, being thoroughly aware of it.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is personal?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Psalm 23 pictures God in the most personal of relational terms, 'my shepherd,' someone who leads, restores, and stays present even 'through the darkest valley,' close enough to reassure with 'your rod and your staff.' Psalm 139 takes the personal dimension even further: God 'examines' and 'knows' the psalmist so thoroughly that he understands his motives 'from far away' and is 'aware of everything I do,' down to words not yet spoken. Together, these psalms describe a God who isn't managing creation from a distance but is intimately acquainted with and present to one individual life.
elements.questionHint: Psalm 139 says God knows the psalmist's motives 'even from far away' and is aware of his words before he speaks them — what kind of relationship involves knowing someone that thoroughly and personally?

elements.passageText: <sup>15</sup> Can a woman forget her baby who nurses at her breast? Can she withhold compassion from the child she has borne? Even if mothers were to forget, I could never forget you!

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is personal?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God reaches for the strongest human bond available, a nursing mother's attachment to her own baby, and then says his own commitment exceeds even that: 'even if mothers were to forget, I could never forget you.' The rhetorical questions assume everyone knows a mother forgetting her nursing child is nearly unthinkable, which makes the final line all the more striking; God is saying his personal attachment to his people surpasses the most intimate, instinctive human relationship anyone could name.
elements.questionHint: God compares his attachment to his people with a nursing mother's bond to her baby, and then says his surpasses even that — why choose the single strongest example of human attachment to make this comparison?

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup> For I know what I have planned for you,’ says the Lord . ‘I have plans to prosper you, not to harm you. I have plans to give you a future filled with hope.

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is personal?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God speaks about specific, individualized plans, 'I know what I have planned for you,' not a generic policy applied uniformly to everyone. The repetition of 'plans' underlines that this isn't vague goodwill but deliberate intention, thought through in advance. Given to exiles in Babylon who had every reason to feel forgotten and anonymous among the nations, this verse insists God's attention toward them is personal and forward-looking, aimed at their genuine welfare rather than harm, even while their present circumstances looked bleak.
elements.questionHint: God says 'I know what I have planned for you,' addressing a specific people rather than making a general statement — what does having specific plans 'for you' suggest about the kind of attention God is giving?

elements.passageText:
6:9 So pray this way: “Our Father in heaven, may your name be honored, ...”


4:6 And because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, who calls “Abba! Father!”

elements.question: How does this verse show that God is personal?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus teaches his disciples to address God as 'Our Father,' a strikingly familial and personal form of address compared to more formal or distant ways ancient people addressed deities. Paul's language in Galatians goes even further into intimacy: the Spirit calls out 'Abba! Father!', an Aramaic term of close, childlike address, closer to 'Papa' than a formal title. That this address is placed by God's own Spirit 'into our hearts' shows the personal relationship isn't something believers work up on their own; it's given to them, prompting the kind of address a child uses with a parent they know well.
