The passive constructions, "regaining of sight," being "set free," point to people receiving something they could not achieve themselves, anointed and sent by "the Spirit of the Lord" through Jesus specifically to bring it about.
elements.questionHint: Jesus lists several kinds of restoration together, good news to the poor, release to captives, sight to the blind, freedom for the oppressed — what does grouping physical healing alongside social and spiritual freedom suggest about how broadly healing is meant here?

elements.passageText: <sup>24</sup> He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we may cease from sinning and live for righteousness. By his wounds you were healed.

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of healing?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The same verse describing substitution ends with a direct healing claim: "by his wounds you were healed." Peter draws this straight from Isaiah's Suffering Servant song and applies it to his readers' actual experience, not a future hope only, but something already true of them, "you were healed," past tense. The healing in view is closely tied to the moral transformation named just before it, ceasing "from sinning" and living "for righteousness," suggesting Peter has primarily spiritual healing in mind, freedom from sin's grip, even though the language is drawn from physical wound-and-cure imagery.
elements.questionHint: Peter says "by his wounds you were healed" right after describing believers ceasing "from sinning and living for righteousness" — given that context, what kind of healing does Peter seem to mean by pairing it with a change in moral behavior rather than physical health?

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup> flowing down the middle of the city’s main street. On each side of the river is the tree of life producing twelve kinds of fruit, yielding its fruit every month of the year. Its leaves are for the healing of the nations.

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of healing?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: In this closing vision of the new creation, healing takes on a permanent, cosmic scope: the leaves of the tree of life "are for the healing of the nations." This tree, producing fruit continuously, "every month of the year," pictures healing not as a one-time event but as an ongoing, abundant, and freely available provision in the eternal city. Significantly, it is "nations," plural and corporate, that are healed here, not just individuals, extending the biblical healing trajectory that began with the Servant's wounds all the way to the full undoing of every fracture, social, spiritual, physical, that sin ever caused among peoples.
elements.questionHint: The tree's leaves bring "healing of the nations," and it bears fruit every month without fail — what does that continuous, abundant supply suggest about healing in the new creation compared to the limited, occasional healings seen earlier in Scripture?

elements.text: 10. Mediation (Legal/Relational Metaphor) – Christ acts as the mediator between God and humanity, bridging the gap caused by sin. His death allows us to come into the presence of a holy God.

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup> But Moses sought the favor of the Lord his God and said, “O Lord, why does your anger burn against your people, whom you have brought out from the land of Egypt with great power and with a mighty hand?

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of mediation?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: After Israel's sin with the golden calf, Moses stands between an angry God and a guilty people, pleading on their behalf: "why does your anger burn against your people?" He doesn't excuse the sin but appeals directly to God, invoking God's own prior actions, "whom you have brought out... with great power," as grounds for mercy. This is mediation in its rawest Old Testament form, a human intercessor stepping into the gap to turn away deserved wrath through prayer and appeal, foreshadowing the greater mediating work of Christ, who intercedes not merely with words but with his own life.
elements.questionHint: Moses asks God why his "anger burns against your people," standing between God's wrath and Israel's guilt — what role is Moses playing by inserting himself into that gap rather than letting judgment simply fall?

elements.passageText: <sup>33</sup> Nor is there an arbiter between us, who might lay his hand on us both,

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of mediation?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Even as a fragment, this line captures Job's lament at the heart of his suffering: he longs for someone able to stand between himself and God, an "arbiter" who could mediate his case, and finds none available. The absence Job names becomes, in the New Testament's later resolution, exactly what Christ supplies, a mediator both able to represent both sides at once and, in Christ's case, actually human and actually divine at the same time. Job's cry for a missing mediator becomes an ache the gospel answers directly.
elements.questionHint: Job complains there is "no arbiter between us" — between himself and God. What kind of person would need to exist to fill that missing role, standing on both sides at once?

elements.passageText: <sup>34</sup> Who is the one who will condemn? Christ is the one who died (and more than that, he was raised), who is at the right hand of God, and who also is interceding for us.

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of mediation?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul stacks up a rapid series of facts about Christ to answer the rhetorical question "who is the one who will condemn?" He "died," was "raised," is "at the right hand of God," and "is interceding for us." That final, present-tense activity is mediation in action: Christ doesn't merely have died for believers in the past; he actively intercedes for them now, from the position of highest authority. The logic of the verse is that no accusation can succeed against those for whom Christ, seated in power, is continually pleading, mediation here functioning as ongoing legal defense against condemnation.
elements.questionHint: Paul lists Christ's death and resurrection but ends on a present-tense action — he "is interceding for us" right now. What does that ongoing, present activity add to what his past death and resurrection already accomplished?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> Jesus replied, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of mediation?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus makes an exclusive claim to mediating access to God: "I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me." The phrase "through me" is the mediating hinge; access to the Father isn't direct or self-achieved, it passes specifically through Jesus. He doesn't merely point toward a way; he claims to be the way itself, meaning mediation here isn't a function Jesus performs alongside other possible routes but the only channel by which anyone actually reaches God.
elements.questionHint: Jesus says no one comes to the Father "except through me" — what does that word "except," ruling out every other route, tell you about how exclusive his role as mediator is meant to be?

elements.passageText: <sup>19</sup> Why then was the law given? It was added because of transgressions, until the arrival of the descendant to whom the promise had been made. It was administered through angels by an intermediary.

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of mediation?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul describes the law's origin as itself mediated: it "was administered through angels by an intermediary," a reference to the tradition that the law was given to Moses through angelic mediation. Paul's point in context is to show the law's more indirect, temporary status compared to God's direct promise to Abraham: the law came through layers of mediation, "through angels," "by an intermediary," and only "until the arrival of the descendant," Christ, to whom the promise belonged. This sets up a contrast the rest of the chapter develops, a law given through secondary mediators versus a promise, and ultimately a mediator, that comes directly and permanently in Christ.
elements.questionHint: Paul notes that the law came "through angels by an intermediary," several layers removed, and only "until" Christ arrived. What does that layered, temporary mediation contrast with regarding how the promise, and ultimately Christ, comes to God's people?

elements.passageText: 5 For there is one God and one intermediary between God and humanity, Christ Jesus, himself human, 6 who gave himself as a ransom for all, revealing God’s purpose at his appointed time.

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of mediation?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This verse states mediation as bare theological fact: "there is one God and one intermediary between God and humanity, Christ Jesus, himself human." The word "one" appears twice, ruling out any other mediator and any plurality of gods; Paul is asserting an exclusive, singular channel between two parties. Crucially, this intermediary is "himself human," meaning he can represent humanity's side genuinely, not merely act as a messenger from God's side. The following clause, his giving himself as a ransom for all, shows that his mediation isn't only representative but also active and costly; he doesn't just stand between, he pays what standing between requires.
elements.questionHint: The verse insists there is "one" God and "one" intermediary, and stresses that this intermediary is "himself human" — why would being genuinely human, not just divine, matter for someone who is supposed to represent humanity's side to God?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> But now Jesus has obtained a superior ministry, since the covenant that he mediates is also better and is enacted on better promises.

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of mediation?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The author compares covenants through the quality of their mediator: Jesus has "obtained a superior ministry" precisely because "the covenant that he mediates is also better." The logic runs both ways: a better mediator secures a better covenant, and a better covenant is "enacted on better promises" because of who mediates it. Mediation here isn't a neutral, mechanical function; the value of what's mediated is bound up with the person doing the mediating, and Jesus's superiority as mediator is what grounds confidence in the promises of the new covenant.
elements.questionHint: The verse says Jesus's ministry is "superior" precisely because "the covenant that he mediates is also better" — what does that link suggest about how the value of a covenant depends on the one who mediates it?

elements.passageText: <sup>15</sup> And so he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the eternal inheritance he has promised, since he died to set them free from the violations committed under the first covenant.

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of mediation?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This verse names Christ specifically as "the mediator of a new covenant" and ties that mediating role directly to his death: it is "since he died" that "those who are called may receive the eternal inheritance he has promised." His mediation isn't a matter of standing between two parties in conversation; it operates by his death dealing with "the violations committed under the first covenant," clearing the obstacle that stood between the people and the promised inheritance. Mediation and sacrifice are fused here; he mediates by dying, not merely by speaking on someone's behalf.
elements.questionHint: The verse says Christ is "the mediator" specifically "since he died" to clear violations under the old covenant — what does that connection tell you about how his mediation works, compared to a mediator who simply negotiates or speaks on someone's behalf?

elements.passageText: <sup>24</sup> and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks of something better than Abel’s does.

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of mediation?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This verse pairs Jesus, "the mediator of a new covenant," with "the sprinkled blood that speaks of something better than Abel's does." Abel's blood, spilled by his brother's violence, cried out from the ground for vengeance, but Christ's sprinkled blood also "speaks," of something better, not a cry for retribution but, in context, a message of grace and access to God. The mediator's role and the blood's voice are named together, showing that Christ mediates the new covenant precisely through this blood, whose message reverses the pattern of blood crying out for judgment.
elements.questionHint: The passage contrasts Christ's blood, which "speaks of something better," with Abel's blood, which cried out for justice against his murderer. What different message does blood that mediates a new covenant speak, compared to blood that cries out for vengeance?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> (My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin.) But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous One,

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of mediation?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John's pastoral purpose, "so that you may not sin," is followed immediately by a provision for when believers do sin: "we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous One." "Advocate" pictures a legal counselor speaking on the accused's behalf, and John specifies where this advocacy happens, "with the Father," meaning access to God's own presence. Christ's qualification for this role is his righteousness; only "the righteous One" can mediate for the unrighteous without conflict of interest. The verse assumes ongoing need, believers do sin, and offers ongoing mediation as the answer.
elements.questionHint: John calls Jesus our "advocate with the Father" specifically because he is "the righteous One" — why would the mediator's own righteousness, rather than just his willingness, matter for his advocacy on behalf of sinners to actually work?

elements.text: 11. Cleansing (Purity Metaphor) – The blood of Christ shed on the cross purifies us from the stain of sin.

elements.passageText: <sup>7</sup> Sprinkle me with water and I will be pure;

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of cleansing?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: David's plea, written after his sin with Bathsheba, pictures cleansing as something done to him by an outside act, "sprinkle me," not something he can accomplish through willpower or resolve. The imagery of sprinkling recalls purification rituals in Israel's worship, applying that external, ceremonial cleansing to David's inward moral guilt. His confidence that he "will be pure" rests entirely on this act being performed, not on any effort of his own; cleansing here is received, requested, and granted, not self-generated.
elements.questionHint: David asks God to "sprinkle" him, using the language of a ritual act done to a person rather than something the person does for themselves — what does that request tell you about David's ability to purify himself from his own sin?

elements.passageText: <sup>18</sup> “Come, let’s consider your options,” says the Lord. “Though your sins have stained you like the color red, you can become white like snow; though they are as easy to see as the color scarlet, you can become white like wool.”

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of cleansing?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God invites Israel into what he frames as reasoned deliberation, "let's consider your options," before making an extraordinary promise: sins "stained... like the color red" or "scarlet" can "become white like snow" or "wool." The color imagery is deliberately vivid and total: scarlet and crimson were notoriously difficult, near-permanent dyes in the ancient world, making the promised change from red to white a picture of complete reversal, not a partial fading. Cleansing here is framed as God's own initiative and invitation, offered even to sin that looks indelible.
elements.questionHint: God compares sin to scarlet and crimson stains, dyes known for being nearly impossible to remove, becoming "white like snow." What does choosing such a stubborn stain as the comparison suggest about how deep the promised cleansing goes?

elements.passageText: <sup>25</sup> I will sprinkle you with pure water and you will be clean from all your impurities. I will purify you from all your idols.

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of cleansing?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God promises a specific ritual action with a comprehensive result: "I will sprinkle you with pure water and you will be clean from all your impurities." As in the cleansing rituals of the law, water applied by sprinkling symbolizes purification, but here the scope is total, "all your impurities," including idols specifically named as the target of this cleansing. This comes in the middle of a larger promise of a new heart and a new spirit, showing that external cleansing from impurity and internal renewal are bound together in God's restoring work; the washing isn't cosmetic but paired with a change of the whole person.
elements.questionHint: God promises cleansing "from all your impurities," specifically naming idols as part of what gets purified — what does pairing water-cleansing with the removal of idols suggest about how thorough this promised purification is meant to be?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> “In that day there will be a fountain opened up for the dynasty of David and the people of Jerusalem to cleanse them from sin and impurity.

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of cleansing?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Zechariah pictures cleansing as an opened, accessible source: "a fountain opened up... to cleanse them from sin and impurity." Unlike a single ritual act performed once, a fountain suggests ongoing, freely flowing availability, cleansing not rationed out sparingly but opened for continual use "for the dynasty of David and the people of Jerusalem." The pairing of "sin and impurity" covers both moral guilt and ceremonial defilement, suggesting the fountain addresses the full range of what separates people from God, made available in "that day," a phrase associated elsewhere in Zechariah with the coming of God's decisive future action.
elements.questionHint: Zechariah pictures cleansing coming from an opened "fountain," not a single washing — what does the image of a continually flowing fountain, rather than a one-time rinse, suggest about the availability of this cleansing?

elements.passageText: <sup>25</sup> Husbands, love your wives just as Christ loved the church and gave himself for her <sup>26</sup> to sanctify her by cleansing her with the washing of the water by the word,

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of cleansing?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul roots the church's cleansing directly in Christ's sacrificial love: he "gave himself for her to sanctify her by cleansing her with the washing of the water by the word." The purpose clause is important; Christ's self-giving has cleansing as its stated goal, tying sacrifice and purification together as one act rather than two separate steps. The phrase "washing of water by the word" suggests that the cleansing happens through the gospel message itself, applied like water, making Christ's sacrificial death effective in the church's life through the proclaimed word.
elements.questionHint: Paul says Christ gave himself "to sanctify her by cleansing her with the washing of the water by the word" — what role does "the word" play in applying the cleansing that his sacrifice accomplished, according to this phrase?

elements.passageText: <sup>14</sup> how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our consciences from dead works to worship the living God.

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of cleansing?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The author builds an argument from lesser to greater, "how much more," to show the superior cleansing power of Christ's sacrifice. Where the old system's blood offerings provided external, ritual cleansing, "the blood of Christ," offered "through the eternal Spirit" and "without blemish," reaches further: it can "purify our consciences from dead works." The target of the cleansing is internal and moral, the conscience, not merely ceremonial, and its purpose is explicitly stated, "to worship the living God," meaning this cleansing removes the guilt that would otherwise bar genuine access to and worship of God.
elements.questionHint: The passage says Christ's blood purifies "our consciences from dead works," not just outward ceremonial defilement like the old sacrifices did — what does targeting the conscience specifically suggest about the depth of this cleansing?

elements.passageText: <sup>22</sup> let us draw near with a sincere heart in the assurance that faith brings, because we have had our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed in pure water.

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of cleansing?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The author describes a two-part cleansing corresponding to inner and outer aspects of a person: "hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience" and "bodies washed in pure water." The sprinkling language recalls the blood rituals of the old covenant now applied to the conscience itself, while the washing evokes the water rites, likely baptism, marking outward identification with that inner cleansing. Because of this double cleansing, believers are told they can "draw near" to God "with a sincere heart in... assurance," cleansing here directly enabling confident access into God's presence rather than the fear and distance sin would otherwise require.
elements.questionHint: The verse pairs hearts "sprinkled clean" with bodies "washed in pure water" — what does having both an inner and outer form of cleansing accomplish for the confidence, "assurance," with which someone can approach God?

elements.passageText: <sup>14</sup> So I said to him, “My lord, you know the answer.” Then he said to me, “These are the ones who have come out of the great tribulation. They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb!

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of cleansing?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This vision answers a question about a vast multitude who have "come out of the great tribulation" with a paradoxical image: "they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb." Ordinarily, blood stains rather than cleans, making this image deliberately startling, the very substance that would soil a garment is what makes these robes pure white. The cleansing described isn't self-achieved through endurance or good works during tribulation; it is credited entirely to the Lamb's blood, applied to those who have come through suffering still trusting in him.
elements.questionHint: The vision says the multitude washed their robes and made them "white" specifically "in the blood of the Lamb" — normally blood stains a garment, so what does it mean that this particular blood makes robes white rather than red?

elements.text: 12. Rescue (Deliverance-from-Danger Metaphor) – Christ saves sinners from peril, particularly sin and death.

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> The spirit of the sovereign Lord is upon me, because the Lord has chosen me. He has commissioned me to encourage the poor, to help the brokenhearted, to decree the release of captives, and the freeing of prisoners,

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of rescue?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This opening line, which Jesus later reads aloud in the Nazareth synagogue, announces that a Spirit-anointed figure is about to describe a mission of rescue, release for captives, comfort for mourners, and good news for the oppressed, developed in the verses that follow this fragment. Even on its own, the claim "the spirit... is upon me" establishes the speaker's authority and empowerment as coming directly from God, not self-appointed, setting up everything that follows as divinely commissioned rescue rather than a human program of reform.
elements.questionHint: This verse opens by grounding everything that follows in the claim that "the spirit of the sovereign Lord is upon me" — what does this specific anointing suggest about the source and authority behind the rescue mission the rest of the passage describes?

elements.passageText: <sup>21</sup> She will give birth to a son and you will name him Jesus, because he will save his people from their sins.”

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of rescue?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The angel's instruction to Joseph gives Jesus's name its explicit meaning: he "will save his people from their sins." The name itself, meaning "the Lord saves," is tied directly to a specific rescue, not primarily from political oppression or physical danger, which many in Israel expected of a messiah, but from sins themselves. This reframes the nature of the rescue at the very moment Jesus's identity is announced: the deepest danger his people need saving from is their own sin, and that rescue is written into his name before his birth.
elements.questionHint: The angel says Jesus will save his people specifically "from their sins" — not from a foreign army or from poverty. What does naming sin as the specific danger being rescued from tell you about what kind of savior this name announces?

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> He delivered us from so great a risk of death, and he will deliver us. We have set our hope on him that he will deliver us yet again,

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of rescue?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul recounts God's rescue in three tenses at once: "he delivered us... he will deliver us... he will deliver us yet again." The repetition of "deliver" ties together Paul's past experience of a "great risk of death," his present confidence, and his future hope into a single, continuous pattern of God's rescuing character. This passage isn't about the cross specifically but reflects the larger biblical pattern the cross establishes: God is a God who delivers his people from mortal danger, and past deliverance becomes grounds for ongoing trust rather than a one-off event.
elements.questionHint: Paul uses the word "deliver" three times, describing past, present, and future rescue — what does stacking the same verb across all three tenses suggest about the reliability and pattern of God's rescuing, rather than it being a single unrepeatable event?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> who gave himself for our sins to rescue us from this present evil age according to the will of our God and Father,

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of rescue?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul compresses the gospel into a single sentence: Christ "gave himself for our sins to rescue us from this present evil age." The rescue in view isn't only from individual sins in isolation but from an entire "age" characterized as "evil," a whole system, era, or way of the world that holds people captive. The rescue happens specifically "for our sins," meaning the mechanism is Christ dealing with sin's guilt, and the result is extraction from bondage to the present world's evil pattern, "according to the will of our God and Father," rooting the whole rescue in God's own plan rather than human effort.
elements.questionHint: Paul says Christ gave himself "to rescue us from this present evil age" — not just from individual sins but from an entire "age." What does describing the rescue in those larger, systemic terms suggest about the scope of what needed to be escaped?

elements.passageText: <sup>13</sup> He delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of the Son he loves,

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of rescue?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul describes rescue as a change of jurisdiction: God "delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of the Son he loves." "Delivered" and "transferred" are paired verbs describing a single decisive move, not just an escape from one place, but a relocation into another, specific kingdom under a specific ruler. The phrase "the power of darkness" names what's being rescued from as an actual dominion with real authority, not merely a bad influence, making the rescue a transfer of allegiance and citizenship as much as a deliverance from danger.
elements.questionHint: Paul pairs two verbs, "delivered... and transferred," describing not just an escape but a move into a new kingdom. What does needing both a deliverance from one power and a transfer into another suggest about what rescue actually involves here?

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus our deliverer from the coming wrath.

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of rescue?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul identifies Jesus specifically as "our deliverer from the coming wrath," locating this future rescue in Jesus's resurrection, "raised from the dead," and anticipated return, "wait for his Son from heaven." The rescue named here is forward-looking, deliverance from a wrath that is still "coming," showing that the cross and resurrection secure not only present forgiveness but also future safety from final judgment. Waiting itself becomes the posture appropriate to this hope: believers live expectantly because the one who will come is the same one already established as their deliverer.
elements.questionHint: Paul calls Jesus "our deliverer from the coming wrath" — wrath that hasn't arrived yet. What does it mean to already call him "deliverer" from a danger that is still future, rather than only from dangers already past?

elements.passageText: <sup>14</sup> Therefore, since the children share in flesh and blood, he likewise shared in their humanity, so that through death he could destroy the one who holds the power of death (that is, the devil), <sup>15</sup> and set free those who were held in slavery all their lives by their fear of death.

elements.question: How does this verse support the metaphor of rescue?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This passage names both the method and the deeper target of Christ's rescue. He shared in "flesh and blood" so that "through death" he could destroy the devil, who "holds the power of death," but the ultimate rescue described goes further still: to "set free those who were held in slavery all their lives by their fear of death." The slavery in view isn't death itself but the fear of it, a psychological and spiritual bondage gripping people "all their lives." By facing death himself and defeating the one wielding it, Christ removes the grounds for that lifelong fear, rescuing people from an internal captivity as much as an external threat.
elements.questionHint: The passage says people were "held in slavery all their lives by their fear of death" — not by death itself but by fear of it. What does defeating the devil's "power of death" do to remove the grounds for that specific, lifelong fear?

elements.text:
Emeka found his answer not in a single sentence but in the whole gallery of pictures the Bible uses for the cross. His legal guilt is dealt with – he is justified, declared not guilty. His estrangement from God is ended – he is reconciled, brought home like the prodigal son. His slavery to sin is broken – he is redeemed, bought back and set free. His shame is answered – he is cleansed, made pure rather than stained. His sickness of soul is met – he is healed, not merely forgiven but restored. His captivity to fear and old habits is ended – he is rescued, delivered from a power greater than himself.

Emeka realised the sentence he’d heard as a boy wasn’t wrong – it just wasn’t the whole picture. The cross is not a single transaction addressing a single problem. It is God’s answer to everything that is broken about being human: guilt and shame, slavery and sickness, estrangement and fear. Whatever Emeka brings to the cross, there is a metaphor there deep enough to meet it.
A Cross-Centred Confidence Scale
