elements.text:
Case Study – Chiamaka (late 20s)

Chiamaka believed the cross mattered. She could explain it to anyone who asked: Jesus died for her sins, took her punishment, made her right with God. That part of the gospel felt settled in her mind.

The resurrection was different. She affirmed it every Easter, sang about the empty tomb, said the words in the creed without hesitation – but if she was honest, it felt more like a happy ending tacked onto the real story than a load-bearing part of her faith. If the cross had already paid for her sin, what exactly was the resurrection for? A miracle to prove Jesus was who He said He was, perhaps. A comforting sign that death isn’t final. But did it actually change anything for her, on an ordinary Tuesday, the way the cross seemed to?

And the ascension confused her even more. Jesus rising into the sky and disappearing from view felt, if anything, like the story trailing off – an exit, not an achievement. She had never heard anyone explain why it mattered that Jesus left.

Chiamaka needed to know: is the empty tomb, and the empty sky, just decoration on top of a gospel that was already complete at the cross – or did Jesus actually achieve something in rising and ascending that she would be missing out on if she skipped straight from Good Friday to now?
Jot down how each verse answers each of the following questions.
1. Why is Jesus’ resurrection so important?

elements.passageText: <sup>14</sup> And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is futile and your faith is empty.

elements.question: Why is Jesus’ resurrection so important?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul draws the plainest possible line: no resurrection, no gospel. He calls the preaching 'futile' — literally without content — and the faith it produced 'empty,' like a container with nothing inside. This isn't a suggestion that resurrection is one helpful feature among many; Paul makes it the hinge on which the entire Christian message turns. Strip it away and you're left with a moral teacher who died and stayed dead, and a message that has nothing left to proclaim. Whatever else Christianity offers — ethics, community, comfort — collapses if this single historical claim is false, which is exactly Paul's point.
elements.questionHint: What does it mean for something Paul calls 'futile' and 'empty' — rather than merely 'less certain' — to describe both the preaching and the faith?

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup> And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is useless; you are still in your sins. <sup>18</sup> Furthermore, those who have fallen asleep in Christ have also perished. <sup>19</sup> For if only in this life we have hope in Christ, we should be pitied more than anyone.

elements.question: Why is Jesus’ resurrection so important?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Here Paul pushes the implication further than in verse 14: without the resurrection, faith isn't just empty, it's 'useless,' because it leaves believers 'still in their sins' — meaning the cross alone, without a risen Christ to validate it, accomplishes nothing for sin. He adds a second casualty: those who died trusting Christ have simply 'perished,' with no hope beyond the grave. And if this life is all Christian hope amounts to, Paul says believers deserve pity more than anyone else on earth — worse off than unbelievers, because they've been building their whole existence on nothing. The resurrection is what keeps Christian hope from becoming the saddest kind of self-deception.
elements.questionHint: Why would being 'still in your sins' depend on whether Christ was raised, rather than simply on whether he died for them?

elements.passageText: <sup>13</sup> But since we have the same spirit of faith as that shown in what has been written, “ I believed; therefore I spoke ,” we also believe, therefore we also speak. <sup>14</sup> We do so because we know that the one who raised up Jesus will also raise us up with Jesus and will bring us with you into his presence.

elements.question: Why is Jesus’ resurrection so important?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul roots his boldness to speak in a specific piece of reasoning: 'we know that the one who raised up Jesus will also raise us up with Jesus.' The same God who acted in Jesus' resurrection is committed to acting the same way toward those united to him — it isn't a separate promise but an extension of the same power and the same intention. That confidence is what lets Paul keep speaking even amid suffering, the context just before this. The resurrection isn't only a past fact to defend; it's the pattern and guarantee for what God will do with believers, ultimately bringing them 'into his presence' alongside Christ.
elements.questionHint: What does linking 'the one who raised up Jesus' to 'will also raise us up' assume about how God treats those united to Jesus?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! By his great mercy he gave us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, <sup>4</sup> that is, into an inheritance imperishable, undefiled, and unfading. It is reserved in heaven for you,

elements.question: Why is Jesus’ resurrection so important?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter doesn't call this merely a hope, but a 'living hope,' and he's specific about its source: it comes 'through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.' A hope grounded in anything else — good intentions, religious effort, wishful thinking — would be static or fragile, but this one is alive because it's tied to an event, a risen person, not an idea. That resurrection also secures something concrete: an inheritance described as imperishable, undefiled, and unfading — three words that each rule out a different way earthly inheritances fail, through decay, corruption, or fading value. Because Jesus was raised, what's waiting for believers in heaven cannot be lost the way everything else eventually is.
elements.questionHint: Why call it a 'living' hope specifically, and what do 'imperishable, undefiled, and unfading' each rule out about the inheritance?

elements.passageText: <sup>31</sup> because he has set a day on which he is going to judge the world in righteousness, by a man whom he designated, having provided proof to everyone by raising him from the dead.”

elements.question: Why is Jesus’ resurrection so important?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul, preaching to Athenian philosophers, presents the resurrection as evidence — 'having provided proof to everyone by raising him from the dead.' The logic runs: God has appointed a day of judgment and a designated judge, and the resurrection is the public credential that certifies Jesus for that role. It isn't just that Jesus survived death; it's that God's raising him functions as a verifiable announcement to 'everyone,' not merely to the disciples. This turns the resurrection into more than personal vindication — it's the basis on which the world will one day be held accountable, because the judge has already been authenticated by an act everyone can examine.
elements.questionHint: What kind of claim does 'proof' function as here — proof of what, specifically, about the 'man' God appointed?

elements.text: 2. How do we know Jesus rose from the dead?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> Now on the first day of the week, at early dawn, the women went to the tomb, taking the aromatic spices they had prepared. <sup>2</sup> They found that the stone had been rolled away from the tomb, <sup>3</sup> but when they went in, they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus. <sup>4</sup> While they were perplexed about this, suddenly two men stood beside them in dazzling attire. <sup>5</sup> The women were terribly frightened and bowed their faces to the ground, but the men said to them, “Why do you look for the living among the dead? <sup>6</sup> He is not here, but has been raised! Remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee, <sup>7</sup> that the Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and on the third day rise again.”

elements.question: How do we know Jesus rose from the dead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The evidence here isn't a single item but several converging details. The women find the tomb open and the body simply gone — not moved, not switched, absent. Then two men in dazzling clothing interpret the empty tomb for them rather than leaving it ambiguous: 'Why do you look for the living among the dead?' presumes he's now alive. Crucially, they anchor this to something Jesus said beforehand in Galilee — that the Son of Man must be crucified and 'on the third day rise again.' The resurrection isn't a surprise improvised after the fact; it fulfills a specific prediction Jesus made in advance, which is part of what makes the empty tomb meaningful rather than merely strange.
elements.questionHint: Why does Luke have the angels remind the women of something Jesus 'told them...in Galilee' rather than just announcing the resurrection on its own?

elements.passageText: <sup>36</sup> While they were saying these things, Jesus himself stood among them and said to them, “Peace be with you.” <sup>37</sup> But they were startled and terrified, thinking they saw a ghost. <sup>38</sup> Then he said to them, “Why are you frightened, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? <sup>39</sup> Look at my hands and my feet; it’s me! Touch me and see; a ghost does not have flesh and bones like you see I have.” <sup>40</sup> When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet. <sup>41</sup> And while they still could not believe it (because of their joy) and were amazed, he said to them, “Do you have anything here to eat?” <sup>42</sup> So they gave him a piece of broiled fish, <sup>43</sup> and he took it and ate it in front of them.

elements.question: How do we know Jesus rose from the dead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Luke stacks up sensory proofs to rule out the most obvious counter-explanation, which the disciples themselves raise: they think they're seeing a ghost. Jesus answers that suspicion directly, point by point — he invites them to look at his hands and feet, to touch him, and states plainly that 'a ghost does not have flesh and bones like you see I have.' Then, almost anticlimactically, he asks for food and eats a piece of fish in front of them. A vision or hallucination doesn't have solid limbs to grip or a digestive system that processes broiled fish. Luke wants readers to see that whatever happened to Jesus, it was bodily and physical, not merely a spiritual appearance or a projection of grief.
elements.questionHint: Why would Jesus specifically address the disciples' fear that he's a 'ghost,' and why does eating fish settle that question in a way that touching might not?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> Then Simon Peter, who had been following him, arrived and went right into the tomb. He saw the strips of linen cloth lying there, <sup>7</sup> and the face cloth, which had been around Jesus’ head, not lying with the strips of linen cloth but rolled up in a place by itself. <sup>8</sup> Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, came in, and he saw and believed. <sup>9</sup> (For they did not yet understand the scripture that Jesus must rise from the dead.) <sup>19</sup> On the evening of that day, the first day of the week, the disciples had gathered together and locked the doors of the place because they were afraid of the Jewish leaders. Jesus came and stood among them and said to them, “Peace be with you.”

elements.question: How do we know Jesus rose from the dead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John lingers over an odd detail: the linen wrappings are still lying there, but the face cloth is 'rolled up in a place by itself' rather than tossed aside. Grave robbers in a hurry don't neatly fold burial cloths — they take the body, wrappings and all, or leave everything in disarray. The orderliness suggests someone left deliberately, not that the body was stolen or moved. John even notes that the beloved disciple 'saw and believed' on the strength of this scene alone, before any appearance. Later that same day, John records, Jesus stands among the disciples behind locked doors — evidence built on both what was left behind in the tomb and what was witnessed afterward.
elements.questionHint: What would grave robbers, in a hurry to remove a body, be unlikely to do with the burial cloths that this scene shows was actually done?

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that by the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead, this man stands before you healthy.

elements.question: How do we know Jesus rose from the dead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter makes this declaration standing before the Jewish authorities in Jerusalem, the very city where Jesus had been crucified only weeks earlier, in front of a man who has just been visibly healed. He doesn't hedge or soften the claim — he names the crucifixion plainly, 'whom you crucified,' and sets God's raising of Jesus directly against it, then points to the healed man as living proof of the power now at work in Jesus' name. This is a public, falsifiable claim made to hostile witnesses who had every motive and opportunity to produce a body or discredit it, not a private testimony offered to friendly ears.
elements.questionHint: Why does it matter that Peter says this to the same authorities, in the same city, so soon after the crucifixion, rather than far away or much later?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve. <sup>6</sup> Then he appeared to more than five hundred of the brothers and sisters at one time, most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep. <sup>7</sup> Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles. <sup>8</sup> Last of all, as though to one born at the wrong time, he appeared to me also.

elements.question: How do we know Jesus rose from the dead?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul lists a chain of specific, named witnesses — Cephas, the Twelve, James, all the apostles — and then more than five hundred people at once, adding a detail that only makes sense as an invitation to check the facts: 'most of whom are still alive.' He's telling the Corinthians that if they doubt him, they can go ask the eyewitnesses themselves, because most were still around to be questioned. Paul even includes his own encounter with the risen Christ, unusual as it was, 'as though to one born at the wrong time,' as part of the same continuous chain of appearances rather than a separate, private experience.
elements.questionHint: Why would Paul mention that most of the five hundred witnesses were 'still alive' rather than simply saying it happened?

elements.text: 3. The Resurrection proclaims Jesus’ victory. What did he achieve?

elements.passageText: <sup>25</sup> He was given over because of our transgressions and was raised for the sake of our justification.

elements.question: The Resurrection proclaims Jesus’ victory. What did he achieve?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul pairs two acts of God as a single unit: Jesus 'was given over because of our transgressions' — that's the cross dealing with sin — 'and was raised for the sake of our justification' — that's the resurrection securing the verdict. The cross alone answers the problem of guilt, but Paul insists the resurrection is what accomplishes justification, as if God's raising Jesus functions as the courtroom announcement that the payment was accepted and the accused is now righteous. Without the resurrection, the cross would be an unconfirmed transaction; with it, believers have a declared, settled status before God. The victory here isn't only over death but over the charge of guilt itself.
elements.questionHint: What is the resurrection doing in this verse that the phrase 'given over because of our transgressions' by itself doesn't already accomplish?

elements.passageText:
19 and what is the incomparable greatness of his power toward us who believe, as displayed in the exercise of his immense strength. 20 This power he exercised in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly realms 21 far above every rule and authority and power and dominion and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come.


6:12 For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the powers, against the world rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavens.

elements.question: The Resurrection proclaims Jesus’ victory. What did he achieve?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul describes the resurrection as an exercise of God's 'immense strength' — the same power that raised Jesus also seated him 'far above every rule and authority and power and dominion,' language that stacks up every conceivable category of spiritual authority underneath Christ's feet. Read alongside 6:12, where Paul names believers' actual opponents as 'the rulers... the powers... the spiritual forces of evil in the heavens,' the point sharpens: the very forces Christians struggle against in this life have already been placed beneath the risen and enthroned Christ. The resurrection isn't just Jesus escaping death — it's God's decisive victory over the hostile spiritual powers that oppose his people, with Christ now ruling above them.
elements.questionHint: Why does Paul use nearly the same list of powers — 'rule and authority and power' in chapter 1, 'rulers... powers' in chapter 6 — in both passages?

elements.passageText: <sup>21</sup> who will transform these humble bodies of ours into the likeness of his glorious body by means of that power by which he is able to subject all things to himself.

elements.question: The Resurrection proclaims Jesus’ victory. What did he achieve?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul locates the resurrection's victory in the future tense here: the same power by which Christ 'is able to subject all things to himself' is the power that will transform 'these humble bodies of ours into the likeness of his glorious body.' The victory Jesus achieved isn't sealed off in the past or confined to his own body — it's a power currently active and cosmic in scope, reaching all the way down to reshaping the ordinary, weak, mortal bodies of believers. What Jesus achieved in his own resurrection becomes the guarantee and the mechanism for what will eventually happen to everyone united to him.
elements.questionHint: What does calling Christ's power sufficient to 'subject all things to himself' suggest about the scope of the transformation promised to 'these humble bodies of ours'?

elements.passageText: <sup>55</sup> “ Where , O death , is your victory? <sup>56</sup> The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.

elements.question: The Resurrection proclaims Jesus’ victory. What did he achieve?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul taunts death directly — 'Where, O death, is your victory?' — because he's just described the resurrection swallowing death up in the verse just before this. Then he explains exactly why death has lost its weapon: 'the sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.' Death's real power was never mere biological ending; it was sin's unresolved verdict backed by the law's condemnation. Because the resurrection vindicates the finished work of the cross, sin's condemning power is broken, and death is left disarmed — still an enemy encountered, but no longer one that can hold anyone permanently, since its sting has been removed.
elements.questionHint: According to Paul, what exactly is death's 'sting' made of, and what would have to happen to that sting for the taunt 'where is your victory' to make sense?

elements.text: 4. How does the Old Testament point forward to Jesus’ Resurrection?

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> You will not abandon me to Sheol;

elements.question: How does the Old Testament point forward to Jesus’ Resurrection?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This short line carries enormous weight: David expresses confidence that God 'will not abandon' him to Sheol, the realm of the dead. Read on its own, it's a statement of trust that death won't have the final say for God's faithful one. Applied to great David's greater Son, it becomes a direct prophecy: God's Holy One would go into death but would not be left there — not simply saved from dying, but rescued out of death after entering it. That's precisely the shape of resurrection rather than mere survival, which is why the apostles later leaned so heavily on this brief verse to explain what happened to Jesus.
elements.questionHint: What's the difference between God keeping someone from dying at all, and God not 'abandoning' someone who has already gone to Sheol?

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> Though the Lord desired to crush him and make him ill, <sup>11</sup> Having suffered, he will reflect on his work,

elements.question: How does the Old Testament point forward to Jesus’ Resurrection?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The passage holds together two things that seem to conflict: the Servant is crushed and made to suffer to the point of death, yet afterward 'he will reflect on his work.' Reflection presupposes conscious existence — you can't look back on what you accomplished if you no longer exist. Isaiah pictures the Servant as one whose suffering ends not in silence but in ongoing life and evaluation of what his suffering achieved. That's the shape of resurrection embedded right in the structure of the prophecy: genuine death giving way to a continued, active existence afterward.
elements.questionHint: How can someone 'reflect on his work' after being crushed and made ill unless something happens to him after the suffering ends?

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup> He will restore us in a very short time;

elements.question: How does the Old Testament point forward to Jesus’ Resurrection?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: In its own context this is Israel's confident hope of national restoration after judgment, but the specific wording — 'a very short time' — carries forward remarkably well into the pattern of Jesus' resurrection: not indefinite exile or abandonment, but a brief, bounded period followed by restoration to life. The verse doesn't describe endless death but death reversed on a short timetable, which is the same shape later readers see fulfilled when Jesus is raised on the third day. It's less a direct prediction naming Jesus than a pattern of God's dealings — brief affliction, swift restoration — that resurrection ultimately fulfills.
elements.questionHint: What does describing the restoration as happening in 'a very short time' rather than after a long or unspecified period suggest about the kind of reversal in view?

elements.passageText:
1:17 The Lord sent a huge fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was in the stomach of the fish three days and three nights.


12:40 For just as Jonah was in the belly of the huge fish for three days and three nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights.

elements.question: How does the Old Testament point forward to Jesus’ Resurrection?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The passage pairs the two halves for us: Jonah spent 'three days and three nights' inside the fish, and Jesus explicitly claims the same span for himself — 'so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights.' Jesus isn't drawing a loose comparison; he's using Jonah's specific ordeal as a predictive sign of his own death and return, matching the exact duration. Jonah's rescue from what was effectively a tomb becomes the pattern Jesus points to in advance, so that when the resurrection happens on schedule, it fulfills a sign Jesus himself had already named.
elements.questionHint: Why does Jesus specify the exact same duration — 'three days and three nights' — rather than just saying Jonah's ordeal is a general parallel to his own?

elements.passageText:
25 As for me, I know that my Redeemer lives,
and that as the last
he will stand upon the earth.
26 And after my skin has been destroyed,
yet in my flesh I will see God,

elements.question: How does the Old Testament point forward to Jesus’ Resurrection?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Job's confession pushes past mere survival of the soul: he insists that 'in my flesh I will see God,' explicitly after his skin 'has been destroyed.' This isn't vague hope for disembodied continuation — Job expects to see God in a body, in some sense still his own, even though his current body will be ruined by death. He also calls God his 'Redeemer' who will 'stand upon the earth' at the last, tying this hope to a future, decisive intervention rather than an abstract afterlife. It's a remarkably early and explicit statement of embodied hope beyond death, anticipating the bodily resurrection Christians later see fulfilled in Christ.
elements.questionHint: Why does Job insist on seeing God 'in my flesh' rather than simply saying his spirit or soul would carry on?

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup> Many of those who sleep in the dusty ground will awake – some to everlasting life, and others to shame and everlasting abhorrence. <sup>3</sup> But the wise will shine like the brightness of the heavenly expanse. And those bringing many to righteousness will be like the stars forever and ever.

elements.question: How does the Old Testament point forward to Jesus’ Resurrection?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Daniel states plainly that those 'who sleep in the dusty ground will awake' — using death as sleep and resurrection as waking, one of the clearest bodily-resurrection statements in the Old Testament. But he doesn't describe a single uniform outcome: some awake 'to everlasting life,' others 'to shame and everlasting abhorrence.' Resurrection here isn't just restoration of life in general; it's tied to a moral reckoning, dividing people by how they lived. The wise and those who turned others to righteousness are promised a shining, star-like glory. This passage gives later resurrection teaching its vocabulary and its structure: bodily waking, everlasting duration, and a judgment built into the resurrection itself.
elements.questionHint: Why does Daniel describe two different destinies at the resurrection — 'everlasting life' and 'shame and everlasting abhorrence' — instead of one shared outcome?

elements.passageText: <sup>12</sup> Therefore prophesy, and tell them, ‘This is what the sovereign Lord says: Look, I am about to open your graves and will raise you from your graves, my people. I will bring you to the land of Israel. <sup>13</sup> Then you will know that I am the Lord , when I open your graves and raise you from your graves, my people. <sup>14</sup> I will place my breath in you and you will live; I will give you rest in your own land. Then you will know that I am the Lord – I have spoken and I will act, declares the Lord .’”

elements.question: How does the Old Testament point forward to Jesus’ Resurrection?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God speaks through Ezekiel using the most literal resurrection imagery imaginable: 'I am about to open your graves and will raise you from your graves,' followed by placing his own 'breath' in them so that 'you will live.' In its immediate setting this pictures Israel's national restoration from exile, not individual bodily resurrection — but the vocabulary God chooses is exactly the vocabulary of graves opening and breath returning to dead bodies. By reaching for resurrection as the picture that best captures restoration, the passage shows how deeply resurrection hope was already embedded in Israel's imagination, ending with a guarantee: 'I have spoken and I will act.'
elements.questionHint: Why would God choose the image of opening graves and breathing life into corpses to describe national restoration, rather than a less dramatic picture?

elements.passageText: <sup>22</sup> I will declare your name to my countrymen! In the middle of the assembly I will praise you! <sup>23</sup> You loyal followers of the Lord, praise him! All you descendants of Jacob, honor him! All you descendants of Israel, stand in awe of him! <sup>24</sup> For he did not despise or detest the suffering of the oppressed; he did not ignore him; when he cried out to him, he responded.

elements.question: How does the Old Testament point forward to Jesus’ Resurrection?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Psalm 22 opens in anguish, 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me,' but the verses here mark a sudden turn: the sufferer now declares God's name 'in the middle of the assembly' and calls the whole community to praise. That shift only makes sense if something has changed his circumstances — the God who seemed absent has in fact 'not despised or detested the suffering of the oppressed' and 'responded' when he cried out. Applied to Christ, whose crucifixion this psalm famously foreshadows, the movement from abandonment to vindicated public praise mirrors the movement from cross to resurrection: suffering that looked God-forsaken is answered, and answered publicly.
elements.questionHint: What change in circumstance would explain the shift from crying out in suffering to declaring God's name publicly 'in the middle of the assembly'?

elements.text: 5. What is the nature of Jesus’ resurrected body (and, by implication, our resurrected bodies)?

elements.passageText: <sup>42</sup> It is the same with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable, what is raised is imperishable. <sup>43</sup> It is sown in dishonor, it is raised in glory; it is sown in weakness, it is raised in power; <sup>44</sup> it is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body.

elements.question: What is the nature of Jesus’ resurrected body (and, by implication, our resurrected bodies)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul uses three paired contrasts — perishable/imperishable, dishonor/glory, weakness/power — before landing on the main one: 'sown a natural body, raised a spiritual body.' Each pair describes the same body undergoing transformation, not one thing being discarded for something unrelated; the verb 'sown' pictures burial like a seed planted, and 'raised' pictures what grows from it, continuous with what went into the ground yet radically changed. 'Spiritual body' doesn't mean immaterial or ghostly — it means a body fully suited to and empowered by the Spirit, no longer subject to decay, shame, or weakness. This is the pattern for every believer's resurrection, following the shape already seen in Christ's own risen body.
elements.questionHint: What does the seed image — 'sown' then 'raised' — suggest about whether the resurrected body is a new, unrelated body or the same body transformed?

elements.passageText: <sup>53</sup> For this perishable body must put on the imperishable, and this mortal body must put on immortality. <sup>54</sup> Now when this perishable puts on the imperishable, and this mortal puts on immortality, then the saying that is written will happen,

elements.question: What is the nature of Jesus’ resurrected body (and, by implication, our resurrected bodies)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's image is clothing, not demolition and replacement: the perishable body 'must put on' the imperishable, the mortal 'must put on' immortality. You put clothes on over something that's still there — the metaphor implies continuity, the same body now covered and completed with a quality it didn't have before, rather than being discarded so a different body can take its place. This is why Paul can speak of 'this perishable' and 'this mortal,' pointing to the actual bodies believers currently have, receiving new properties rather than being replaced by something else entirely. The transformation is real and total, but it happens to the very body sown in death.
elements.questionHint: What does the image of 'putting on' something imply about the relationship between the old, mortal body and the new, immortal one?

elements.passageText: <sup>20</sup> But our citizenship is in heaven – and we also await a savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ, <sup>21</sup> who will transform these humble bodies of ours into the likeness of his glorious body by means of that power by which he is able to subject all things to himself.

elements.question: What is the nature of Jesus’ resurrected body (and, by implication, our resurrected bodies)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul ties believers' future bodies directly to a pattern already realized: Christ will transform 'these humble bodies of ours into the likeness of his glorious body.' The template for what resurrected bodies will be like isn't speculation — it's Christ's own risen and glorified body, already historically real and witnessed. Believers aren't waiting for an unknown outcome; they're waiting for their ordinary, weak, mortal ('humble') bodies to be conformed to a body that already exists. The passage also frames this hope around citizenship 'in heaven,' from which this transforming savior comes, tying resurrection hope to the return of Christ rather than to death being escaped by some other route.
elements.questionHint: Whose body does Paul point to as the pattern or 'likeness' that believers' bodies will eventually be transformed into?

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup> Dear friends, we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet been revealed. We know that whenever it is revealed we will be like him, because we will see him just as he is.

elements.question: What is the nature of Jesus’ resurrected body (and, by implication, our resurrected bodies)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John admits the details aren't fully revealed yet — 'what we will be has not yet been revealed' — but he's certain of one thing: 'we will be like him, because we will see him just as he is.' The seeing and the becoming are tied together; encountering Christ in his full, unveiled reality is itself what completes believers' transformation into his likeness. This holds back from over-specifying what resurrected bodies will look like in detail, while still anchoring the hope firmly in Christ himself as both the goal and the means — being made like him by finally seeing him without the limits that now obscure that vision.
elements.questionHint: What connection does John draw between 'we will see him just as he is' and 'we will be like him' — why link seeing to becoming?

elements.passageText: <sup>39</sup> Look at my hands and my feet; it’s me! Touch me and see; a ghost does not have flesh and bones like you see I have.” <sup>40</sup> When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet.

elements.question: What is the nature of Jesus’ resurrected body (and, by implication, our resurrected bodies)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus rules out a ghost or purely spiritual appearance in the most concrete terms available: 'a ghost does not have flesh and bones like you see I have.' He doesn't just assert this — he offers his hands and feet to be looked at and touched. The resurrected body, in other words, is a real physical body with actual bones and flesh, not a vision, a spirit, or a symbolic presence. Whatever changes happened in the resurrection, materiality wasn't one of the casualties; Jesus retains a tangible, examinable body, which sets the baseline expectation for what believers' own resurrected bodies will also be — genuinely physical, not merely spiritual in some ethereal sense.
elements.questionHint: What specific physical features does Jesus point to as proof he isn't a ghost, and why would a ghost lack them?

elements.passageText: <sup>27</sup> Then he said to Thomas, “Put your finger here, and examine my hands. Extend your hand and put it into my side. Do not continue in your unbelief, but believe.”

elements.question: What is the nature of Jesus’ resurrected body (and, by implication, our resurrected bodies)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus tells Thomas to examine his hands and put his hand into his side, meaning the wounds from the crucifixion are still visibly present in the resurrected body. This is a striking detail: resurrection doesn't erase the marks of what Jesus suffered, it carries them forward as identifying features. The scars establish continuity of identity — this is the same body that was crucified, not a substitute or a fresh creation — while also standing as permanent testimony to what he accomplished. Thomas is invited from unbelief to belief on the basis of tangible, verifiable evidence built into the very body of the risen Christ.
elements.questionHint: Why would Jesus' resurrected body still bear the wounds of crucifixion instead of being made completely unmarked and new?

elements.passageText: <sup>19</sup> On the evening of that day, the first day of the week, the disciples had gathered together and locked the doors of the place because they were afraid of the Jewish leaders. Jesus came and stood among them and said to them, “Peace be with you.”

elements.question: What is the nature of Jesus’ resurrected body (and, by implication, our resurrected bodies)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The detail that the doors were 'locked' because of fear, and that Jesus simply 'came and stood among them' anyway, points to a resurrected body with new, unexplained capacities alongside its physicality. Locked doors were no barrier to his presence, yet elsewhere in the same appearances he's touched, he eats, he has flesh and bones. John doesn't resolve the tension for readers — he simply records both kinds of evidence side by side. The resurrected body seems to be genuinely physical while no longer bound by ordinary physical limitations in the way it was before death, a combination that defies easy categorization but which John presents as simple fact.
elements.questionHint: How could Jesus be standing 'among them' inside a room whose doors John specifically says were 'locked'?

elements.passageText: <sup>11</sup> Moreover if the Spirit of the one who raised Jesus from the dead lives in you, the one who raised Christ from the dead will also make your mortal bodies alive through his Spirit who lives in you.

elements.question: What is the nature of Jesus’ resurrected body (and, by implication, our resurrected bodies)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul locates the future resurrection of believers in the present, ongoing activity of the Holy Spirit: the same Spirit 'who raised Christ from the dead' already 'lives in you,' and it's through that indwelling Spirit that God 'will also make your mortal bodies alive.' The resurrection of the body isn't detached from the Spirit's current work in believers — it's the culmination of it. This means the nature of the resurrected body is Spirit-produced and Spirit-empowered, following the exact same divine action and agent that raised Jesus himself. The Spirit already at work in mortal bodies now is the guarantee of what will eventually be done to those same bodies.
elements.questionHint: What role does the Spirit 'who lives in you' play now, according to this verse, that connects directly to what will happen to 'your mortal bodies' later?

elements.passageText: <sup>30</sup> When he had taken his place at the table with them, he took the bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to them. <sup>31</sup> At this point their eyes were opened and they recognized him. Then he vanished out of their sight.

elements.question: What is the nature of Jesus’ resurrected body (and, by implication, our resurrected bodies)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This scene at Emmaus combines ordinary and extraordinary in one moment. Jesus does something entirely mundane — takes bread, blesses it, breaks it, gives it — and it's in that familiar gesture that 'their eyes were opened and they recognized him,' as though recognition itself required a kind of unveiling, not just clearer eyesight. Then, just as abruptly, 'he vanished out of their sight.' The resurrected Jesus can be present, physical, and recognizable, yet his appearing and disappearing aren't governed by ordinary means of travel or perception. Luke doesn't explain the mechanics; he simply shows a body that is real enough to share a meal and yet free from the constraints an ordinary body would have.
elements.questionHint: Why does Luke say their eyes 'were opened' to recognize Jesus, as if recognition needed something more than just looking at him?

elements.text: 6. The Ascension – what does Jesus’ return to Heaven tell us?

elements.passageText: <sup>25</sup> So he is able to save completely those who come to God through him, because he always lives to intercede for them.

elements.question: The Ascension – what does Jesus’ return to Heaven tell us?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The writer grounds Jesus' complete, ongoing power to save in his continued life: he 'is able to save completely... because he always lives to intercede for them.' The saving isn't a one-time transaction filed away in the past; it's sustained by a living priest who never stops interceding on behalf of those who come to God through him. That means the ascension isn't Jesus retiring from active involvement — it's him taking up a permanent priestly role in heaven, continuously representing believers before God. 'Completely' covers both the beginning and the ongoing follow-through of salvation, secured precisely because Christ's intercession never lapses or needs to be repeated by someone else.
elements.questionHint: What does linking the ability to 'save completely' to the fact that Jesus 'always lives to intercede' suggest about why an ongoing, living priest matters?

elements.passageText:
24 For Christ did not enter a sanctuary made with hands – the representation of the true sanctuary – but into heaven itself, and he appears now in God’s presence for us.


25 And he did not enter to offer himself again and again, the way the high priest enters the sanctuary year after year with blood that is not his own, 26 for then he would have had to suffer again and again since the foundation of the world. But now he has appeared once for all at the consummation of the ages to put away sin by his sacrifice. 27 And just as people are appointed to die once, and then to face judgment, 28 so also, after Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many, to those who eagerly await him he will appear a second time, not to bear sin but to bring salvation.

elements.question: The Ascension – what does Jesus’ return to Heaven tell us?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The writer contrasts what Christ did with what the earthly high priest had to keep doing: the high priest enters 'year after year' with borrowed blood and must repeat the ritual endlessly, but Christ 'entered... into heaven itself' once and 'appears now in God's presence for us.' The ascension is what completes the sacrifice — it isn't merely Jesus leaving earth, it's the true high priest carrying his finished work into the true, heavenly sanctuary rather than a man-made copy. Because this happened 'once for all,' there's no repetition needed, no return trip to deal with sin again; his next appearance is described as being for salvation, not for another round of atonement.
elements.questionHint: What contrast does the passage draw between what the earthly high priest does 'year after year' and what Christ did by entering 'heaven itself' — why does 'once for all' matter?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> I glorified you on earth by completing the work you gave me to do. <sup>5</sup> And now, Father, glorify me at your side with the glory I had with you before the world was created.

elements.question: The Ascension – what does Jesus’ return to Heaven tell us?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus prays this just before his arrest, framing what's about to happen as the completion of a task: 'I glorified you on earth by completing the work you gave me to do.' Then he asks for something specific — not new glory, but restoration: 'glorify me at your side with the glory I had with you before the world was created.' The ascension, in light of this prayer, is Jesus returning to a glory that already belonged to him prior to his incarnation, now sought again because the assigned work is finished. It isn't promotion to a new status so much as resumption of what the Son had eternally, now on the far side of accomplished redemption.
elements.questionHint: What does asking for the glory Jesus 'had with you before the world was created' say about where the ascension is actually taking him — somewhere new, or somewhere he'd already been?

elements.passageText: 21 And this prefigured baptism, which now saves you – not the washing off of physical dirt but the pledge of a good conscience to God – through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, 22 who went into heaven and is at the right hand of God with angels and authorities and powers subject to him.

elements.question: The Ascension – what does Jesus’ return to Heaven tell us?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter ties baptism's saving significance to 'the resurrection of Jesus Christ,' and then immediately extends the thought to where the resurrected Christ now is: he 'went into heaven and is at the right hand of God with angels and authorities and powers subject to him.' The ascension is presented as the moment Christ's authority over every spiritual power becomes settled fact — not a future hope but a present reality, described in the same breath as his resurrection. Angels, authorities, and powers, categories that could otherwise be seen as threatening or rival forces, are placed under him. The ascension, then, isn't retreat from the world but installation into supreme authority over it.
elements.questionHint: What does it mean that 'angels and authorities and powers' are described as already 'subject to him' rather than something still to be conquered?

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> As a result God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, <sup>10</sup> so that at the name of Jesus every knee will bow – in heaven and on earth and under the earth – <sup>11</sup> and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord to the glory of God the Father.

elements.question: The Ascension – what does Jesus’ return to Heaven tell us?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The passage opens with 'as a result,' pointing back to the self-emptying obedience just described — the exaltation is God's response to the humiliation, not an independent event. 'As a result God exalted him' to the highest possible status, giving him 'the name that is above every name,' and the purpose clause that follows is total in scope: every knee bowing 'in heaven and on earth and under the earth,' every tongue confessing 'Jesus Christ is Lord.' The ascension is the concrete enactment of this exaltation — Christ visibly taking up the position that matches the name and authority he's just been given, with universal acknowledgment as the intended, eventual outcome.
elements.questionHint: What does 'as a result' tell us about the relationship between Christ's exaltation described here and what came immediately before it?

elements.text: 7. What benefits are ours because of His completed work?

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup> There are many dwelling places in my Father’s house. Otherwise, I would have told you, because I am going away to make ready a place for you. <sup>3</sup> And if I go and make ready a place for you, I will come again and take you to be with me, so that where I am you may be too.

elements.question: What benefits are ours because of His completed work?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus frames his departure as purposeful, not merely departure for its own sake: he's 'going away to make ready a place' among the 'many dwelling places' in his Father's house. And the point isn't simply that a place will exist — it's reunion: 'I will come again and take you to be with me, so that where I am you may be too.' The benefit of the ascension, on this account, is preparatory: Christ goes ahead in order to secure a place and then return for his people, so that his own location becomes theirs. Ascension isn't Jesus leaving believers behind; it's Jesus going ahead of them toward a shared destination.
elements.questionHint: What's the stated purpose of Jesus 'going away' according to this passage, and what does he promise will eventually happen 'so that where I am you may be too'?

elements.passageText: <sup>7</sup> But I tell you the truth, it is to your advantage that I am going away. For if I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you, but if I go, I will send him to you.

elements.question: What benefits are ours because of His completed work?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus makes a claim that would sound backwards on the surface: his physical absence is actually 'to your advantage.' He explains why directly — 'if I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you.' His ascension isn't a loss to be merely endured; it's the necessary condition for the Holy Spirit's coming, which Jesus presents as a net gain rather than a consolation prize. Christ's bodily presence, limited to one place at a time, gives way to the Spirit's presence, given to all believers everywhere. The benefit named here is specific and causal: no ascension, no Spirit; ascension precisely in order that the Spirit might come.
elements.questionHint: Why would Jesus describe his own departure as being 'to your advantage,' and what does he say directly depends on his going away?

elements.text:
Chiamaka came to see that the resurrection wasn’t decoration on top of a finished gospel – it was the proof that the payment had been accepted. The cross without the resurrection would just be a good man’s tragic death; the resurrection is God’s public verdict that the debt was actually paid, the wages of sin actually defeated, the tomb actually beaten. Without it, as Paul says, her faith would be futile and she would still be in her sins. With it, she has a living hope, not a hopeful theory.

And the ascension, she realised, was not Jesus leaving the story – it was Jesus stepping into the next scene. He didn’t disappear; He was enthroned, given the name above every name, seated at the Father’s right hand where He now intercedes for her, and from where He will one day return. Because He ascended, He could send His Spirit to be with her always, rather than being limited to one place at one time. Because He ascended, He is preparing a place for her. The empty tomb and the empty sky are not the story trailing off – they are Christ’s coronation.
A Living Hope Scale

elements.instruction: How much difference does the resurrection and ascension actually make to your everyday faith? Tick the box that best fits.
statements: I think of the resurrection as central to my faith, not just a happy ending to Easter
I could explain to a friend why the resurrection matters, beyond simply proving who Jesus is
I live with a genuine ’living hope’ about death and the future, not just a vague optimism
I understand why it was good for me that Jesus ascended, rather than staying visibly on earth
I remember that Jesus is currently interceding for me, right now, as my ascended High Priest
My confidence before God rests on the fact that Jesus rose, not only that He died

elements.question: Before this study, did the resurrection feel like a load-bearing part of your faith, or more like a comforting extra? Has that changed?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Your reflection…

elements.question: What difference does it make to you personally that Jesus’ resurrected body was physical and real, not merely a spiritual idea?

chapters.chapterTitle: Salvation Applied: How Salvation is Received

elements.text:
Case Study – Tobenna (early 20s)

Tobenna trusted Christ at a youth camp when he was sixteen. He remembers the moment clearly: the altar call, the tears, the sense of relief. But five years on, he has started to unravel that memory with anxious questions he can't quite put down.

Did he choose God, or did God choose him first? If God chose him, why does he still sometimes feel nothing when he prays? He was told he was “born again” – but if that's true, why does he still sin the same old sins, sometimes worse than before? A friend at university recently told him bluntly that real faith always produces a changed life, and that if Tobenna was still struggling the way he was, maybe he'd never really been saved at all. That comment has sat in his chest for weeks.

He also can't work out how all the pieces fit together. Is he saved because he believed, or because God regenerated him first so that he could believe? Is salvation a single moment in the past, a daily process, or a future hope he's still waiting for? And if perseverance is required to prove he's really saved, how can he ever be sure – today, this week – that he actually is?

Tobenna needed to see the whole shape of salvation, not just the moment at the altar: what God does, what he does, and how all of it fits together from calling to glory.
Jot down how each verse supports each of the following aspects of salvation.
1. Effectual Calling. That God draws individuals to Christ by His Spirit.

elements.passageText: <sup>44</sup> No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him, and I will raise him up at the last day.

elements.question: How does this verse support the doctrine of effectual calling?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus makes coming to him conditional on something beyond the person's own initiative: "unless the Father who sent me draws him." The word "draws" describes a decisive pull, not a polite invitation left to chance — nobody wanders to Christ under their own power, they are drawn there by the Father's action. This is effectual calling in miniature: the call doesn't just present an option, it actually brings the person. Jesus ties this directly to certainty of final salvation too, promising to "raise him up at the last day," so the one who is drawn is guaranteed to be kept all the way to resurrection.
elements.questionHint: The verse says no one 'can' come unless drawn — what does the word 'draws' suggest about whether this is a suggestion or something more forceful and effective?

elements.passageText: <sup>30</sup> And those he predestined, he also called; and those he called, he also justified; and those he justified, he also glorified.

elements.question: How does this verse support the doctrine of effectual calling?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul links four verbs into an unbroken sequence — predestined, called, justified, glorified — and everyone who appears in one step appears in the next. Nobody is called who fails to end up justified; the calling here isn't a mere offer that some accept and others don't, it's a link in a chain that reaches all the way to glorification. That's the essence of effectual calling: it's not simply God inviting, but God summoning in a way that actually produces the result. The certainty is built into the grammar itself, since Paul describes the whole sequence in the past tense, as an accomplished fact rather than a hoped-for outcome.
elements.questionHint: Look at how each verb in the chain leads to the next without exception — what does that unbroken sequence suggest about whether a 'called' person could end up not justified?

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> God is faithful, by whom you were called into fellowship with his son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

elements.question: How does this verse support the doctrine of effectual calling?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul roots the call in God's own faithfulness rather than in the strength of the hearer's response: "God is faithful, by whom you were called." The reliability of the calling depends on God's character, not on the Corinthians' consistency. And the call doesn't just summon them to a decision — it draws them "into fellowship with his Son," a real, ongoing relationship of shared life with Christ. So the calling described here is both effective, because it's anchored in God's unfailing faithfulness, and relational, because its goal is communion with Jesus, not merely information about him.
elements.questionHint: Why does Paul ground the call in the phrase 'God is faithful' rather than in anything the Corinthians themselves had done — whose reliability makes the call take hold?

elements.passageText: <sup>14</sup> He called you to this salvation through our gospel, so that you may possess the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.

elements.question: How does this verse support the doctrine of effectual calling?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This verse describes both the means and the goal of the call. The means is stated plainly — "through our gospel" — meaning the call reaches people as the good news is preached, not apart from it. The goal is just as specific: "so that you may possess the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ," a definite outcome rather than a vague possibility. Effectual calling shows up here in that gap between means and goal being closed: God's call through the gospel is aimed at, and secures, actual possession of Christ's glory, not simply an offer that leaves the outcome undetermined.
elements.questionHint: What phrase tells you the instrument God uses to call people ('through our ___'), and what specific outcome does Paul say this call is aimed at achieving?

elements.text: 2. Regeneration (New Birth). That God takes the initiative, acting in us to bring us to new life in Christ, renewing our hearts and spirits.

elements.passageText: <sup>26</sup> I will give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will remove the heart of stone from your body and give you a heart of flesh.

elements.question: How does this verse support the doctrine of regeneration (new birth)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Every verb in this promise belongs to God: "I will give... I will put... I will remove... give." There is no clause where the exiled Israelites clean up their own hearts first — God performs surgery on the inside, replacing dead unresponsiveness with living responsiveness. Calling it a "heart of stone" describes something inert and unmoved by God's word, while a "heart of flesh" can feel, respond, and obey. This is the Old Testament seedbed for regeneration: God doesn't merely improve the old heart, he removes it and supplies a new one, and he does it entirely by his own initiative.
elements.questionHint: Who is the one performing every action in this verse ('I will give,' 'I will put,' 'I will remove') — does the change start with the person or with God?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> Jesus replied, “I tell you the solemn truth, unless a person is born from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God.”

elements.question: How does this verse support the doctrine of regeneration (new birth)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus states an absolute condition: "unless a person is born from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God." Seeing the kingdom doesn't come first and birth follow as a description of it — the new birth has to happen before anyone can perceive or enter what God is doing. That ordering is the heart of regeneration: it is not a response a person works up after glimpsing spiritual truth, but the miraculous origin that makes such sight possible in the first place, as mysterious and unearned as one's first, natural birth.
elements.questionHint: In the phrase 'unless... he cannot see,' which comes first according to Jesus — being born again, or perceiving the kingdom of God?

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup> So then, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; what is old has passed away – look, what is new has come!

elements.question: How does this verse support the doctrine of regeneration (new birth)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul doesn't describe gradual self-improvement here; he describes an entirely new creation. Being "in Christ" — the union that grounds the change — results in a person for whom "what is old has passed away" completely, replaced by something Paul insists has already "come." The verbs are decisive and complete, not in-progress. This is regeneration described from the inside: it isn't a New Year's resolution to do better, it's a change of nature so total that the old identity is said to be gone and a new one has taken its place.
elements.questionHint: What does calling someone a 'new creation' rule out compared to just calling them 'improved,' and what phrase ties this change to being 'in Christ'?

elements.passageText: <sup>23</sup> You have been born anew, not from perishable but from imperishable seed, through the living and enduring word of God.

elements.question: How does this verse support the doctrine of regeneration (new birth)?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter locates the origin of new birth in a "seed" — but not the ordinary, perishable kind that produces natural life. This seed is imperishable because it is nothing less than "the living and enduring word of God." The durability of the new birth follows directly from the durability of its source: since the word that produced it never decays, the life it generates cannot decay either. Regeneration, in other words, isn't a spark that might fizzle out — its permanence is guaranteed by the very nature of what planted it.
elements.questionHint: What does Peter identify as the 'seed' that produces this new birth, and why does calling it 'imperishable' matter for how secure the resulting life is?

elements.text: 3. Repentance & Faith. Turning away from sin and turning toward Christ in trust.

elements.passageText:
1:15 He said, “The time is fulfilled and the kingdom of God is near. Repent and believe the gospel!”


2:38 Peter said to them, “Repent, and each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.

elements.question: How does this verse support the doctrine of repentance & faith?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus pairs two commands as a single response to the good news: "Repent and believe the gospel." Repentance is a turning away, and believing is a turning toward — together they form the complete response to the announcement that "the kingdom of God is near." Peter's words in Acts fill in what follows: repentance leads to baptism, to "forgiveness of your sins," and to receiving "the gift of the Holy Spirit." Read together, the two passages show repentance and faith as inseparable companions, with real, tangible results — pardon and the Spirit's presence — attached to the turn.
elements.questionHint: In Mark, what two verbs does Jesus join with 'and' as the proper response to his announcement, and in Acts what two gifts does Peter say follow after repenting?

elements.passageText: <sup>21</sup> testifying to both Jews and Greeks about repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus.

elements.question: How does this verse support the doctrine of repentance & faith?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Luke's summary of Paul's preaching pairs two responses with two different objects: "repentance toward God, and faith in our Lord Jesus." Repentance is aimed at God because it addresses the wrong relationship — rebellion against him that needs to be turned from. Faith, by contrast, is aimed specifically "in" Jesus, because it's a matter of personal trust placed in a person, not just agreement with facts about God in general. The two prepositions do real work: one describes turning away from a broken relationship, the other describes turning toward and resting in the one who can fix it.
elements.questionHint: Notice the two different prepositions Luke uses — repentance is 'toward' whom, and faith is 'in' whom — what does that difference tell you about what each response addresses?

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> because if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.

elements.question: How does this verse support the doctrine of repentance & faith?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul names two actions that go together: confessing "with your mouth" and believing "in your heart." The heart-belief concerns a specific truth — that God raised Jesus from the dead — while the mouth-confession concerns another — that Jesus is Lord. Neither one substitutes for the other; Paul doesn't say private conviction alone saves, nor does he say a verbal claim alone saves. Saving faith here is both inward conviction about the resurrection and outward acknowledgment of Christ's lordship, a whole-person response rather than a merely intellectual one.
elements.questionHint: What two actions does Paul pair — one done 'with your mouth' and one 'in your heart' — and what specific truth does each one affirm?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> Now without faith it is impossible to please him, for the one who approaches God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.

elements.question: How does this verse support the doctrine of repentance & faith?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The author states faith's necessity in the starkest terms: "without faith it is impossible to please him." But he also specifies what that faith must include — not vague spirituality, but the conviction "that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him." Faith here isn't simply believing facts about God's existence; it's trusting that God responds to those who pursue him. That second half matters as much as the first, because a person could affirm God's existence without ever approaching him — this verse insists that real faith moves toward God expecting to be met.
elements.questionHint: What two specific things does the verse say a person 'must believe' — is it only that God exists, or something more about how he responds to seekers?

elements.text: 4. Justification. Being declared righteous by God through faith in Christ.

elements.passageText: <sup>23</sup> for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. <sup>24</sup> But they are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.

elements.question: How does this verse support the doctrine of justification?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul places the universal problem and its solution back to back: "all have sinned," yet believers "are justified freely by his grace." That word "freely" does heavy lifting — it rules out any contribution from the sinner's own effort or merit as the basis for the verdict. The means is specified too: "through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus," so the free gift has a real cost behind it, just not one paid by the recipient. Justification, as Paul describes it here, is a legal declaration given as an unearned gift, purchased by Christ's redemption rather than by anything the sinner brings.
elements.questionHint: What word does Paul use to describe how believers 'are justified' — and what does that word rule out as the basis for God's declaration?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> Therefore, since we have been declared righteous by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,

elements.question: How does this verse support the doctrine of justification?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul draws a direct line from justification to peace: "since we have been declared righteous by faith, we have peace with God." Notice the verdict comes first, described as an accomplished fact — "declared righteous" — and the peace follows as its consequence, not the other way around. This is a legal, relational change, not merely a felt one; the hostility between God and the sinner is ended because the sinner's status before God has actually changed. Peace with God, then, rests on a settled verdict, which is exactly why it can be a confident possession rather than a fragile feeling.
elements.questionHint: Does 'peace with God' come from a change in feeling or from the legal status described as being 'declared righteous by faith' — which one does Paul say produces the other?

elements.passageText: <sup>16</sup> yet we know that no one is justified by the works of the law but by the faithfulness of Jesus Christ. And we have come to believe in Christ Jesus, so that we may be justified by the faithfulness of Christ and not by the works of the law, because by the works of the law no one will be justified.

elements.question: How does this verse support the doctrine of justification?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul hammers a single point three times in one sentence: no one is justified "by the works of the law," and "by the works of the law no one will be justified." The repetition is the argument — he's not leaving room for law-keeping to share credit with faith. Set against that threefold denial is the positive alternative, repeated just as emphatically: justification comes "by the faithfulness of Jesus Christ." The sheer redundancy of Paul's wording shows how important it was to him that the Galatians not slip works back into the basis for their standing before God.
elements.questionHint: Count how many times in this single verse Paul repeats some version of 'not by works of the law' — what does that repetition tell you about how strongly he wanted to make this point?

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup> and be found in him, not because I have my own righteousness derived from the law, but because I have the righteousness that comes by way of Christ’s faithfulness – a righteousness from God that is in fact based on Christ’s faithfulness.

elements.question: How does this verse support the doctrine of justification?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul distinguishes two possible sources of righteousness and rejects the first outright: not "my own righteousness derived from the law." In its place he sets a righteousness that comes "by way of Christ's faithfulness" — one he calls, twice over, a righteousness "from God" rather than from himself. The repetition of "Christ's faithfulness" at the end underscores where the righteousness actually originates. Justification, in Paul's own words about his own hopes, means trading a righteousness he could produce for one he could only receive, based entirely on what Christ has done rather than on Paul's own record.
elements.questionHint: What contrast does Paul draw between 'my own righteousness derived from the law' and the righteousness he now has — whose faithfulness does he say the second one is based on?

elements.text: 5. Adoption. Becoming adopted as sons and daughters of God.

elements.passageText: <sup>15</sup> For you did not receive the spirit of slavery leading again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba, Father.”

elements.question: How does this verse support the doctrine of adoption?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul contrasts two spirits and two postures: "the spirit of slavery leading again to fear" against "the Spirit of adoption." A slave relates to a master through obligation and dread; the adopted child relates through intimacy, crying out "Abba, Father" — a term of close, trusting address. The change isn't just in status but in felt relationship: adoption doesn't merely rescue from slavery, it installs a completely different kind of nearness to God. The cry itself, spontaneous and confident, is presented as evidence that the fearful, servile relationship has genuinely given way to a filial one.
elements.questionHint: What two spirits does Paul contrast, and what does the cry 'Abba, Father' reveal about the kind of relationship adoption produces compared to slavery?

elements.passageText:
3:26 For in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God through faith.


4:4 But when the appropriate time had come, God sent out his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, 4:5 to redeem those who were under the law, so that we may be adopted as sons with full rights.

elements.question: How does this verse support the doctrine of adoption?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul states sonship's basis plainly — "in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God through faith" — and then in Galatians 4 explains the mechanism behind it. God's Son was sent, "born under the law," with a stated purpose: "to redeem those who were under the law, so that we may be adopted as sons with full rights." Adoption isn't an afterthought tacked onto redemption; it's the very goal Paul says redemption was aimed at achieving. Christ's incarnation and law-keeping exist, in this text, so that adoption — with all its legal privileges — could actually happen.
elements.questionHint: What purpose does Paul give (introduced by 'so that') for why Christ was sent to redeem those under the law — what was redemption ultimately aimed at producing?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> He did this by predestining us to adoption as his sons through Jesus Christ, according to the pleasure of his will –

elements.question: How does this verse support the doctrine of adoption?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Ephesians traces adoption back before any human response at all: God's act of "predestining us to adoption as his sons through Jesus Christ" happened "according to the pleasure of his will." The motive named here isn't anything foreseen or earned in the adopted — it's something located entirely in God himself, his own pleasure and will. That phrase removes adoption from the category of a reward and places it in the category of a gift planned out of God's own delight, decided before the adopted children ever existed to do anything deserving or undeserving of it.
elements.questionHint: What does the phrase 'according to the pleasure of his will' locate as the reason for adoption — something in the adopted person, or something in God himself?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> (See what sort of love the Father has given to us: that we should be called God’s children – and indeed we are! For this reason the world does not know us: because it did not know him.

elements.question: How does this verse support the doctrine of adoption?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: John doesn't just report a title; he marvels at it: "see what sort of love the Father has given to us: that we should be called God's children." Then he adds a clause that refuses to let the point be taken as merely honorary — "and indeed we are!" That insistence matters, because the whole verse could otherwise be read as a courtesy title rather than a genuine relationship. John wants his readers to grasp both the astonishing scale of the love behind adoption and the plain reality of the status it confers, not just its language.
elements.questionHint: After saying believers are 'called God's children,' what short phrase does John add to insist this is a real status, not just a nice-sounding label?

elements.text: 6. Union with Christ. The believer's spiritual union with Christ by faith.

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> For if we have become united with him in the likeness of his death, we will certainly also be united in the likeness of his resurrection.

elements.question: How does this verse support the doctrine of union with Christ?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul links two unions with a strong guarantee: "if we have become united with him in the likeness of his death, we will certainly also be united in the likeness of his resurrection."
