Carefully obey all the law my servant Moses charged you to keep. Do not swerve from it to the right or to the left, so that you may be successful in all you do. <sup>8</sup> This law scroll must not leave your lips. You must memorize it day and night so you can carefully obey all that is written in it. Then you will prosper and be successful. <sup>9</sup> I repeat, be strong and brave! Don’t be afraid and don’t panic, for I, the Lord your God, am with you in all you do.”

elements.question: What does this verse teach about human responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God's charge to Joshua repeats the imperative "be strong and brave" three times, paired with a specific task: "carefully obey all the law." Joshua's success is tied directly to his own diligence — he must not "swerve... to the right or to the left," must "memorize it day and night," and "then you will prosper and be successful." The link between obedience and outcome shows this isn't fatalistic waiting on God to act alone; God's presence, "I... am with you in all you do," accompanies Joshua's responsibility rather than replacing it.
elements.questionHint: Notice the "so that" and "then you will" language — what does it show about the connection between Joshua's own obedience and what happens to him?

elements.passageText:
8 He has told you, O man, what is good,
and what the Lord really wants from you:
He wants you to carry out justice, to love faithfulness,
and to live obediently before your God.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about human responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Micah reduces the whole matter to three concrete, doable actions: "carry out justice, love faithfulness, and live obediently before your God." These aren't abstract postures but a plain expectation for daily conduct within reach of any person — the verse says God has already "told you... what is good," meaning ignorance isn't the issue. Responsibility here is framed as already knowing what is required and simply doing it, without excuse, since the standard has been made plain rather than hidden.
elements.questionHint: What does it mean that God has already "told you... what is good" — how does that remove one possible excuse for not doing it?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> Then the Lord said to Cain, “Why are you angry, and why is your expression downcast? <sup>7</sup> Is it not true that if you do what is right, you will be fine? But if you do not do what is right, sin is crouching at the door. It desires to dominate you, but you must subdue it.”

elements.question: What does this verse teach about human responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God confronts Cain with a direct connection between action and outcome: "if you do what is right, you will be fine." Sin is pictured as a crouching, desiring predator, but the final word is command, not fate: "you must subdue it." Even with sin actively "desir[ing] to dominate" him, Cain retains the capacity and the duty to master it — God doesn't excuse him in advance or treat the temptation as irresistible. The responsibility to resist sits with Cain himself, right at the threshold, before he acts.
elements.questionHint: Even though sin "desires to dominate" Cain, what does the command "you must subdue it" assume about Cain's own ability to respond?

elements.passageText: <sup>41</sup> “I do not accept praise from people, <sup>42</sup> but I know you, that you do not have the love of God within you. <sup>43</sup> I have come in my Father’s name, and you do not accept me. If someone else comes in his own name, you will accept him. <sup>44</sup> How can you believe, if you accept praise from one another and don’t seek the praise that comes from the only God?

elements.question: What does this verse teach about human responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus diagnoses the real obstacle to belief as a matter of misplaced desire, not incapacity: "you do not have the love of God within you," and "you accept praise from one another" instead of "the praise that comes from... God." His question, "How can you believe, if...," makes their unbelief a consequence of what they have chosen to value — human approval over God's — rather than something imposed on them from outside. The responsibility for refusing him lies in the priorities they themselves have cultivated.
elements.questionHint: What does Jesus's question "How can you believe, if you accept praise from one another" suggest about the actual cause of their unbelief?

elements.passageText: <sup>51</sup> “You stubborn people, with uncircumcised hearts and ears! You are always resisting the Holy Spirit, like your ancestors did! <sup>52</sup> Which of the prophets did your ancestors not persecute? They killed those who foretold long ago the coming of the Righteous One, whose betrayers and murderers you have now become! <sup>53</sup> You received the law by decrees given by angels, but you did not obey it.”

elements.question: What does this verse teach about human responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Stephen's accusation is unrelenting in placing blame on his hearers' own choices: "stubborn people," "uncircumcised hearts and ears," "you are always resisting the Holy Spirit." He traces a pattern — their ancestors persecuted the prophets, and they themselves "have now become" the betrayers and murderers of the Righteous One. Receiving "the law by decrees given by angels" only sharpens the charge, since possessing revelation and still failing to obey it shows the failure was theirs in the face of real advantage, not a lack of opportunity or knowledge.
elements.questionHint: What does it mean that Stephen calls them "always resisting" — is this something being done to them, or something they are actively doing?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> Therefore I exhort you, brothers and sisters, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a sacrifice—alive, holy, and pleasing to God—which is your reasonable service. <sup>2</sup> Do not be conformed to this present world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may test and approve what is the will of God—what is good and well-pleasing and perfect.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about human responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul frames the Christian life as something believers must actively pursue: "present your bodies as a sacrifice," "be transformed by the renewing of your mind." The commands — do not be conformed, but be transformed — put the responsibility for resisting the world's pattern and cultivating a renewed mind on the believer, even though the appeal is grounded in "the mercies of God" already given. The goal, to "test and approve... the will of God," implies ongoing discernment and effort on the reader's part, not passive reception of a settled outcome.
elements.questionHint: What do the two commands "do not be conformed" and "be transformed" ask of the reader personally, and how are they tied to "the renewing of your mind"?

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup> So I say this, and insist in the Lord, that you no longer live as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their thinking. <sup>25</sup> Therefore, having laid aside falsehood, each one of you speak the truth with his neighbor because we are members of one another.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about human responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul "insist[s] in the Lord" on a break with a former way of life — "no longer live as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their thinking." That verb "insist" signals urgency and expectation of compliance, not mere suggestion. Having "laid aside falsehood," believers are then commanded to "speak the truth," a deliberate, repeated choice grounded in the fact that "we are members of one another." The passage puts concrete, everyday behavior — how one thinks and speaks — squarely under personal obligation.
elements.questionHint: What does Paul's word "insist" suggest about how seriously believers are expected to take putting off old thinking and speaking truthfully?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> Therefore, just as you received Christ Jesus as Lord, continue to live your lives in him, <sup>7</sup> rooted and built up in him and firm in your faith just as you were taught, and overflowing with thankfulness. <sup>8</sup> Be careful not to allow anyone to captivate you through an empty, deceitful philosophy that is according to human traditions and the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about human responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul commands believers to "continue to live your lives in him," an ongoing, active responsibility pictured as being "rooted and built up... firm in your faith." The warning, "be careful not to allow anyone to captivate you," makes vigilance a personal duty — being deceived by "empty, deceitful philosophy" is something a believer must guard against, not something that simply happens regardless of effort. Both the verbs of growth and the call to watchfulness fall on the reader, not on some automatic process.
elements.questionHint: What does the command "be careful not to allow anyone to captivate you" imply about the believer's own role in guarding against deception?

elements.passageText: <sup>5</sup> So put to death whatever in your nature belongs to the earth: sexual immorality, impurity, shameful passion, evil desire, and greed which is idolatry. <sup>6</sup> Because of these things the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience. <sup>7</sup> You also lived your lives in this way at one time, when you used to live among them. <sup>8</sup> But now, put off all such things as anger, rage, malice, slander, abusive language from your mouth. <sup>9</sup> Do not lie to one another since you have put off the old man with its practices <sup>10</sup> and have been clothed with the new man that is being renewed in knowledge according to the image of the one who created it.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about human responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's commands here are blunt and active: "put to death" the old ways, "put off" anger and slander, don't "lie to one another." These are verbs of deliberate, effortful action against one's own sinful patterns, not descriptions of something that happens automatically. Even though believers have already "put off the old man" and "been clothed with the new," the ongoing task of putting sin to death and being "renewed in knowledge" is still set before them, with the warning that "the wrath of God is coming" on exactly these practices when they go unchecked.
elements.questionHint: What is the tension between describing something as already true ("you have put off the old man") and still commanding it as an action ("put to death," "put off")?

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup> Finally then, brothers and sisters, we ask you and urge you in the Lord Jesus, that as you received instruction from us about how you must live and please God (as you are in fact living) that you do so more and more. <sup>2</sup> For you know what commands we gave you through the Lord Jesus.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about human responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul reminds the Thessalonians that they already know "what commands we gave you," and urges them to keep living in a way that pleases God, "that you do so more and more." The phrase "as you are in fact living" acknowledges real progress already made, but "more and more" shows the expectation of continued growth isn't optional or automatic — it requires ongoing attention to instructions already received. Responsibility here is about persevering and increasing in what one already knows to do, not resting on past obedience.
elements.questionHint: What does the phrase "more and more" suggest about whether current obedience is enough, or whether continued effort is still expected?

elements.passageText: <sup>7</sup> The one who has an ear had better hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who conquers, I will permit him to eat from the tree of life that is in the paradise of God.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about human responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The call "the one who has an ear had better hear" places responsibility on the individual listener to actually attend to what the Spirit says — hearing isn't guaranteed just because ears exist. The promise to "the one who conquers" implies genuine struggle and effort resulting in victory, with the reward of eating "from the tree of life" following as a consequence of overcoming, not an unconditional gift bestowed apart from that overcoming.
elements.questionHint: What does the phrase "had better hear" imply is at stake if someone simply has ears but doesn't actually listen?

elements.text: 2. Divine Sovereignty.

elements.passageText:
1 The intentions of the heart belong to a man,
but the answer of the tongue comes from the Lord. 4 The Lord has worked everything for his own ends—
even the wicked for the day of disaster. 9 A person plans his course,
but the Lord directs his steps. 33 The dice are thrown into the lap,
but their every decision is from the Lord.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about divine sovereignty?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: This cluster of proverbs pairs human activity with divine determination at every level, from speech to plans to random chance: humans have "intentions," but "the answer of the tongue comes from the Lord"; a person "plans his course, but the Lord directs his steps"; even "the dice are thrown into the lap, but their every decision is from the Lord." The proverb about the wicked being "worked... for the day of disaster" pushes this further, extending God's purposeful oversight even over evil people's outcomes. The repeated "but" construction shows human planning and speaking are real, yet ultimately subordinate to what the Lord directs.
elements.questionHint: What does the repeated pattern — a person does one thing, "but the Lord" does another — suggest about how these proverbs relate human intention to the actual outcome?

elements.passageText:
21 There are many plans in a person’s mind,
but it is the counsel of the Lord that will stand.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about divine sovereignty?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The proverb doesn't deny that people have "many plans" — that plurality is acknowledged plainly. But it sets those many human plans against a single, settled outcome: "it is the counsel of the Lord that will stand." The contrast between "many" and one prevailing purpose underscores that human intentions are numerous and often competing, while God's purpose is what actually holds in the end regardless of how many alternative plans people devise.
elements.questionHint: What is the significance of contrasting "many plans" (plural) with "the counsel of the Lord" (singular) that "will stand"?

elements.passageText:
24 The steps of a person are ordained by the Lord—
so how can anyone understand his own way? 1 The king’s heart is in the hand of the Lord like channels of water;
he turns it wherever he wants.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about divine sovereignty?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The first proverb states plainly that "the steps of a person are ordained by the Lord," then draws the natural, humbling conclusion: "how can anyone understand his own way?" — human self-understanding is limited precisely because there's a hidden divine ordering behind one's path. The second image, of a king's heart as "channels of water" that the Lord "turns... wherever he wants," pictures even the most powerful human will as pliable in God's hands, redirected as easily as irrigation water, without denying it is genuinely the king's own heart and decisions being described.
elements.questionHint: What does comparing the king's heart to "channels of water" suggest about how directly God can move even the most powerful human will?

elements.passageText:
7 I am the one who forms light
and creates darkness;
the one who brings about peace
and creates calamity.
I am the Lord, who accomplishes all these things.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about divine sovereignty?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God claims direct authorship over the full range of experience, not just the pleasant half: he "forms light and creates darkness," brings "peace" and creates "calamity." The verse resists dividing reality into a sphere God controls and a rival sphere outside his control — "I am the Lord, who accomplishes all these things" leaves nothing external to his sovereign action. This is stark, comprehensive language that refuses to let calamity be explained apart from God's own agency, even while it doesn't spell out here how that squares with human or other moral responsibility for evil.
elements.questionHint: Why might Isaiah pair opposites like "light/darkness" and "peace/calamity" rather than only crediting God with the pleasant half of each pair?

elements.passageText:
10 who announces the end from the beginning
and reveals beforehand what has not yet occurred;
who says, ‘My plan will be realized,
I will accomplish what I desire;’ 11 who summons an eagle from the east,
from a distant land, one who carries out my plan.
Yes, I have decreed,
yes, I will bring it to pass;
I have formulated a plan,
yes, I will carry it out.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about divine sovereignty?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God speaks with total confidence about outcomes still future: he "announces the end from the beginning" and "reveals beforehand what has not yet occurred." His stated intention isn't a hope but a certainty — "My plan will be realized, I will accomplish what I desire" — repeated with the emphatic "yes, I have decreed... yes, I will bring it to pass." Even the specific historical agent, "an eagle from the east," is described as one who "carries out my plan," meaning a human figure's actions are folded into and accomplish God's own predetermined purpose.
elements.questionHint: What does it mean that a specific human figure, "an eagle from the east," is described as the one who "carries out my plan" — whose plan is actually being fulfilled through that person's actions?

elements.passageText: <sup>48</sup> When the Gentiles heard this, they began to rejoice and praise the word of the Lord, and all who had been appointed for eternal life believed.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about divine sovereignty?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Luke links belief directly to a prior divine action: "all who had been appointed for eternal life believed." The order in the sentence matters — appointment precedes and grounds belief, rather than belief earning appointment afterward. At the same time, the text doesn't erase the Gentiles' own response; they "began to rejoice and praise the word," an evident act of their own hearts. Luke simply states both together without resolving exactly how the appointing and the believing relate, letting divine sovereignty and human response sit side by side in a single sentence.
elements.questionHint: In the sentence, which comes first — being "appointed for eternal life" or having "believed" — and what might that ordering suggest?

elements.passageText: <sup>28</sup> And we know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose, <sup>29</sup> because those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that his Son would be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters. <sup>30</sup> And those he predestined, he also called; and those he called, he also justified; and those he justified, he also glorified.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about divine sovereignty?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul traces an unbroken chain from God's own initiative to its final result: "those whom he foreknew he also predestined... those he predestined, he also called; and those he called, he also justified; and those he justified, he also glorified." Every verb in that chain has God as the subject and the believer as the object — this is not a partnership described in balanced terms but a sequence entirely driven by God's action from beginning to end. The promise that "all things work together for good" for those "called according to his purpose" rests on this same prior, divine initiative rather than on human achievement.
elements.questionHint: Who is the subject performing every verb in the chain "foreknew... predestined... called... justified... glorified" — and what does that grammar suggest about where the initiative lies?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> Blessed is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms in Christ. <sup>4</sup> For he chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world that we may be holy and unblemished in his sight in love. <sup>5</sup> He did this by predestining us to adoption as his sons through Jesus Christ, according to the pleasure of his will – <sup>6</sup> to the praise of the glory of his grace that he has freely bestowed on us in his dearly loved Son. <sup>7</sup> In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace <sup>8</sup> that he lavished on us in all wisdom and insight. <sup>9</sup> He did this when he revealed to us the secret of his will, according to his good pleasure that he set forth in Christ, <sup>10</sup> toward the administration of the fullness of the times, to head up all things in Christ – the things in heaven and the things on earth. <sup>11</sup> In Christ we too have been claimed as God’s own possession, since we were predestined according to the one purpose of him who accomplishes all things according to the counsel of his will <sup>12</sup> so that we, who were the first to set our hope on Christ, would be to the praise of his glory. <sup>13</sup> And when you heard the word of truth (the gospel of your salvation) – when you believed in Christ – you were marked with the seal of the promised Holy Spirit, <sup>14</sup> who is the down payment of our inheritance, until the redemption of God’s own possession, to the praise of his glory.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about divine sovereignty?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul stacks up phrases that all point to God's initiative prior to any human response: God "chose us... before the foundation of the world," did this "according to the pleasure of his will," and works out "the one purpose of him who accomplishes all things according to the counsel of his will." Nothing here is contingent on foreseen human merit — the choosing happens before anyone existed to earn it. Yet the passage also describes a real human moment of response — "when you heard... when you believed... you were marked with the seal" — placing genuine hearing and believing within the unfolding of a plan set long before.
elements.questionHint: What does it mean that God chose "before the foundation of the world," before anyone existed to do anything, and how does that relate to the later phrase "when you believed"?

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> Not only that, but when Rebekah had conceived children by one man, our ancestor Isaac— <sup>11</sup> even before they were born or had done anything good or bad (so that God’s purpose in election would stand, not by works but by his calling)— <sup>12</sup> it was said to her, “The older will serve the younger,” <sup>13</sup> just as it is written: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” <sup>14</sup> What shall we say then? Is there injustice with God? Absolutely not! <sup>15</sup> For he says to Moses: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.” <sup>16</sup> So then, it does not depend on human desire or exertion, but on God who shows mercy. <sup>17</sup> For the scripture says to Pharaoh: “For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I may demonstrate my power in you, and that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth.” <sup>18</sup> So then, God has mercy on whom he chooses to have mercy, and he hardens whom he chooses to harden. <sup>19</sup> You will say to me then, “Why does he still find fault? For who has ever resisted his will?” <sup>20</sup> But who indeed are you—a mere human being—to talk back to God? Does what is molded say to the molder, “Why have you made me like this?” <sup>21</sup> Has the potter no right to make from the same lump of clay one vessel for special use and another for ordinary use? <sup>22</sup> But what if God, willing to demonstrate his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience the objects of wrath prepared for destruction? <sup>23</sup> And what if he is willing to make known the wealth of his glory on the objects of mercy that he has prepared beforehand for glory— <sup>24</sup> even us, whom he has called, not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles?

elements.question: What does this verse teach about divine sovereignty?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul goes out of his way to remove any human basis for God's choice between Jacob and Esau — the choice was made "even before they were born or had done anything good or bad," precisely "so that God's purpose in election would stand, not by works but by his calling." He anticipates and rejects the charge of injustice ("Is there injustice with God? Absolutely not!") and roots mercy entirely in God's own will: "it does not depend on human desire or exertion, but on God who shows mercy." The potter-and-clay image pushes this further still — the molded thing has no standing to interrogate the molder — making this one of the most unqualified statements of divine sovereignty over human destiny in Scripture, deliberately answering the objection that it seems unfair.
elements.questionHint: Why does Paul specify that the choice was made "before they were born or had done anything good or bad" — what possible explanation is he deliberately ruling out?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> For you are a people holy to the Lord your God. He has chosen you to be his people, prized above all others on the face of the earth. <sup>7</sup> It is not because you were more numerous than all the other peoples that the Lord favored and chose you—for in fact you were the least numerous of all peoples. <sup>8</sup> Rather it is because of his love for you and his faithfulness to the promise he solemnly vowed to your ancestors that the Lord brought you out with great power, redeeming you from the place of slavery, from the power of Pharaoh king of Egypt.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about divine sovereignty?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Moses is emphatic that Israel's chosen status has nothing to do with anything they brought to the table — in fact, "you were the least numerous of all peoples." God's choosing is traced instead to causes entirely within himself: "his love for you and his faithfulness to the promise he solemnly vowed to your ancestors." The repeated denial, "not because you were more numerous," closes off the obvious human explanation, leaving God's own prior commitment and affection as the sole ground of election.
elements.questionHint: What reason does Moses explicitly rule out for why God chose Israel, and what does he offer instead as the real cause?

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup> Do not think to yourself after the Lord your God has driven them out before you, “Because of my own righteousness the Lord has brought me here to possess this land.” It is because of the wickedness of these nations that the Lord is driving them out ahead of you. <sup>5</sup> It is not because of your righteousness, or even your inner uprightness, that you have come here to possess their land. Instead, because of the wickedness of these nations, the Lord your God is driving them out ahead of you in order to confirm the promise he made on oath to your ancestors, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. <sup>6</sup> Understand, therefore, that it is not because of your righteousness that the Lord your God is about to give you this good land as a possession, for you are a stubborn people!

elements.question: What does this verse teach about divine sovereignty?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Moses repeats the warning three times in slightly different words — "not because of my own righteousness," "not because of your righteousness," "it is not because of your righteousness" — to make absolutely sure Israel doesn't misread the conquest as a reward for merit. The real cause lies elsewhere entirely: "the wickedness of these nations" and God's determination "to confirm the promise he made on oath." The blunt closing description of Israel as "a stubborn people" removes any lingering suspicion that they deserved this gift, underlining that the land's transfer runs on God's own purposes and prior promise.
elements.questionHint: How many times does Moses deny that Israel's own righteousness is the reason for the land, and what does that repetition suggest about how tempting the wrong conclusion would be?

elements.passageText:
32 With his hands he covers the lightning
and directs it against its target.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about divine sovereignty?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Elihu's image is startlingly intimate: God covers the lightning "with his hands" and personally "directs it against its target." Lightning, one of the most unpredictable and uncontrollable natural forces from a human vantage point, is pictured here as precisely aimed by God's own hand rather than random or self-governing. The verse asserts a kind of moment-by-moment, targeted control over even the most chaotic-seeming natural events.
elements.questionHint: What does it mean that God is pictured as directing lightning "against its target" rather than simply letting it strike at random?

elements.passageText:
24 The Lord of Heaven’s Armies makes this solemn vow:
“Be sure of this:
Just as I have intended, so it will be;
just as I have planned, it will happen. 27 Indeed, the Lord of Heaven’s Armies has a plan,
and who can possibly frustrate it?
His hand is ready to strike,
and who can possibly stop it?

elements.question: What does this verse teach about divine sovereignty?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God's vow is framed as an unbreakable equation between intention and reality: "just as I have intended, so it will be; just as I have planned, it will happen." There's no gap here between what God wills and what actually occurs. The rhetorical questions that follow — "who can possibly frustrate it?... who can possibly stop it?" — aren't really questions but assertions that no opposing power, human or otherwise, has the capacity to overturn what God has determined to do.
elements.questionHint: What is the effect of the rhetorical questions "who can possibly frustrate it?" and "who can possibly stop it?" — are they inviting an answer, or ruling one out?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> If an alarm sounds in a city, do people not fear? If disaster overtakes a city, is the Lord not responsible?

elements.question: What does this verse teach about divine sovereignty?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Amos asks two parallel rhetorical questions that both expect the answer "of course" — if an alarm sounds, people naturally fear, and likewise, if disaster hits a city, the Lord is behind it. By putting a city-wide "disaster" in the same breath as an obvious cause-and-effect like an alarm causing fear, Amos treats divine responsibility for calamity as just as self-evident, refusing to let disaster be explained as some unrelated, godless accident.
elements.questionHint: What kind of answer does the question "is the Lord not responsible?" expect — yes or no — and what does that reveal about Amos's assumption?

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup> “I have revealed your name to the men you gave me out of the world. They belonged to you, and you gave them to me, and they have obeyed your word.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about divine sovereignty?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus describes his disciples in Father-given, Father-owned terms: "the men you gave me out of the world. They belonged to you, and you gave them to me." Their coming to Jesus is traced back to an act of the Father's giving, prior to and underlying their presence with the Son. Yet the verse ends by noting a genuine human act of theirs — "they have obeyed your word" — so the disciples' own obedience is real and named, even as their belonging to Jesus in the first place is credited to the Father's prior gift.
elements.questionHint: Notice the sequence — "they belonged to you," "you gave them to me," "they have obeyed" — which action comes first, and whose is it?

elements.text: 3. Sovereignty and Responsibility together.

elements.passageText: <sup>20</sup> As for you, you meant to harm me, but God intended it for a good purpose, so he could preserve the lives of many people, as you can see this day.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about how sovereignty and responsibility fit together?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Joseph doesn't deny his brothers' guilt — "you meant to harm me" stands as a flat statement of their real, culpable intention. But he sets alongside it, without canceling it, God's own purpose in the same event: "God intended it for a good purpose, so he could preserve the lives of many people." The same historical act — selling Joseph into slavery — carries two intentions simultaneously, an evil human one and a good divine one, and Joseph holds both as true at once rather than letting one erase the other.
elements.questionHint: How can the very same act be described as something the brothers "meant" for harm and something God "intended" for good — does one explanation cancel out the other?

elements.passageText: <sup>23</sup> this man, who was handed over by the predetermined plan and foreknowledge of God, you executed by nailing him to a cross at the hands of Gentiles.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about how sovereignty and responsibility fit together?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter names two things in the very same breath: Jesus "was handed over by the predetermined plan and foreknowledge of God," and yet "you executed by nailing him to a cross" — real human hands did the killing. The sentence doesn't soften either side to relieve the tension; God's plan and foreknowledge stood behind the event, while the specific human agents who carried it out are held fully guilty for what they did. Peter clearly expects his listeners to feel the weight of "you executed him" even as he affirms it happened under God's predetermined plan.
elements.questionHint: How does Peter hold together "the predetermined plan... of God" and "you executed" in the very same sentence — does naming God's plan let the human actors off the hook?

elements.passageText: <sup>37</sup> Everyone whom the Father gives me will come to me, and the one who comes to me I will never send away. <sup>39</sup> Now this is the will of the one who sent me—that I should not lose one person of every one he has given me, but raise them all up at the last day. <sup>40</sup> For this is the will of my Father—for everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him to have eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day. <sup>44</sup> No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him, and I will raise him up at the last day. <sup>65</sup> Because of this I told you that no one can come to me unless the Father has allowed him to come.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about how sovereignty and responsibility fit together?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus repeats a pattern throughout this passage: those the Father "gives" to him will come, and "no one can come to me unless the Father... draws him" or "unless the Father has allowed him to come." Coming to Jesus is not something people simply generate out of their own initiative; it requires the Father's prior drawing or granting. Yet Jesus also describes a real human action — "the one who comes," "everyone who looks on the Son and believes" — treating the coming and believing as genuine acts even while insisting they only happen because the Father enables them.
elements.questionHint: According to verse 44, what has to happen before "no one can come" becomes possible — what does "draws him" suggest about the source of that ability?

elements.passageText: <sup>12</sup> So then, my dear friends, just as you have always obeyed, not only in my presence but even more in my absence, continue working out your salvation with awe and reverence, <sup>13</sup> for the one bringing forth in you both the desire and the effort—for the sake of his good pleasure—is God.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about how sovereignty and responsibility fit together?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's command and his explanation sit right next to each other in a way that refuses to separate them: "work out your salvation," followed immediately by the reason — God is "the one bringing forth in you both the desire and the effort." The imperative to work is real and active; Paul doesn't say let God work instead of you. But the very desire and effort a believer exercises are themselves traced to God's own operation, "for the sake of his good pleasure." This is one of the tightest pairings in Scripture of human effort commanded and divine enabling credited, in the very same two verses.
elements.questionHint: What does it mean that God is described as producing "both the desire and the effort" — the very things Paul just commanded believers to exercise?

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> For we are his workmanship, having been created in Christ Jesus for good works that God prepared beforehand so we may do them.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about how sovereignty and responsibility fit together?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul calls believers God's "workmanship," a term suggesting they are made, not self-made, "created in Christ Jesus for good works." Yet those good works aren't optional decoration — they are works "God prepared beforehand so we may do them," meaning believers are still expected to actually walk in and perform them. The preparation is God's; the doing is still something "we" do, even though the opportunity and design behind it originated entirely with God ahead of time.
elements.questionHint: What is the difference between God preparing the good works "beforehand" and believers being the ones who actually "do them" — whose action is each part?

elements.passageText: <sup>14</sup> A woman named Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from the city of Thyatira, a God-fearing woman, listened to us. The Lord opened her heart to respond to what Paul was saying.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about how sovereignty and responsibility fit together?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Luke describes Lydia in ordinary human terms first — "a dealer in purple cloth," "a God-fearing woman" already inclined toward worship — and then adds the decisive divine act: "The Lord opened her heart to respond." Her attentive "listen[ing]" is her own, but Luke credits the actual capacity to respond to what Paul said to a specific divine action on her heart, suggesting that even a receptive, God-fearing person's positive response required this opening from the Lord.
elements.questionHint: What does it mean that Luke doesn't just say Lydia listened and believed, but specifically says "The Lord opened her heart" so that she could respond?

elements.passageText: <sup>21</sup> And you were at one time strangers and enemies in your minds as expressed through your evil deeds, <sup>22</sup> but now he has reconciled you by his physical body through death to present you holy, without blemish, and blameless before him— <sup>23</sup> if indeed you remain in the faith, established and firm, without shifting from the hope of the gospel that you heard. This gospel has also been preached in all creation under heaven, and I, Paul, have become its servant.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about how sovereignty and responsibility fit together?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul describes reconciliation as something God has already accomplished — "he has reconciled you by his physical body through death" — using completed, finished language for what God did. But he immediately attaches a condition to the ultimate goal of presenting them "holy, without blemish, and blameless": "if indeed you remain in the faith, established and firm... without shifting from the hope of the gospel." The reconciling act is God's finished work, yet continuing steadfastly in that faith is placed as the believers' own ongoing responsibility, tied directly to that "if."
elements.questionHint: What does the word "if" attached to "you remain in the faith" suggest about the relationship between what God has already done and what believers must continue doing?

elements.passageText: <sup>19</sup> However, God’s solid foundation remains standing, bearing this seal: “The Lord knows those who are his,” and “Everyone who confesses the name of the Lord must turn away from evil.”

elements.question: What does this verse teach about how sovereignty and responsibility fit together?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The "seal" on God's foundation carries two inscriptions facing opposite directions: "The Lord knows those who are his" speaks to God's own sovereign knowledge of his people, while "everyone who confesses the name of the Lord must turn away from evil" places a moral demand squarely on the individual. Both are stamped on the same foundation, as if security in God's knowledge and the obligation to turn from evil are meant to be held together rather than treated as alternatives — knowing you belong to the Lord doesn't dissolve the "must" that follows.
elements.questionHint: The seal has two sides — one about God's knowledge, one about human conduct with "must turn away from evil" — why might both be needed on the same foundation?

elements.passageText: <sup>21</sup> The Lord said to Moses, “When you go back to Egypt, see that you do before Pharaoh all the wonders I have put under your control. But I will harden his heart and he will not let the people go.” <sup>12</sup> But the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not listen to them, just as the Lord had predicted to Moses. <sup>1</sup> The Lord said to Moses, “Go to Pharaoh, for I have hardened his heart and the heart of his servants, in order to display these signs of mine before him, and in order that in the hearing of your son and your grandson you may tell how I made fools of the Egyptians and about my signs that I displayed among them, so that you may know that I am the Lord.”

elements.question: What does this verse teach about how sovereignty and responsibility fit together?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God states plainly, ahead of time, "I will harden his heart," and the narrator later confirms "the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart... just as the Lord had predicted." God even explains a purpose behind it — "in order to display these signs of mine" and "so that you may know that I am the Lord." These verses place the hardening's ultimate cause and predicted certainty on God's own action and stated intention; taken alone, without yet showing Pharaoh's own earlier hardening, they emphasize God's sovereign hand behind Pharaoh's resistance and its purpose in revealing who God is.
elements.questionHint: What does it mean that God predicts the hardening in advance, "I will harden," and then the narrator confirms it happened "just as the Lord had predicted"?

elements.passageText: <sup>15</sup> But when Pharaoh saw that there was relief, he hardened his heart and did not listen to them, just as the Lord had predicted. <sup>32</sup> But Pharaoh hardened his heart this time also and did not release the people. <sup>34</sup> When Pharaoh saw that the rain and hail and thunder ceased, he sinned again: both he and his servants hardened their hearts.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about how sovereignty and responsibility fit together?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: In these verses, the very same hardening is described the other way around: "Pharaoh saw... he hardened his heart," "Pharaoh hardened his heart this time also," "he sinned again: both he and his servants hardened their hearts." Here Pharaoh is the grammatical subject doing the hardening himself, in direct response to what he sees — relief from a plague, or its ceasing. Read alongside Exodus 4:21 and 9:12, where God says "I will harden his heart," this pairing shows Scripture describing the same reality from both directions: Pharaoh's own repeated, willful resistance and God's sovereign hardening are both affirmed, without the text explaining exactly how the two relate.
elements.questionHint: Who is the subject of the verb "hardened" in these verses, compared to the earlier passage in Exodus 4:21 and 9:12 — what changes?

elements.passageText: <sup>27</sup> All things have been handed over to me by my Father. No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son decides to reveal him. <sup>28</sup> Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about how sovereignty and responsibility fit together?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus claims an exclusive, sovereign control over revelation itself: "no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son decides to reveal him." Knowing God the Father is not something people can achieve on their own initiative — it depends on the Son's own decision to reveal. Yet in the very next breath, Jesus issues a wide-open, personal invitation: "Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened." The sovereign gatekeeping of revelation and the genuine, open call to come sit side by side without Jesus treating them as contradictory.
elements.questionHint: How does the exclusivity of "anyone to whom the Son decides to reveal him" sit next to the open invitation, "Come to me, all you"?

elements.passageText: <sup>28</sup> We proclaim him by instructing and teaching all people with all wisdom so that we may present every person mature in Christ. <sup>29</sup> Toward this goal I also labor, struggling according to his power that powerfully works in me.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about how sovereignty and responsibility fit together?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul describes his own strenuous labor — "instructing and teaching all people with all wisdom," "I also labor, struggling" — using vivid, effortful language that leaves no doubt this is real personal exertion toward a real goal, "to present every person mature in Christ." But he immediately locates the source of his capacity to do this outside himself: he struggles "according to his power that powerfully works in me." Paul's labor is genuinely his own, yet he attributes its strength to God's power actively operating within him as he does it.
elements.questionHint: What is the relationship between Paul's own "struggling" and the phrase "his power that powerfully works in me" — whose effort is it, and whose power fuels it?

elements.passageText: <sup>3</sup> because we recall in the presence of our God and Father your work produced by faith and labor motivated by love and endurance inspired by hope in our Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>4</sup> We know, brothers and sisters loved by God, that he has chosen you, <sup>5</sup> in that our gospel did not come to you merely in words, but in power and in the Holy Spirit and with deep conviction (surely you recall the character we displayed when we came among you to help you). <sup>6</sup> And you became imitators of us and of the Lord when you received the message with joy that comes from the Holy Spirit, despite great affliction.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about how sovereignty and responsibility fit together?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul recalls the Thessalonians' "work produced by faith and labor motivated by love and endurance inspired by hope" — real, observable human activity springing from genuine inward conviction. In the same breath, he grounds their identity in God's prior action: "he has chosen you." Their receiving the gospel "with joy... despite great affliction" and becoming "imitators" shows an active, costly human response, even as Paul traces the whole situation back to God having already chosen them beforehand.
elements.questionHint: How does Paul move from "he has chosen you" to describing their visible "work," "labor," and "endurance" — are these treated as alternatives, or as connected?

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup> Therefore, brothers and sisters, make every effort to be sure of your calling and election. For by doing this you will never stumble into sin. <sup>11</sup> For thus an entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ, will be richly provided for you.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about how sovereignty and responsibility fit together?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter commands active effort aimed at something already granted: "make every effort to be sure of your calling and election." The calling and election are described as already theirs, yet confirming or "be[ing] sure" of them requires diligent human pursuit — "by doing this you will never stumble." The reward, "an entrance into the eternal kingdom," is explicitly tied to that same effort being "richly provided," meaning Peter treats vigorous human diligence as the means by which an already-given election is confirmed and its promised future secured.
elements.questionHint: If election is already something Peter assumes is theirs, why does he still command them to "make every effort" to be sure of it?

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup> Therefore, dear friends, since you have been forewarned, be on your guard that you do not get led astray by the error of these unprincipled men and fall from your firm grasp on the truth.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about how sovereignty and responsibility fit together?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Peter's warning assumes real spiritual danger and a real capacity to fall: believers can be "led astray" and can "fall from your firm grasp on the truth" if they are not vigilant. Being "forewarned" carries an implied responsibility to act on that warning — "be on your guard" — as if the outcome genuinely depends on whether they heed it. The passage doesn't suggest their standing is so secure that carelessness is safe; it treats watchfulness as something believers must actively maintain against "the error of these unprincipled men."
elements.questionHint: What does the command "be on your guard" assume about whether falling away is genuinely possible for someone who has already been "forewarned"?

elements.passageText: <sup>20</sup> But you, dear friends, by building yourselves up in your most holy faith, by praying in the Holy Spirit, <sup>21</sup> maintain yourselves in the love of God while anticipating the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that brings eternal life. <sup>22</sup> And have mercy on those who waver; <sup>23</sup> save others by snatching them out of the fire; have mercy on others, coupled with a fear of God, hating even the clothes stained by the flesh. <sup>24</sup> Now to the one who is able to keep you from falling, and to cause you to stand, rejoicing, without blemish before his glorious presence, <sup>25</sup> to the only God our Savior through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, power, and authority, before all time, and now, and for all eternity. Amen.

elements.question: What does this verse teach about how sovereignty and responsibility fit together?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jude piles up active commands — "building yourselves up," "praying," "maintain yourselves in the love of God," "have mercy," "snatching them out of the fire" — placing real, effortful responsibility on believers both for their own perseverance and for rescuing others. Yet the letter closes by ascribing the actual power to preserve entirely to God: "to the one who is able to keep you from falling, and to cause you to stand... rejoicing." The same passage that commands vigorous human effort ends by crediting God alone with the power that makes that standing secure.
elements.questionHint: How do the many imperatives — "build," "pray," "maintain," "snatch" — in verses 20-23 relate to the doxology's claim that God is "able to keep you from falling" in verse 24?

elements.text: 4. Some final, related thoughts.

elements.passageText: <sup>29</sup> Secret things belong to the Lord our God, but those that are revealed belong to us and our descendants forever, so that we might obey all the words of this law.

elements.question: What does this verse teach us in these final, related thoughts on sovereignty and responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Moses draws a clean line between two categories: "secret things" that "belong to the Lord" alone, and "those that are revealed" which "belong to us." The purpose clause at the end — "so that we might obey" — shows why the distinction matters: God hasn't disclosed everything, but what he has disclosed is given precisely so his people can act on it. Human responsibility is thus bounded by revelation; people are accountable for what's revealed, not for the secrets God has kept to himself.
elements.questionHint: What does the purpose clause "so that we might obey" tell you about why God gives us the "revealed" things rather than leaving everything secret?

elements.passageText:
4 “Where were you
when I laid the foundation of the earth?
Tell me, if you possess understanding.

elements.question: What does this verse teach us in these final, related thoughts on sovereignty and responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God's opening question to Job is pointedly unanswerable by any human: "Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?" The question doesn't invite information — Job wasn't there, and both speaker and listener know it. By asking Job to "tell me, if you possess understanding," God exposes the built-in limits of human knowledge next to his own, placing Job's entire complaint about God's dealings within a much smaller frame of comprehension than Job had assumed he occupied.
elements.questionHint: Since Job obviously wasn't present "when I laid the foundation of the earth," what is the real purpose behind God asking him this question?

elements.passageText:
2 “Will the one who contends with the Almighty correct him?
Let the person who accuses God give him an answer!” 8 Would you indeed annul my justice?
Would you declare me guilty so that you might be right?

elements.question: What does this verse teach us in these final, related thoughts on sovereignty and responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God confronts Job's complaint with two pointed questions that expose what was actually at stake in his arguing: "will the one who contends with the Almighty correct him?" and "would you declare me guilty so that you might be right?" The second question in particular names the real danger in Job's position — defending his own righteousness had begun to require making God the guilty party instead. God's questions press Job to see that a human, however wronged he feels, is in no position to correct or indict the Almighty in order to vindicate himself.
elements.questionHint: What does God's question "would you declare me guilty so that you might be right?" reveal about what Job's self-defense was actually costing?

elements.passageText:
3 When I look up at the heavens, which your fingers made,
and see the moon and the stars, which you set in place, 4 Of what importance is the human race, that you should notice them?
Of what importance is mankind, that you should pay attention to them?

elements.question: What does this verse teach us in these final, related thoughts on sovereignty and responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The psalmist looks at the heavens — "the moon and the stars, which you set in place" — and the sheer scale of it produces a genuine question about human significance: "Of what importance is mankind, that you should pay attention to them?" This isn't rhetorical dismissal but real wonder; set against a universe God made and arranged with his own "fingers," human beings seem impossibly small, and yet the very fact that God does "notice" and "pay attention" is what the psalmist marvels at, not denies.
elements.questionHint: Is the psalmist's question about human smallness meant to conclude that God doesn't care, or to marvel that he pays attention anyway?

elements.passageText:
13 Who comprehends the mind of the Lord,
or gives him instruction as his counselor? 14 From whom does he receive directions? Who teaches him the correct way to do things,
or imparts knowledge to him,
or instructs him in skillful design?

elements.question: What does this verse teach us in these final, related thoughts on sovereignty and responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Isaiah stacks rhetorical questions that all expect the same answer — no one: "Who comprehends the mind of the Lord?" "From whom does he receive directions?" "Who teaches him?" Each question rules out any external source for God's wisdom or plans; he needs no counselor, no instructor, no one to impart understanding to him. The effect is to place God's own counsel in a category entirely apart from and unaccountable to any created mind, human wisdom included.
elements.questionHint: What answer do these rhetorical questions expect — is there anyone at all who instructs or advises God, according to the passage?

elements.passageText:
25 “To whom can you compare me? Whom do I resemble?”
says the Holy One. 26 Look up at the sky!
Who created all these heavenly lights?
He is the one who leads out their ranks;
he calls them all by name.
Because of his absolute power and awesome strength,
not one of them is missing. 27 Why do you say, Jacob,
Why do you say, Israel,
“The Lord is not aware of what is happening to me;
my God is not concerned with my vindication”? 28 Do you not know?
Have you not heard?
The Lord is an eternal God,
the Creator of the whole earth.
He does not get tired or weary;
there is no limit to his wisdom.

elements.question: What does this verse teach us in these final, related thoughts on sovereignty and responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God challenges any comparison to himself — "To whom can you compare me?" — then points to the stars as evidence: he "calls them all by name," and "not one of them is missing" because of "his absolute power and awesome strength." The passage turns directly to address Israel's specific complaint, quoted almost verbatim — "The Lord is not aware... not concerned with my vindication" — and answers it by appealing to God's identity as "the Creator of the whole earth" who "does not get tired" and whose wisdom has "no limit." The complaint of feeling forgotten is met not with a quick fix but with the reminder of exactly who this God is.
elements.questionHint: How does the passage answer Israel's specific complaint, "the Lord is not aware of what is happening to me" — with a solution to the problem, or with a reminder of who God is?

elements.passageText:
9 One who argues with his Creator is in grave danger,
one who is like a mere shard among the other shards on the ground!
The clay should not say to the potter,
“What in the world are you doing?
Your work lacks skill!”

elements.question: What does this verse teach us in these final, related thoughts on sovereignty and responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Isaiah pictures a piece of pottery daring to interrogate its maker — "What in the world are you doing? Your work lacks skill!" — and calls this "grave danger," comparing the objector to "a mere shard among the other shards on the ground," insignificant and easily broken. The absurdity of clay critiquing the skill of the potter who shaped it is the point: creatures arguing with their Creator about how he has made or ordered things occupy an impossible position, one the text treats as genuinely perilous rather than merely unwise.
elements.questionHint: What makes it absurd, according to the image, for "the clay" to accuse the potter of lacking skill — what does the clay actually know about the potter's design?

elements.passageText:
9 Remember what I accomplished in antiquity!
Truly I am God, I have no peer;
I am God, and there is none like me, 10 who announces the end from the beginning
and reveals beforehand what has not yet occurred;
who says, ‘My plan will be realized,
I will accomplish what I desire;’

elements.question: What does this verse teach us in these final, related thoughts on sovereignty and responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God grounds his uniqueness in his track record and his foreknowledge together: "remember what I accomplished in antiquity," and "there is none like me," followed by the claim that he "announces the end from the beginning" and "reveals beforehand what has not yet occurred." His stated resolve — "My plan will be realized, I will accomplish what I desire" — isn't offered as one possibility among others but as the singular, guaranteed outcome, precisely because no other being shares this combination of comprehensive foreknowledge and unmatched power to bring it about.
elements.questionHint: What two things does God claim about himself here — his past accomplishments and his knowledge of the future — and how do they together support "there is none like me"?

elements.passageText:
12 The Lord is the one who by his power made the earth.
He is the one who by his wisdom established the world.
And by his understanding, he spread out the skies.

elements.question: What does this verse teach us in these final, related thoughts on sovereignty and responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Jeremiah credits the entire structure of creation to God's own attributes acting directly: "by his power made the earth," "by his wisdom established the world," "by his understanding, he spread out the skies." Each clause pairs a specific divine quality with a specific creative act, building a picture of a world that isn't accidental or self-organized but the deliberate product of God's power, wisdom, and understanding working together — foundational for trusting that the same God who ordered the physical world also orders human affairs within it.
elements.questionHint: Notice how each clause pairs a divine attribute — power, wisdom, understanding — with a specific act of creation. What does that pairing suggest about how intentional creation is?

elements.passageText:
35 All the inhabitants of the earth are regarded as nothing.
He does as he wishes with the army of heaven
and with those who inhabit the earth.
No one slaps his hand
and says to him, “What have you done?”

elements.question: What does this verse teach us in these final, related thoughts on sovereignty and responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: After his humbling, Nebuchadnezzar confesses a strikingly absolute view of God's rule: "all the inhabitants of the earth are regarded as nothing" next to him, and "he does as he wishes with the army of heaven and... those who inhabit the earth." The closing image — "no one slaps his hand and says to him, 'What have you done?'" — pictures total unaccountability to any created being; God's actions among nations and individuals face no higher court that can call him to answer, a lesson this once-proud king learned only through his own downfall.
elements.questionHint: What does the image of "no one slaps his hand" suggest about whether any human being, even a king, has the standing to demand an explanation from God?

elements.passageText:
11 God has made everything fit beautifully in its appropriate time,
but he has also placed ignorance in the human heart
so that people cannot discover what God has ordained,
from the beginning to the end of their lives.

elements.question: What does this verse teach us in these final, related thoughts on sovereignty and responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: The Teacher holds two things together without smoothing them out: God has made "everything fit beautifully in its appropriate time" — there is a real, good order behind events — yet he "has also placed ignorance in the human heart" so that people "cannot discover what God has ordained." The beauty of the order and human inability to perceive its full shape are both attributed directly to God's own doing; the not-knowing isn't a defect to be overcome by more effort but something built into the human condition by God himself, which is part of why this tension is never fully resolved in Ecclesiastes.
elements.questionHint: What does it mean that God himself "placed ignorance in the human heart" — is not fully understanding God's ordained plan a human failure, or something God built in?

elements.passageText: <sup>25</sup> For the foolishness of God is wiser than human wisdom, and the weakness of God is stronger than human strength.

elements.question: What does this verse teach us in these final, related thoughts on sovereignty and responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul's paradox flips ordinary categories on their head: "the foolishness of God is wiser than human wisdom, and the weakness of God is stronger than human strength." Even naming something "foolish" or "weak" about God is a rhetorical concession to human standards of judgment, only to show those standards fail entirely when set beside God — what looks like God's lesser move still outperforms humanity's greatest wisdom and strength. The verse leaves human ability, at its very best, permanently outmatched.
elements.questionHint: Why might Paul deliberately use the words "foolishness" and "weakness" to describe God, when he clearly doesn't believe God is actually foolish or weak?

elements.passageText: <sup>14</sup> You do not know about tomorrow. What is your life like? For you are a puff of smoke that appears for a short time and then vanishes. <sup>15</sup> You ought to say instead, “If the Lord is willing, then we will live and do this or that.”

elements.question: What does this verse teach us in these final, related thoughts on sovereignty and responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: James confronts confident human planning with the fragility of life itself: "you do not know about tomorrow," and existence is no sturdier than "a puff of smoke that appears for a short time and then vanishes." His remedy isn't fatalistic passivity but a specific verbal reorientation — "you ought to say instead, 'If the Lord is willing, then we will live and do this or that.'" People still plan and act, "do this or that," but James wants every plan explicitly subordinated to a will greater and more certain than their own uncertain grasp of the future.
elements.questionHint: What does James actually tell people to say instead of confidently asserting their plans — does he tell them to stop planning, or to reframe how they speak about it?

elements.passageText:
8 “Indeed, my plans are not like your plans,
and my deeds are not like your deeds,” says the Lord, 9 for just as the sky is higher than the earth,
so my deeds are superior to your deeds
and my plans superior to your plans.

elements.question: What does this verse teach us in these final, related thoughts on sovereignty and responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: God states the gap between his ways and human ways in the starkest possible terms: "my plans are not like your plans," and the difference is measured cosmically — "just as the sky is higher than the earth, so my deeds are superior to your deeds." This isn't a claim that God's plans are merely somewhat better; the sky-earth comparison signals a difference in kind, not just degree, meaning human plans cannot be used as a reliable measuring stick for evaluating or predicting what God's plans will be.
elements.questionHint: What kind of difference does the "sky is higher than the earth" comparison suggest — a difference of degree, or a difference of kind?

elements.passageText:
33 Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how unfathomable his ways! 34 For who has known the mind of the Lord,
or who has been his counselor? 35 Or who has first given to God
that God needs to repay him? 36 For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever! Amen.

elements.question: What does this verse teach us in these final, related thoughts on sovereignty and responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul breaks into worship rather than explanation at this point — "the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments." After all the argument of Romans 9-11 about election and mercy, Paul's conclusion is not a tidy formula but awe at what remains genuinely "unfathomable." His rhetorical questions — "who has known the mind of the Lord?" "who has first given to God?" — insist that no one can claim to have fully worked God out or put him in anyone's debt; the fitting response, after all the reasoning, is doxology: "from him and through him and to him are all things."
elements.questionHint: After chapters of careful argument about election, why does Paul end not with a tidy conclusion but with an outburst of praise and unanswerable questions?

elements.passageText: <sup>8</sup> But God demonstrates his own love for us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

elements.question: What does this verse teach us in these final, related thoughts on sovereignty and responsibility?
elements.answerPlaceholder: Remember to answer the question from the passage
elements.sampleAnswer: Paul locates the proof of God's love not in human worthiness but squarely in the timing: "while we were still sinners, Christ died for us." The love precedes and doesn't wait on any change in the objects of it — it's demonstrated in action, at the point of maximum human unworthiness, rather than offered as a reward for having become good first. This grounds the whole discussion of sovereignty and responsibility in one concrete historical act, showing that whatever roles divine initiative and human response play elsewhere, the starting point of it all is God's love acting toward people who had done nothing to deserve it.
elements.questionHint: What does it mean that Christ died for people "while we were still sinners" rather than after they had improved — what does that timing say about the basis of God's love?

elements.text:
Uche found that the Bible never resolves the tension by cutting off one side. It never treats sovereignty and responsibility as rivals to be balanced fifty-fifty, and it never lets either one cancel the other. Genesis 50:20 held both at once, in a single verse, about a single set of events: Joseph's brothers meant it for evil, God meant it for good. Not half-meant by each. Fully meant by both, on different levels. Acts 2:23 does the same with the cross itself: Jesus was handed over by God's set plan and foreknowledge, and put to death by the hands of lawless men. Both true. Neither cancels the other.

He realised his prayers were never in competition with God's plan – they are part of how God's plan unfolds. God ordains the means as well as the ends, and prayer is one of the ordained means. His evangelism is not pointless because God has already chosen who will respond – God's sovereign choice works through, not around, Uche opening his mouth. Paul held this exact tension together without apparent strain: work out your own salvation, for it is God who works in you.

Uche didn't get a tidy formula for how the two things fit together – the Bible doesn't quite give one. But he got something more solid than a formula: the settled conviction that God is genuinely sovereign over all things, and Uche is genuinely responsible for his choices, and that the mystery of how those two truths interlock is not a contradiction to be solved but a depth to be trusted, from a God whose thoughts are higher than his.
A Sovereignty & Responsibility Scale

elements.instruction: How do you actually hold divine sovereignty and human responsibility together in daily life? Tick the box that best fits.
statements: I pray freely and expectantly, without feeling that it contradicts God's sovereignty
I sometimes feel my choices don't really matter, since God has already decided everything
I am motivated to share my faith with others, trusting God to work through my efforts
I take full responsibility for my sin, rather than blaming it on God's plan or ordination
I find genuine comfort, not fatalism, in knowing that God is sovereign over my circumstances
I am able to hold both truths together without needing to fully resolve how they fit

elements.question: Before this study, did you lean more toward emphasising God's sovereignty or human responsibility? What pulled you that way?
